Title: Comment on the housing tax agreement
text: OPINION DANMARKS NATIONALBANK'S COMMENT ON THE HOUSING TAX AGREEMENT May 3, 2017 Governor Lars Rohde says: "The agreement reinstates from 2022 a link between housing taxes and the value of homes. At that time, this has a stabilizing effect on house prices and thus the economy." "Some elements of the agreement are pulling in the opposite direction: Chapter 5 of the agreement sets the stage for an additional process whereby housing taxation is reduced if, over time, housing taxes have increased more than anticipated. This will be done in a situation of high house prices and can thus dilute the positive stabilising effects of the agreement. Freezing future increases in housing taxes is less important in this context, but pulling in the same direction." "The permanent tax rebate to existing homeowners gives them a strong incentive to stay and will thus reduce mobility in the housing market." "In Denmark, we have a well-functioning financial market that can provide credit to homeowners who, after noticeable increases in the value of the home, have to pay more in housing tax. It is therefore not obvious to freeze the future housing tax increase, which means that the state acts as a bank for households." Page 1 of 1
text_original: UDTALELSE NATIONALBANKENS KOMMENTAR TIL BOLIGSKATTEAFTALE 3. maj 2017 Nationalbankdirektr Lars Rohde udtaler: "Med aftalen genindfres fra 2022 en sammenhng mellem boligskatterne og boligernes vrdi. Det har til den tid en stabiliserende effekt p boligpriserne og dermed samfundskonomien." "Nogle elementer i aftalen trkker i modsat retning: I aftalens kapitel 5 lgges op til en ekstra proces, hvorefter boligbeskatningen sttes ned, hvis boligskatterne over tid er steget mere end forudsat. Det vil i givet fald ske i en situation med hje boligpriser og kan dermed udvande de positive stabiliserende effekter i aftalen. Indefrysning af fremtidige stigninger i boligskatten har i den sammenhng mindre betydning, men trkker i samme retning." "Den permanente skatterabat til eksisterende boligejere giver disse en strk tilskyndelse til at blive boende og vil dermed mindske mobiliteten p boligmarkedet." "Vi har i Danmark et velfungerende finansielt marked, som kan yde kredit til boligejere, der efter mrkbare stigninger i boligens vrdi skal betale mere i boligskat. Det er derfor ikke oplagt med en indefrysning af den fremtidige boligskattestigning, der betyder, at staten agerer bank for husholdningerne." Page 1 of 1

Title: Speech by Governor Christian Kettel Thomsen at the Board Association's anniversary conference
text: SPEECH Governor Christian Kettel Thomsen's speech to the Association of Board Directors' Anniversary Conference on Monetary Policy DANMARKS NATIONALBANK 11. j 2023 THE SPOKEN WORD COUNTS Introduction Thank you for the invitation to speak here at the Board Association's 10th anniversary conference. Board work has evolved significantly over the past decade, so that today there are far more professional boards. The Board Association has made a major contribution to this - for the benefit of the individual company and for the benefit of business development in Denmark. My focus today is on inflation; how we got here and why we are in a different place than in the 70s. In addition, I will touch on monetary policy and deglobalization, which I know takes up a lot of space in your board work. *** Inflation *** In Denmark and many other countries around the world, inflation has risen sharply - and it is today our common most important macroeconomic challenge. The high inflation is essentially the result of a significant mismatch between demand and supply. The imbalances have arisen in connection with the large fluctuations during the pandemic. The repeated lockdowns challenged the global production of goods and meant long delivery times. At the same time, we have seen a sharp increase in global demand. This is due to an almost synchronous reopening of the economies globally and very accommodative fiscal and monetary policy. The combination of high demand and reduced supply has thus pushed up price development worldwide. Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and the resulting political tensions and sanctions, have pushed further. This is particularly true for energy and food prices, where very high increases last year further increased inflation. At the same time, we have seen quite tight labour markets in both the EU, the United States and Denmark. Extraordinarily high inflation has peaked*** To reduce the pressure in the economy, the central banks of most countries have tightened monetary policy sharply over the past year. They have done this to get rid of inflation. However, experience shows that it takes some time for higher interest rates to have a full impact on activity in society. Central banks can therefore have only limited influence on inflation in the short term, but they can prevent inflation from being embedded in forward wage and price expectations. Central banks therefore take a strong stance on medium-term inflation expectations. Expectations are important as a measure of confidence that central banks can and will fight inflation. And here, most data indicate that medium-term inflation expectations - among consumers, financial markets and experts - are still well anchored around an inflation rate of around 2 per cent. The extraordinarily high inflation now seems to have peaked. This is due to three main factors: Firstly, energy prices have fallen from a very high level. In fact, energy no longer contributes to inflation. Second, economic activity has been dampened by a sharp fall in real wages and higher interest rates. And thirdly, lower freight rates and lower raw material prices and better tender conditions and less pressure on prices contribute. But core inflation - i.e. inflation calculated without energy and unprocessed food - will still be high in the coming years. Among other things, due to indirect effects from energy and higher wage increases. Core inflation is interesting because it excludes the prices of the goods that typically fluctuate the most. And therefore it is a better measure of underlying price pressures in the economy. High sustained price increases may lead to a shift in inflation expectations, which could lay the seeds for a wage-price spiral. That is what we must avoid. The last time we were in a similar situation was in the 1970s*** It is natural to compare the current situation with that of the 1970s and 1980s. At that time, energy prices and geopolitical turmoil also played a key role in boosting inflation. At the same time, fiscal policy was also supportive of economic activity at that time. But there are also important differences. Substantial progress has been made in the area of monetary policy. Today, the leading central banks are independent of the political system, with a clear mandate to ensure stable prices. For example, the US and European central banks have explicit targets of inflation of around 2% over the medium term. The political decision to make central banks independent of policy decisions has given greater credibility to their commitment to achieving their inflation targets. And this is particularly important in the fight against inflation, because inflation depends, among other things, on expectations of future price increases. In Denmark, we conduct a fixed exchange rate policy, so that the Danish krone is pegged to the euro. Thus, the inflation target for the European Central Bank, ECB, will also be the focal point for inflation in Denmark. We are importing low and stable inflation in the slightly longer term, so to speak, from the ECB. We are therefore in a better place to fight inflation today than we were in the 1970s. And it is also our clear expectation that the major central banks will ensure that monetary policy brings inflation back to its targets. The ECB has also been determined in its actions and communications to bring inflation down. For example, to remove a potential barrier to interest rate policy, the ECB has established a special purchase facility. It must be possible to use this to prevent an unwanted and uncontrolled widening of the interest rate spread between, for example, southern European countries and Germany, even if the interest rate is raised. And recently, the ECB has communicated clearly that monetary policy should not deal with, for example, banking turmoil; Financial stability must be addressed with other instruments. Deglobalization*** However, there is a risk that we will look into a global economy with greater fluctuations in both growth and inflation in the coming years. After several decades of almost taking globalisation for granted, the world is now facing the risk of less globalisation. The pandemic, Russia's war in Ukraine and especially rivalry between the United States and China may lead to a greater focus on security at the expense of efficiency in global value chains. This could then trigger a shift where global companies diversify suppliers and focus on obtaining important inputs from places they feel more trusted. Such a shift could lead to higher input prices and lower efficiency. We should not be blind to the fact that there may be good security policy considerations about more self-sufficiency in critical products and infrastructure within the EU, for example. But it is important to avoid it becoming just an excuse for classic protectionism. We must therefore bear in mind the benefits we have had from globalisation, not least in terms of living standards. Globalisation has led to a stronger exchange of ideas and culture. Globalisation has also led to a sharp increase in trade and competition. This has contributed to increased growth globally. Today, companies can sell their goods globally rather than within narrower geographies. Similarly, the workforce has gone global. This has provided access to labour in countries with lower wages than in the West, which has enabled increased production at relatively lower costs. Globalization has also led to technological advances spreading more rapidly globally, as countries and companies have had to adapt to global competition. This has contributed to the development of new technologies and innovations. Overall, globalisation has thus led to increased prosperity and growth globally. But there are also negative consequences of globalisation. There is evidence that some population groups, such as the less educated in the Western world, have benefited less from the gains of globalisation. This is partly due to increased competition and pressure on wages for low-paid workers. An example of the increasing income inequality is in the United States. Here, the real average wage has risen by about 75 per cent since the beginning of the 1970s. At the same time, the real median salary can increase by about 35 percent. This is thus an example of how the benefits of globalisation are not necessarily widely distributed in society. If we look at home, Denmark - as a small, open economy - has benefited from globalisation. This is both in the form of increased demand for Danish goods and services and in the form of Danish companies' and consumers' access to cheaper goods produced abroad. Increased opportunities for foreign labour in Denmark have also meant that situations of overheating in the labour market have been avoided to a greater extent. This has helped to ensure that cyclical pressures on wages do not destroy a cyclical upturn and lead to or amplify a subsequent recession. This has supported the Danish economy and contributed to the increase in employment in Denmark by more than 400,000 over the past ten years. If someone had predicted it 10 years ago, I would probably have said that it was not possible and that the labour market would boil over. In Denmark, the Danish social model has helped to distribute the benefits of globalisation widely in society. In practice, this is done by trade unions and employers in industry - i.e. the part of the economy that is typically most export-focused - negotiating wages in light of the competitive situation, among other things. The result of the industrial negotiations then forms the basis for the negotiations in the rest of the private labour market. And the development in total private wages in turn forms the basis for wages in the public sector and for the regulation of most transfer incomes. This has supported a positive view of the opportunities of globalisation rather than its disadvantages - both among the social partners and among the population. For example, many Danish trade unions focus on productivity as a source of real wage growth. An example is at Danish Metal, where Claus Jensen has been out saying "Dear companies ... get some more robots". I think that it is a rather unique Danish view that Claus Jensen is expressing here. Where automation in some places abroad is perceived more as something that removes jobs. This is only possible because there has been a focus on broad distribution of the benefits. This translates into a relatively low income inequality in Denmark than in, for example, the United States. What does this mean for monetary policy*** If protectionist tendencies gain ground, it can reduce efficiency and increase costs. This will lead to lower productivity growth and real growth - both in Denmark and globally. This will also have implications for monetary policy. Globalisation has - as I have mentioned - contributed to a significant increase in world trade. This has meant almost constant growth in supply, which has supported monetary policy and contributed to a long period of relatively low and stable inflation. In other words, central banks have been able to focus on stabilising inflation by managing demand  without having to take into account major supply-side disturbances. If globalisation is reduced, we may face the risk of repeated global supply shocks. We have seen this not least in recent times, where the pandemic and war have demonstrated that critical supplies depend on stable global conditions. In a world with more supply side disturbances, it is even more important that fiscal policy and monetary policy push in the same direction and thus not work against each other. We believe that this is generally the case in Denmark, where a relatively restrictive fiscal policy is being pursued in the wake of the pandemic. However, in many other European countries, financial policy is still trying to compensate consumers and businesses for higher prices. This helps to keep demand under control and, in isolation, increases both the size and duration of the pressure on prices. This is not appropriate and increases the need to tighten monetary policy. In other words: When fiscal policy is accommodative, monetary policy must be tightened further to keep inflation low and stable. Let me conclude by quoting ECB President Christine Lagarde: 'Central banks will provide stability in an age that is anything but stable'. Thank you for the floor.
text_original: TALE Nationalbankdirektr Christian Kettel Thomsens tale til Bestyrelsesforeningens jubilumskonference om pengepolitik DANMARKS NATIONALBANK 11. j 2023 DET TALTE ORD GLDER Introduktion Tak for invitationen til at tale her ved Bestyrelsesforeningens 10-rs jubilumskonference. Bestyrelsesarbejdet har udviklet sig betydeligt det seneste rti, s der i dag er langt mere professionelle bestyrelser. Det har Bestyrelsesforeningen i hj grad bidraget til - til gavn for den enkelte virksomhed og til gavn for erhvervsudviklingen i Danmark. Mit fokus i dag er p inflation; hvordan vi kom hertil, og hvorfor vi str et andet sted end i 70'erne. Derudover vil jeg komme ind p pengepolitik og deglobalisering, som jeg ved fylder rigtig meget i jeres bestyrelsesarbejder. *** Inflation *** I Danmark og mange andre lande verden over er inflationen steget kraftigt - og den er i dag vores flles vigtigste makrokonomiske udfordring. Den hje inflation er i bund og grund et resultat af et betydeligt mismatch mellem eftersprgsel og udbud. Ubalancerne er opstet i forbindelse med de store udsving under pandemien. De gentagne nedlukninger udfordrede den globale produktion af varer og betd lange leveringstider. Side 1 af 7 Samtidig har vi set en kraftig stigning i den globale eftersprgsel. Det skyldes en nsten synkron genbning af konomierne globalt og meget lempelig fi- nans- og pengepolitik. Kombinationen af hj eftersprgsel og reduceret udbud har alts skubbet til prisudviklingen verden over. Ruslands invasion af Ukraine, og de afledte politiske spndinger og sanktio- ner, har skubbet yderligere p. Det glder isr for energi- og fdevarepriserne, hvor meget hje stigninger sidste r yderligere gede inflationen. Samtidig har vi set ganske stramme arbejdsmarkeder i bde EU, USA og i Danmark. ***Den ekstraordinrt hje inflation har toppet*** For at reducere presset i konomien har centralbankerne i de fleste lande strammet pengepolitikken kraftigt det seneste r. Det har de gjort for at f bugt med inflationen. Det tager dog erfaringsmssigt noget tid, fr de hjere renter slr fuldt igennem p aktiviteten i samfundet. Centralbanker kan derfor kun i begrnset omfanget pvirke inflationen p kort sigt, men de kan forhindre, at inflationen indlejres i de fremadrettede ln- og prisforventninger. Centralbanker forholder sig derfor i hj grad til forventningerne til inflatio- nen p mellemlang sigt. Forventningerne er vsentlige som ml for tilliden til, at centralbankerne kan og vil bekmpe inflationen. Og her peger de fleste data p, at de mellemfristede inflationsforventninger - blandt forbrugere, finansielle markeder og eksperter - stadig er velforan- krede omkring en inflation p ca. 2 pct. Den ekstraordinrt hje inflation ser nu ud til at have toppet. Det skyldes overordnet tre faktorer: For det frste er energipriserne faldet fra et meget hjt niveau. Faktisk bi- drager energien ikke lngere til inflationen. For det andet er den konomiske aktivitet blevet dmpet af et stort fald i realln og hjere renter. Og for det tredje, s bidrager blandt andet lavere fragtrater og lavere rva- repriser og bedre udbudsbetingelser og et mindre pres p priserne. Side 2 af 7 Men kerneinflationen - alts inflationen opgjort uden energi og uforarbej- dede fdevarer - den vil stadig vre hj de kommende r. Blandt andet p grund af indirekte effekter fra energien og hjere lnstigninger. Kerneinflation er interessant, fordi den ekskluderer priserne p de varer, der typisk svinger mest. Og derfor er den et bedre ml for det underliggende prispres i konomien. Hje vedvarende prisstigninger kan give skred i inflationsforventningerne, som kan lgge kimen til en ln-pris-spiral. Det er dt, vi skal undg. ***Sidst vi stod i en lignende situation, var i 1970'erne*** Det er nrliggende at sammenligne den aktuelle situation med den, vi havde i 1970'erne og 1980'erne. Dengang spillede energipriser og geopolitisk uro ogs en nglerolle i at stte skub i inflationen. Samtidig var finanspolitikken ogs dengang understttende for den konomiske aktivitet. Men der er ogs vigtige forskelle. Der er sket vsentlige fremskridt p det pengepolitiske omrde. I dag er de toneangivende centralbanker uafhngige af det politiske system med et klart mandat om at sikre stabile priser. For eksempel har den amerikanske og den europiske centralbank eksplicitte ml om en inflation p omkring 2 pct. p mellemlangt sigt. At man politisk har besluttet at gre centralbankerne uafhngige af politiske beslutninger, har givet strre trovrdighed omkring deres forpligtelse til at n deres inflationsml. Og det er isr vigtigt i bekmpelse af inflation, fordi inflation bl.a. afhnger af forventningerne til fremtidens prisstigninger. Herhjemme frer vi fastkurspolitik, s den danske krone er knyttet til euroen. Dermed bliver inflationsmlet for Den Europiske Centralbank, ECB, ogs omdrejningspunkt for inflation i Danmark. Vi importerer s at sige lav og sta- bil inflation p lidt lngere sigt fra ECB. Vi str derfor et bedre sted i forhold til at bekmpe inflationen i dag, end vi gjorde i 1970'erne. Og det er ogs vores klare forventning, at de store centralbanker vil sikre, at pengepolitikken bringer inflationen tilbage p deres mlstninger. Side 3 af 7 ECB har ogs i sine handlinger og kommunikation vret fast besluttet p at bringe inflationen ned. For at fjerne en potentiel barriere for rentepolitikken har ECB fx etableret et srligt opkbsinstrument. Det skal kunne bruges til at forhindre unsket og ukontrolleret udvidelse af rentespndet mellem fx sydeuropiske lande og Tyskland, selvom renten hves. Og for nylig har ECB kommunikeret klart og tydeligt om, at pengepolitikken ikke skal hndtere fx bankuro; finansiel stabilitet skal hndteres med andre instrumenter. ***Deglobalisering*** Der er dog en risiko for, at vi ser ind i en global konomi med strre ud- sving i bde vkst og inflation de kommende r. Efter flere rtier, hvor vi nsten har taget globalisering som en selvflge, str verden nu over for en risiko for mindre globalisering. Pandemien, Ruslands krig i Ukraine og isr rivalisering mellem USA og Kina kan fre til et strre fokus p sikkerhed p bekostning af effektivitet i de glo- bale vrdikder. Det kan s udlse et skift, hvor globale virksomheder diversificerer leveran- drer og fokuserer p at indhente vigtige input fra steder, de fler mere til- lid til. Et sdant skift kan fre til hjere inputpriser og lavere effektivitet. Vi skal ikke vre blinde for, at der kan vre gode sikkerhedspolitiske over- vejelser om mere selvforsyning med kritiske produkter og infrastruktur in- den for fx EU. Men det er vigtigt at undg, at det blot bliver en undskyldning for klassisk protektionisme. Derfor skal vi huske p, hvilke fordele vi har haft af globali- seringen - ikke mindst for levestandarden. Globaliseringen har frt til en strkere udveksling af ideer og kultur. Globa- liseringen har ogs frt til kraftigt get handel og konkurrence. Det har bi- draget til get vkst globalt. Virksomhederne kan i dag afstte deres varer globalt frem for inden for mere snvre geografier. Tilsvarende er arbejdsstyrken blevet global. Det har givet adgang til ar- bejdskraft i lande med lavere lnninger end i vesten, hvilket har muliggjort get produktion med relativt lavere omkostninger. Side 4 af 7 Globaliseringen har ogs frt til, at teknologiske fremskridt er bredt hurti- gere ud globalt, da lande og virksomheder har vret ndt til at tilpasse sig den globale konkurrence. Det har bidraget til udvikling af nye teknologier og innovationer. Samlet set har globaliseringen dermed frt til get velstand og vkst glo- balt. Men der er ogs negative konsekvenser af globaliseringen. Der er tegn p, at nogle befolkningsgrupper, ssom mindre uddannede i den vestlige verden, har fet mindre gavn af globaliseringens gevinster. Det skyldes blandt andet get konkurrence og pres p lnningerne for lavtln- nede arbejdere. Et eksempel p den stigende indkomstulighed er i USA. Her er den reale gennemsnitsln steget med omkring 75 pct. siden begyndelsen af 1970'erne. Samtidig er den reale medianln kan steget med omkring 35 pct. Det er dermed et eksempel p, at globaliseringens gevinster ikke ndven- digvis fordeler sig bredt i samfundet. Vender vi blikket herhjem, har Danmark - som en lille, ben konomi - nydt godt af globaliseringen. Det er bde i form af get eftersprgsel efter danske varer og tjenester og i form af danske virksomheders og forbrugeres adgang til billigere varer, der er produceret i udlandet. get mulighed for udenlandsk arbejdskraft herhjemme har ogs betydet, at situationer med overophedning p arbejdsmarkedet i hjere grad har kun- net undgs. Det har bidraget til, at et konjunkturbetinget pres p lnningerne ikke de- lgger et konjunkturopsving og frer til eller forstrker en efterflgende lavkonjunktur. Det har understttet dansk konomi og vret medvirkende til, at beskfti- gelsen herhjemme er steget med mere end 400.000 over de seneste ti r. Hvis nogen havde forudsagt det for 10 r siden, s ville jeg nok have sagt, at det ikke var muligt, og at arbejdsmarkedet ville koge over. Herhjemme har den danske samfundsmodel medvirket til at fordele globali- seringens gevinster bredt i samfundet. Side 5 af 7 I praksis sker det, ved at fagforeninger og arbejdsgivere i industrien - alts den del af konomien, der typisk er mest eksportfokuseret - forhandler om lnninger i lyset af bl.a. konkurrencesituationen. Resultatet fra industriforhandlingerne udgr s grundlaget forforhandlin- gerne p resten af det private arbejdsmarked. Og udviklingen i de samlede private lnninger udgr igen grundlaget for lnningerne i den offentlige sektor og for reguleringen af de fleste overfr- selsindkomster. Det har understttet et positivt syn p globaliseringens muligheder frem for dens ulemper - bde hos arbejdsmarkedets parter og hos befolkningen. For eksempel har mange danske fagforeninger fokus p produktivitet som kilde til reallnsfremgang. Et eksempel er hos Dansk Metal, hvor Claus Jensen har vret ude at sige "Kre virksomheder ...f nogle flere robotter". Jeg tror, at det er en ret unik dansk opfattelse, som Claus Jensen her giver udtryk for. Hvor automatisering nogle steder i udlandet mere opfattes som noget, der fjerner jobs. Det er kun muligt fordi der netop har vret fokus p bred fordeling af ge- vinsterne. Det slr sig ud i en relativ lav indkomstulighed i Denmark end i fx USA. ***Hvad betyder det for pengepolitikken*** Vinder protektionistiske tendenser frem, kan det reducere effektiviteten og ge omkostningerne. Det vil fre til lavere produktivitetsvkst og realvkst - bde i Danmark og globalt. Det vil ogs have konsekvenser for pengepolitikken. Globaliseringen har - som jeg har nvnt - bidraget med betydeligt vok- sende verdenshandel. Det har betydet nsten konstant voksende udbud, som har understttet pengepolitikken og bidraget til en lang periode med relativt lav og stabil inflation. Centralbankerne har med andre ord kunnet fokusere p at stabilisere inflati- onen ved at styre eftersprgslen - uden at skulle tage hjde for store for- styrrelser p udbudssiden. Side 6 af 7 Mindskes globaliseringen, kan vi st over for risikoen for gentagne globale udbudschok. Det har vi ikke mindst set i den seneste tid, hvor pandemi og krig har de- monstreret, at kritiske forsyninger afhnger af stabile globale forhold. I en verden med flere forstyrrelser p udbudssiden er det endnu mere vig- tigt, at finanspolitikken og pengepolitikken skubber i samme retning og alts ikke modarbejder hinanden. Det mener vi generelt er tilfldet i Danmark, hvor der fres en relativt re- striktiv finanspolitik oven p pandemien. Men i mange andre europiske lande forsger man stadig via finanspolitik- ken at kompensere forbrugere og virksomheder for de hjere priser. Det er med til at holde hnden under eftersprgslen og ger isoleret set bde strrelsen og varigheden af presset p priserne. Det er ikke hensigtsmssigt og ger behovet for at stramme pengepolitik- ken. Sagt p en anden mde: Nr finanspolitikken er lempelig, skal pengepolitik- ken strammes yderligere for at holde inflationen lav og stabil. Lad mig afslutningsvist citere ECB's formand Christine Lagarde: "Centralban- ker skal [nok] srge for stabilitet i en tidsalder, der er alt andet end stabil". Tak for ordet. Side 7 af 7

Title: Speech to the Confederation of Danish Industry's business policy summit
text: The spoken word applies. Confederation of Danish Industry's Business Policy Summit 25 September 2008 Cyclical Outlook Danmarks Nationalbank Governor Nils Bernstein After some years of high growth, the Danish economy is slowing down. Growth was close to zero in the first half of the year and the housing market is very sluggish. The slowdown has come a little faster than we initially expected. Nevertheless, the Danish economy is still working above its capacity limit and will do so all the way into 2010. The labour market is very strong, with an unemployment rate of only 1.6 per cent of the labour force. There are nearly 45,000 jobs available, judging by the number of job postings online. So there is continued buoyancy in parts of the economy. The growth slowdown in the overall economy therefore reflects an adjustment in which activity is gradually finding a sustainable bearing after some years of strong recovery. Such an adjustment is necessary and leaves no room for economic policy easing. The fire is still well under way, and there is no need to throw more firewood on. Global growth is also slowing. The expectation is that the recession will be as strong in Europe as in the United States. For the rest of the current year, growth will be very subdued. Only sometime during 2009 can we hope that it starts to turn, but the uncertainty is great. Progress in emerging economies will also decline, but from a high level, and mainly due to a slowdown in export markets and high commodity prices. The global economy is currently suffering from high inflation and financial turmoil. The increase in consumer prices is primarily due to rising energy and food prices. The rate of price appreciation is expected to slow somewhat over the autumn, partly as a result of declines in the price of oil  from a peak of nearly 150 a barrel in July. The moderation in global growth is moderating the rate of price appreciation. However, there is still a great deal of uncertainty about the path of inflation. The pass-through to core inflation, i.e. excluding food and energy, has so far been limited, and the rate of wage growth in developed countries remains subdued. At the same time, household expectations for inflation have fallen especially in the United States. 2 The euro area has also seen a decline, but inflation expectations are still above 2%. It is crucial for the world economy's ability to recover from low growth relatively quickly that a devastating price-wage spiral can be avoided. *** What began last summer with some problems in the U.S. housing market has evolved into a financial crisis of historic proportions in the United States, with offshoots to the entire global financial system. Denmark has also been affected. The key words are uncertainty and lack of confidence, which have dried up the markets for liquidity between banks. This has particularly affected financial institutions that have traditionally financed themselves directly in the capital markets, while those that have a deposit base are better off. U.S. authorities have had to intervene over the past month to prevent the collapse of a number of major players in the U.S. financial market. These are first housing finance institutions Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae, as well as the world's largest insurance company, AIG. The investment banks Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have been transformed into bank holding companies. This gives access to the Fed's credit facilities, but at the same time means more tight regulation. Merrill Lynch was taken over by Bank and America, while Lehman Brothers was allowed to go into receivership. Thus, within a week, the American investment banks disappeared from the world map. Despite these measures, the downturn continued, and the US authorities last week had to throw out a lifebuoy to the entire financial system to prevent a total meltdown. An element of the plan is the creation of a new institution in the form of a fund that will buy the poor and illiquid credits of banks. The plan will add liquidity to the market and should restore confidence in the sector. The establishment cost is provisionally set at 700 billion. This does not necessarily reflect the final losses. These depend entirely on the extent to which the assumed claims result in losses in the end. There is no doubt, however, that this bailout plan, which must first go through Congress, could be very expensive for the U.S. Treasury. The immediate market reaction to the plan was positive only since more cautious, and it is still far too early to sound the alarm. 3 One consequence of the crisis in the United States has been a drying up of the international dollar liquidity market. In line with other central banks around the world, Danmarks Nationalbank has now been given the opportunity to lend dollars to Danish banks using a so-called swap agreement with the US National Bank. In Denmark, a number of financial institutions have come into difficulties as a result of the tightening of access to liquidity in money and capital markets that has been a consequence of the global financial crisis. In order to support the stability of the financial system, Danmarks Nationalbank has expanded the banks' and mortgage banks' loan access and also had to intervene with targeted liquidity support, and with direct takeover in one case - Roskilde Bank. Recent events in the Danish banking sector are disturbing. Not so much the ability of the overall system to broker funding if we carry ourselves sensibly. However, the fact that so relatively early in the business cycle slowdown we are seeing individual banks that are so exposed to distressed property arrangements that, in combination with the fact that it has generally become more difficult to obtain funding to cover the growing deposit deficit, they get into difficulties or have to anticipate difficulties. Although these banks in their local area may be important, their direct importance to the Danish economy is not decisive. The problem, however, is that dealing with the difficulties faced by those banks may affect access to funding for well-run banks and thus indirectly endanger financial stability. How strong this correlation is, it is difficult to assess in advance. But the current situation in the money and capital markets does not encourage experimentation. The legitimate interest of the press may compound the problems for individual institutions. Danmarks Nationalbank's line is clear: we will use the instruments at our disposal to ensure that the financial system works and that well-run banks do not run into liquidity difficulties. If that means that in specific situations we have to go further than we would under normal market conditions, then we must do so. You ask yourself: How on earth did we end up in this situation? What could we have done differently? These are important questions to clarify and learn from. But let's concentrate in the first place on maneuvering safely ashore. Then we'll take the sea interrogation later and learn from it. *** 4 Even though we in Denmark have our own financial problems and are affected by the events around us, so far the Danish real economy has only to a lesser extent been affected by the global growth slowdown. The decline in the Danish growth rate is primarily determined by domestic conditions. Exports, not least industrial exports, grew nicely in the first part of the year. Going forward, the slowdown in our export markets will have an impact on exports, but the order intake in the industry remains at a decent level. The professions' view of the economy has generally become less optimistic. In August, industry confidence indicators were close to average over an extended historical period. This reflects the fact that the professions are now approaching the normal situation with more subdued expectations for the future. Looking at the industry in isolation, business confidence remains significantly more positive than during the two recessions of the early 1980s and 1990s, respectively. Employment growth has continued throughout the past part of 2008. Since the end of 2003, unemployment has fallen by an average of 2,000 people per month, and this trend has continued over the summer. However, the shortage of labor is no longer as pronounced as in the past. Within the industry, the number of companies reporting labour shortages is back to a more normal level. In construction, there are still quite a few companies reporting labour shortages. Also in large parts of the public sector, as well as in many service professions, there is a shortage of available hands. The large number of vacancies means that there is hardly any prospect of any sudden and violent increase in unemployment. However, we expect the bottom to be reached this autumn and that the unemployment rate will increase by about 50,000 people by 2010. That will increase the unemployment rate from 1.6 to 3.3. It will help to take the pressure off the labor market. I shouldn't blame anyone if they smile: it's been said before that unemployment has now bottomed out. And yet it has continued to decline. Taking into account that some of those who change jobs also appear in the unemployment statistics, there may not be many long-term unemployed left. Despite decent wage growth, household disposable incomes will rise only slightly this year as a result of high inflation and rising interest rates. Along with declines in house prices and stock prices, this has led to a slowdown in consumption growth. This is evident in retail sales, which have fallen in recent months after moving sideways at a high level for a period of time. Consumer confidence, too, has fallen significantly, but mostly as 5 following concern about the country's economy. Own finances are still highly trusted. Danish consumers act sensibly. With the prospect of some slowdown and much talk of worse times, it's not surprising that consumers are holding back a bit, even though they still have a solid economy. Looking ahead, we expect a further slowdown in private consumption, but several factors are holding hand during private consumption  including the strong labour market and the solid wealth position of households. The wealth position may have deteriorated slightly lately due to declines in the price of owner-occupied homes and shares, but from a longer-term perspective, the deterioration is modest. Household wealth is still significantly above 2003 levels, when the cyclical recovery took off. Free values have recently fallen not only as a result of falling cash prices, but also as a result of continued decent growth in the new loan. Also, growth in unsecured loans in the home remains high. This suggests that not all households have yet adapted to a situation of lower growth. A delayed adoption of the budget and the spring strike in large parts of the public sphere means that we are currently on very uncertain ground when the growth in public consumption is to be made up. The preliminary figures for government consumption growth in the first half of the year look surprisingly low. In the upcoming budget negotiations, the Danish Parliament should follow the same cautious behaviour as consumers. Looking ahead, one of the uncertainties in the cyclical assessment is the development in the housing market. Price declines in the capital region have spread to other parts of the country this spring. In addition to the development of interest rates, the market is currently largely driven by psychology. Expectations of further price declines are holding buyers back. Buyers who already own a house do not dare to buy until the old one is sold. It provides a self-reinforcing effect, with the supply of homes for sale piling up. The situation may worsen when unemployment starts to rise. It is uncertain how large and elongated a price correction we will see. It is not unlikely that the period of falling prices, both nominally and real, will extend over the next few years. However, nothing suggests dramatic price declines nationwide. There is probably a risk that the fall in prices will be stronger than there is a real economic basis for. It is far from clear that, in a slightly longer perspective, cash prices are generally overvalued. In terms of price, the housing market is divided into two, each with its own price level. In the Capital Region of Denmark, with approximately 25 per cent of owner-occupied housing. 6 late, is a typical m2 price for a detached house of DKK 22,000. In the rest of the country, one m2 can be obtained for half. These prices are inclusive of the price of the plot. If the cost of new construction in relation to the price of existing homes is used as a benchmark for cash prices in the long term, there does not seem to be any serious overestimation, if any, in the majority of the country. The market price of a typical residential building is today in the range of DKK 10-15,000 per m2, and then the cost of the plot comes on top of that. The argument assumes that there are vacant building plots available to a significant extent. In the metropolitan area, which to a greater extent than the rest of the country is expanded, new construction prices do not provide a guideline for the price level to the same extent. However, the spread between cash prices in the metropolitan area and the rest of the country had become too large. Historically, housing investment has followed real cash prices closely, and is therefore expected to slow down somewhat in the coming years. Despite the slowdown, this does not change the fact that the level of housing investment will remain at a high level from a longer-term perspective. The same applies to business investment, where the investment ratio will fall from a high to a more normal level. The pressures on the labour market are not surprisingly reflected in strong wage developments. According to the Danish Employers' Association, the employees' hourly earnings in the industry in the second quarter were 4.7 per cent higher than in the same period last year. This can be compared to a rate of wage increase for our competitors of 3.2 per cent. On top of that, the effective krone exchange rate has risen by just over 3 per cent. This development has been going on for some time, and it puts considerable pressure on the international competitiveness of Danish companies. Government employees' salaries increased in the second quarter by more than 5% compared to the previous year. In a situation where the rate of wage growth compared to our competitors is already high, it is important that wage pressures in the public sector not exposed to competition do not rub off on private wages. But that's easier said than done. Inflationary pressures are also seen in consumer prices. Despite high consumer price inflation, underlying inflation has also remained moderate at home. There seems to be a tendency for firms to initially let price increases on inputs in production squeeze profit margins rather than fully passing on commodity price increases in sales prices. This keeps inflation down in the first place, but is obviously not sustainable in the long run. This means that stronger underlying inflationary pressures can be expected later, in line with the recovery of profit margins. It is confirmed by the latest figures. 7 The Danish economy is currently working on its capacity limit with labour shortages. We expect GDP growth of around 1% both this year and next year, with a decline to 0.5% in 2010. That's significantly lower than we've been used to in recent years, but reflects, as I said, a necessary slowdown to ease capacity pressures. It is illusory to think that, through an expansionary fiscal policy, it should be possible to avoid some increase in unemployment. It is only a question of whether we accept a slight increase in the coming years through responsible economic policy, or whether we should have a potentially even greater increase in unemployment in the long term through continued growth in wage growth and loss of competitiveness. ***
