Title: Declining borrowing need in Europe
text: Declining borrowing need in Europe Speech by Jens Thomsen, Member of the Board of Governors of Danmarks Nationalbank European Government Bond Summit, Brussels, Belgium, 25 October 2007 Introduction [Slide 1] I am delighted to be here today to offer some remarks on an issue that is of great interest to me and of relevance to the participants of the European Government Bond Summit. I am chairman of the "The Thomsen group", officially known as Economic and Financial Committee, sub-committee on EU Government Bonds and Bills Market. The mandate of the group is to further promote the integration and a better functioning of EU government bond markets. In the following, I would like to address my speech to a topical issue that has been surrounding the EU government debt markets. In the past decade public finances in Europe have improved and central-government debt decreased, partly due to increased budget discipline in order to enter the euro but recently also aided by accelerated economic growth, privatisations of government-owned entities and lower interest cost. [Slide 2] In most EU-15 countries the government debt has decreased during the past decade. Ireland, Belgium and Denmark have experienced decreases of around 40 percentage points of GDP. In recent years the tendency of falling debt has spread to other countries such as Germany. The Federal Government of Germany announced in June 2007, that they will start to reduce issuance due to a favourable development in tax receipts. A forecast for the year 2008 shows that government debt will decline in almost all EU countries. [Slide 3] In the new EU countries the debt is generally low and stable except for Bulgaria that has reduced its debt considerably. In EU the Maastricht Treaty has had a disciplinary effect on government debt, but also outside EU debt reduction has been a general objective. [Slide 4] Notwithstanding the tendency of decreasing debt, the euro area issued government bonds close to euro 1500 billion in 2006 of which almost half was AAA rated. In fact, there has been an increase in euro area issuance in recent years although redemptions and change in duration profile may also have contributed to an increase in the issuance volume. 2 Decreasing debt has implications for government debt management and government bond markets. It is these implications I am going to touch upon today, first from a government debt management point of view and then from a bond market point of view. In my view government surpluses should be welcomed. In the following, when I speak about the challenges from surpluses and falling debt, please keep that in mind. Under no circumstances do I think that the re-emergence of deficits or of increasing debt is the right solution to these challenges. Challenges for debt managers of a low borrowing requirement [Slide 5] As central-government debt decreases the government borrowing requirement is reduced or even disappears. It is possible to stop borrowing and no longer issue government bonds. The overall objectives of the government debt policy should be taken into consideration when deciding if the government should stop or continue issuing bonds. In particular, the decision should take into account the primary objective of government debt management, namely to finance debt at the lowest longterm cost while taking risks into account and ensuring access to the financial markets, both in short and long term. Consider what would happen if the need to borrow returns and the government bond market has closed down from lack of issuance. Then a new market and a new issuance program must be established. This could be costly as a premium most likely must be paid for a period of time. Furthermore, the secondary government debt policy objective of supporting a well-functioning domestic financial market should be taken into consideration. The question here is whether there are substitutes that may take over the functions of domestic government bonds. [Slide 6] If government surpluses continue, the government has two choices: Continue or discontinue issuance. Each choice presents its own challenges and consequences. If the government believes that the low borrowing requirement is to be short lived and re-entry in the government bond market is costly, it is sensible to continue issuance and maintain a government securities market to ensure later access to funding. Closing down an issuance program only to re-open within a short period of time may well be excessively costly. The same conclusion would be reached if the government believes that a domestic bond market is crucial to maintain well-functioning financial markets. 3 If the continuation of issuance is decided upon, the issuance strategy needs to be focused on maintaining the liquidity needed to support the market. One way to achieve a sufficient minimum outstanding amount in each government security is to consolidate issuance in fewer securities, narrowing the number of lines and closing less important issuance programmes. Furthermore, more active use of buybacks and switches could further concentrate "scarce" liquidity, if market conditions permit. In countries where public borrowing is segmented on several entities, centralisation of public borrowing at the central government level may also enhance liquidity. It is possible to discontinue issuance if no borrowing requirement is expected for the foreseeable future and domestic government bonds play no unique role in the financial markets. In that case the debt will gradually expire. Temporary borrowing requirement could be handled by other means, e.g. syndications. Of course, a return of a permanent borrowing requirement would imply costly re-establishment of a domestic bond market. [Slide 7] Some countries outside the EU with a prolonged period of government surplus, e.g. Australia, New Zealand and Norway, have continued to issue government bonds to maintain a given level of outstanding gross debt. The issuance in these countries is continued to maintain a level of gross debt of 10 to 20 per cent of GDP. In 2002, the Australian Office of Financial management (AOFM) prepared a review in the light of the decrease of the central government debt from approximately 20 per cent of GDP in 1995 to approximately 5 per cent of GDP. The outcome of the review1 concluded that it was necessary to maintain a liquid government bond market in order to support the Australian government bond futures market. Otherwise the financing costs for Australia's private sector would probably be higher. Market implications of the falling government debt [Slide 8] In stable times on the financial markets it is easy to forget the differences between government bonds and other financial instruments. However, the past months' flight to quality has served as a reminder that government securities are not quite the same as other securities. A falling supply of government bonds could affect financial markets, in particular as government bonds hold specific roles and are not easily replaced by substitutes in the domestic market. 1 Australian Government Budget 2003-04, Budget Paper No.1, Statement 7 4 In the euro area and in the EU countries with a currency pegged to the euro, the other countries' euro denominated government bonds are near substitutes to domestic government bonds. The following arguments relate to government security markets in countries with own currency. The typical roles mentioned with regard to domestic government bonds are: price reference for financial products, allowing pricing of other instru- ments and of specific risks, as well as supporting a market for hedging a long term investment vehicle, as a reflection of the government's will- ingness to pay a fixed interest rate a safe haven in times of financial instability. These roles rely on sufficient liquidity in the government bond markets. [Slide 9] The leeway in containing a temporary shortfall in the borrowing requirement and still maintaining liquidity differs between small and large countries. In the larger countries the absolute size means that there is more scope for adjustments while maintaining sufficient liquidity. [Slide 10] Government debt managers can actively support liquidity and strengthen market efficiency for trading government securities. One possibility is to expand the range of available buy-back instruments, for instance alternating between on-tap, auctions and switches. Another possibility is to widen the scope for securities lending facilities, including looking at terms and costs. [Slide 11] If government bonds become illiquid or disappear entirely, it does not mean that these roles will not be fulfilled. Surely financial markets will create private alternatives to government securities or existing alternatives will step in. In that respect, the feature most difficult to replicate is probably the credit-worthiness. There is a lack of evidence of developed financial markets operating in absence of a government debt market. The crux of the matter is how well the alternative instruments, e.g. interest rate swaps, asset backed securities, foreign government securities and corporate bonds will handle these roles compared to government bonds. Some countries operating as financial centres e.g. Singapore and Hong Kong have initiated a government securities 5 programme, even though they do not need issuance to finance government expenditures. In my view it is not possible to make a general statement on whether issuance should be continued or discontinued. It depends on the domestic financial market characteristics such as size and level of development, but also on proximity to other financial markets. In the euro area and in the EU countries with a currency pegged to euro, the adjustment to a market without a national government debt market will probably be less complicated, if other countries' issuance support a liquid euro bond and swap market. Outside the euro area the disappearance of government bonds could pose a greater challenge. In that case the solution could be a continuation of issuance to maintain a domestic government bond market. An example, albeit geographically far away, is Australia, where the continuation of a futures market, based on government bonds, was deemed so important that issuance was continued without a borrowing requirement. The Future [Slide 12] If there is one thing we can learn from the past, it is that the future is hard to predict. As I mentioned earlier, there are expectations of government budget surpluses in Europe in the next couple of years. In the medium term, one should remember that the favourable business cycle has been a positive contributor in many countries. [Slide 13] In the longer run, however, demographic issues clearly point in the direction of a deterioration of public finances. The old age dependency ratio  that is the retired (65 years) as a percentage of the working aged (20-64 years)  is estimated to increase from 29 per cent in year 2007 to 58 per cent in year 2050. A significant increase is expected already from year 2020. This means that unless the retirement age is increased, there will be a pressure on public finances and very likely a higher borrowing requirement. With this trend in mind, it seems to me too early to call off government debt in Europe.

Title: Speech at DLR Kredit's Annual General Meeting, 25 April 2007
text: Basis of speech. The spoken word applies. Nils Bernstein DLR Kredit's Annual General Meeting, 25 April 2007  The Danish economy in an international perspective Thank you for the invitation to speak today. Today I want to talk about the Danish economy in an international perspective. I will start with some observations on globalization. Then I will turn to the internationalization of financial markets. Finally, I will turn my attention to some of the financial products that have come to us from outside and are currently offered to private Danish investors. The Danish economy has traditionally had an international aim characterized by great trade with the outside world. It has been more than 100 years since agriculture was hit by globalization. We owe much of our prosperity to the international division of labour. Developments in these years have only made the international perspective even more relevant. The world is characterized by ever greater international exchange of goods and services, investments, information, people, food habits, culture, etc. The societal changes have been extensive, and this helps to explain why globalization is one of the great topics of debate of the time. *** Globalization has evolved in waves of shorter or longer duration over the past few centuries. The golden periods, in particular, seem to have been marked by great technological advances in transport and communications. They have also been characterised by an international political environment which has been conducive to free trade and to the free mobility of capital and people. In these years, it is as if globalization has been given an extra breath. Populous nations such as China and India have become part of the global market economy. Technological advances in, for example, the IT field have fundamentally changed the way companies organise production. The free movement of capital has hardly been better than it is right now. As a consequence of these changes, the gains of international division of labour have been increased. Low-tech production has moved to those countries that have their comparative advantage in labor-intensive production. Production in more developed countries has been further concentrated on- 2 kring high-tech products. At the same time, the outsourcing of services, rather than just the production of goods, has been increasing rapidly. Today, cross-border trade in services accounts for 20 per cent of world trade. An indicator of the increasing economic integration between the countries of the world is the fact that world trade is growing faster than world production as measured by GDP (slide 2). This has been the case continuously since the end of World War II. Compared to other developed countries, the Danish economy has gained "double" on globalization. On the one hand, an export-oriented economy such as the Danish one has benefited from the general increase in international trade. But in addition, Denmark has experienced an improved exchange ratio. Many Danish companies have managed to sell their products at ever-increasing prices, while import prices have stagnated. The Danish exchange ratio has been increasing over the past 15 years, also when energy is disregarded (slide 3). For the EU as a whole, on the other hand, the exchange ratio has remained unchanged since 1990. Exchange conditions in Sweden and Finland have deteriorated over the period, while the economic development of the two countries has been characterised by high growth. A contributing factor is a strong productivity improvement in some of the products where these countries have a comparative advantage, including in telecommunications. When Denmark has experienced an improvement in the exchange ratio, it can be attributed to the fact that the business structure has been continuously adjusted. Precisely because Danish society shows great willingness to change, Danish has succeeded 3 economy to remain competitive. The willingness to change will also be an important element for the Danish economy in the future, when we may be challenged even more than today on the production of high-tech and other "knowledge-intensive" products. The flexibility of the Danish economy is due to several factors. It has been important not to seek to keep artificially alive industries and individual companies in decline through political means. At the same time, as a result of a flexible labour market and continuing education efforts, we have been able to move labour resources around. In Denmark, the average length of employment per job is approximately 4.8 years, which is low in a European context (slide 4). With a workforce of around 2.9 million people, this corresponds to approximately 600,000 job changes in Denmark per year. A special aspect of globalisation has been cross-border financial integration. It is not only international trade in goods and services that has risen sharply. Developments in international capital movements have been exponential. For example, the volume of trades in US securities between the US and the rest of the world has grown by a factor of 200 between 1980 and 2006. Over the same period, U.S. foreign trade has grown by a factor of 11 and U.S. nominal GDP by a factor of 5 (slide 5). It has been crucial to the increase, as we have seen, that capital movements around the world have become increasingly liberalised. There has been talk of 4 a gradual process, which especially gained momentum in the 1980s. Within the framework of the EU, much has been done to promote the free movement of capital. The removal of exchange rate uncertainty related to the introduction of the euro has further contributed to increasing financial integration within euro area countries. In recent years, new common framework conditions have also been developed for European securities markets. The globalisation of financial markets opens up for a more efficient use of capital with potentially large gains for the world economy. For investors, a more integrated financial market implies greater investment opportunities. Capital will have the opportunity to move into new markets with higher returns, and a larger financial market will allow for a better opportunity to spread its risk. In addition, borrowers are given the opportunity to raise capital from a deeper and wider circle of investors. The overall effect is a more efficient use of capital. Capital is used where the effect is greatest. With financial integration, however, new risks have emerged at the same time. Major financial imbalances across countries can be financed as long as financial markets have confidence in developments. But the day the trust disappears, it can go very fast. Continuously from 2002 until today, the United States has been able to finance a current account deficit of around 4-7% of GDP (slide 6). During this period, U.S. consumer and investment demand has persistently been significantly greater than its income. This has been made possible by large foreign capital injections. But what if these capital injections cease suddenly? That will lead to sharply rising U.S. interest rates and a markedly weaker dollar. In such a scenario, there is a risk that the adjustment will be very costly for large parts of the world economy. There will be an abrupt adjustment in the prices of a number of financial assets, and this will drag on real economic adjustments. Fortunately, most are of the opinion that the risk of an abrupt adaptation is decreasing, but still present. Denmark has also taken part in global financial integration. Danish companies regularly buy up foreign companies, and foreign companies buy Danish companies. The sale of TDC to an international 5 private equity last year was, even in an international context, one of the largest transactions of this kind ever. The development in the Danish securities markets testifies to increasing financial integration  especially with the euro area countries. Statistical analyses show that interest rate changes on 10-year Danish government bonds closely follow corresponding German interest rate changes (slide 7). Danish, German, English and Japanese interest rate changes also correlate relatively closely with interest rate changes in the world's most important bond market  the U.S. Treasury bond market (slide 8). In recent years, convergence has increased noticeably. Investors seem to be increasingly viewing the major bond markets worldwide as one market. Compared to bonds, stocks are of a more heterogeneous structure, and the integration of stock markets across countries is less advanced. However, it is clear that stock indices in the US, the euro area and at home are influenced by common factors (slide 9). 6 Denmark's integration into global financial markets is indisputable. And this is a development that brings us much benefit. But it is also obvious that we cannot shield ourselves from external events to the same extent as in the past. I mentioned earlier the risk of suddenly complicating the financing of the U.S. balance of payments deficit. Such an abrupt adjustment would necessarily also have some repercussions in Denmark, e.g. via a decrease in exports. Another example of a global financial phenomenon that is considered by some to pose a threat to global financial stability is the so-called yen "carry" trade. The yen-carry trade is an investment strategy in which an investor borrows money at low interest rates in Japanese yen and subsequently places the money at a higher interest rate in, for example, American securities. Although the scope of the yen-carry trading strategy is impossible to quantify with any great precision, the strategy undoubtedly attracts many investors. This is due to a significant interest rate spread, of around 3 percentage points, between yen and dollar claims (slide 10). Practitioners of the yen-carry strategy are a motley bunch. They range from Japanese housewives who invest in mutual funds, which place themselves in New Zealand and Australian dollar bonds, to hedge funds, to farmers in Eastern Europe who finance themselves in the yen. Whether the yen-carry strategy poses a global risk depends largely on the popularity of the strategy. If there are sudden changes in the strategy's assumptions, which means that investors at the same time flock towards the exit, it will  if the sums are otherwise large enough  lead to strong movements in exchange rates and interest rates. Movements that will propagate further in the global financial system and ultimately also require adjustments in the real economy. The yen deal, according to economic theory, should not pay off over long periods of time. Adjustments in economies mean that interest rate differentials over time are offset by exchange rate changes  in this case by a yen strengthening. However, the fact is that for long periods of time the strategy has paid off. Exchange rates that are not rooted in fixed exchange rate regimes are notoriously difficult to 7 foretell. This also applies to the yen, which for long periods of time has been continuously weakened against the dollar  perhaps precisely as a result of the fact that more and more investors have been attracted to the yen-carry trade, meaning an ongoing sale of the yen. However, there is much to suggest that one should be cautious about this kind of speculation, even if the strategy has been advantageous for long periods. The Yencarry strategy is risky. The problem arises if the yen is strongly and abruptly strengthened. Investors will then incur heavy losses. Many investors' attempts to get out of the same type of position will only reinforce the yen's appreciation. It will create further losses. That's exactly what happened in 1998. The yield spread between yen and dollar claims also attracted many investors to the yen-carry trade back then. Then in just 3 days the yen strengthened by 13 per cent. This, among other things, inflicted heavy losses on a number of hedge funds (slide 11). Compared to the normal price fluctuations of the yen, the strengthening during this period was an almost impossible event according to the probability distributions that are usually used. But that's how it can go, and that's how it goes sometimes. This is the background to the strategy's comparison with the collection of small coins in front of a steamroller (slide 12). Economists have a concept called "fat tails." It is the term for the statistical phenomenon that extreme events occur more frequently than the most commonly used probability distribution would suggest. Fat tails can hurt investors when they hit. *** 8 Financial integration has not only brought global systemic change and new opportunities for professional investors. The development has also given rise to rapid financial innovation with completely new opportunities for private investors. I think that some in this Chamber are familiar with the principles behind the carry investment strata that I just mentioned. We also have our own little version of that strategy. In our case, the strategy is carried out by private borrowers, often farmers it is said, who, rather than taking out loans in Danish kroner, choose to do so in Swiss francs. A lower level of interest rates on Swiss claims than on Danish ones means that this will be advantageous  at least as long as the Swiss franc is not strengthened too much rather than the crown (slide 13). Banks' lending to households in Swiss francs has steadily increased since 2001 and is currently estimated at almost 20 mia.kr. (slide 14). However, during 2006, the increase in Swiss franc lending flattened and net lending turned negative late in the year (slide 15). At the same time, the Swiss franc had weakened to its lowest level in 8-9 years across the Danish kroner. The decline in net lending may be due to expectations of a reversal of the Swiss franc's weakening. This is confirmed by statistical analyses on data for a number of years. The analyses find a significant correlation between a weakening Swiss franc and declining net lending. 9 It is interesting that the Danish carry speculators have a different reaction pattern than the yen carry speculators. The yen carry speculators run out of their position when the yen is strengthened. They are apparently afraid that the strengthening heralds a forthcoming major adjustment in the exchange rate. Our domestic Swiss franc speculators increase their positions when the Swiss franc is strengthened. They apparently believe that the strengthening is temporary. Of course, the Danish Swiss franc carry loan strategy does not pose a threat to the global financial system. In addition, it is far too small and insignificant. Instead, the risk relates to the financial situation of the individual borrowers if the Swiss franc is strengthened rather than kroner. It will also hurt if the fat tails are turned away. Another new type of financial products that we have been presented with at home in recent years is the so-called indexed bonds. Bank sales of this type of bond have grown sharply since its inception in 1998. At the beginning of April this year, the outstanding volume listed on the Copenhagen Stock Exchange was 52 mia.kr. (slide 16). In Danmarks Nationalbank's next quarterly review, we will present an analysis of this product. Let me mention some of the results now. The product consists partly of a relatively safe bond investment and partly of an option investment. The option investment is linked to developments in, for example, stocks, exchange rates or commodities. The product has expanded the investment universe for private investors. We can now all speculate whether it is the copper price or the Australian dollar that is on the rise. 10 The indexed bonds are distinguished by the fact that any loss is often limited to a relatively small share of the amount invested. However, this is not sufficient to make it a sensible investment. The indexed bonds are illiquid and often have a complicated structure that can be difficult to figure out for most people. What is available in return for this complexity? A high return? Not necessarily. At Danmarks Nationalbank, we have reviewed 67 indexed bonds with a nominal value of approximately 18 mia.kr. The bonds have all been listed on the Copenhagen Stock Exchange, but have now been redeemed. The average annual yield on these bonds has been around 2.5% weighted in relation to the maturity and nominal outstanding amount of the bonds. Almost half of the bonds were associated with a negative or no return, while about 15% of the bonds had an annual return of 10% or more (slide 17). The 67 indexed bonds have had an average annual excess return compared to Danish government bonds of similar duration of around 0.1 percentage points. When investing in a Danish government bond, a liquid, risk-free and quite uncomplicated bond is purchased, the nominal return of which is also known at the time of purchase. In comparison, the indexed bonds have slightly more credit risk, much less liquidity and a much more fluctuating return. In relation to the risks assumed, a historical average annual excess return of 0.1 percentage points must be characterised as small. Borrowing Swiss francs and investing in indexed bonds, like most other investment decisions, are associated with financial risks. I can only call for investment decisions to be made with careful consideration of the risks contained. Globalisation is a positive development, and it has been especially true for Denmark, because we have been able to adapt quickly. Financial markets are an area where the consequences of globalisation are most evident. Financial markets today react as closely interconnected vessels. It is wise to remember that it can also have unpleasant consequences when you as a private investor or borrower move into these markets.
text_original: Grundlag for talen. Det talte ord glder. Nils Bernstein DLR Kredits generalforsamling, 25. april 2007  Dansk konomi i et internationalt perspektiv Tak for invitationen til at tale i dag. Jeg vil i dag tale om dansk konomi i et internationalt perspektiv. Jeg vil starte med nogle betragtninger om globaliseringen. Derefter vil jeg vende mig mod internationaliseringen af de finansielle markeder. Til sidst vil jeg vende blikket mod nogle af de finansielle produkter, som er kommet til os udefra og i dag udbydes til private danske investorer. Dansk konomi har traditionelt haft et internationalt sigte prget af stor samhandel med omverdenen. Det er mere end 100 r siden, at landbruget blev ramt af globaliseringen. Den internationale arbejdsdeling skylder vi meget af vores velstand. Udviklingen i disse r har kun gjort det internationale perspektiv endnu mere relevant. Verden prges af stadig strre international udveksling af varer og tjenester, investeringer, information, mennesker, madvaner, kultur mv. De samfundsmssige forandringer har vret omfattende, og det er med til at forklare, hvorfor globalisering er et af tidens store debatemner. *** Globaliseringen har udviklet sig i blger af kortere eller lngere varighed gennem de sidste par rhundreder. De gyldne perioder synes isr at have vret prget af store teknologiske fremskridt inden for transport og kommunikation. De har ogs vret kendetegnet ved et internationalt politisk milj, som har virket befordrende for frihandel og for fri mobilitet for kapital og mennesker. I disse r er det som om, globaliseringen har fet et ekstra pust. Folkerige nationer som Kina og Indien er blevet en del af den globale markedskonomi. Teknologiske fremskridt p fx it-omrdet har ndret grundlggende ved den mde, virksomheder indretter produktionen p. Kapitalens frie bevgelighed har nppe heller haft bedre kr end netop nu. Som en konsekvens af disse forandringer er gevinsterne ved international arbejdsdeling blevet forget. Lavteknologisk produktion er flyttet til de lande, som har deres komparative fordel i arbejdskraftintensiv produktion. Produktionen i mere udviklede lande er blevet yderligere koncentreret om- 2 kring hjteknologiske produkter. Samtidig har outsourcing af tjenesteydelser, frem for blot vareproduktion, vret strkt tiltagende. I dag udgr grnseoverskridende handel med tjenesteydelser 20 pct. af verdenshandlen. En indikator for den stigende konomiske integration mellem verdens lande er det faktum, at verdenshandlen vokser hurtigere end verdens produktion mlt ved BNP (slide 2). Det har vret tilfldet uafbrudt siden afslutningen p 2. verdenskrig. Sammenlignet med andre industrilande har dansk konomi vundet "dobbelt" p globaliseringen. Dels har en eksportorienteret konomi som den danske haft gavn af den generelle stigning i den internationale samhandel. Men derudover har Danmark oplevet et forbedret bytteforhold. Mange danske virksomheder har formet at afstte deres produkter til stadigt stigende priser, mens importpriserne er stagneret. Det danske bytteforhold har vret stigende de sidste 15 r, ogs nr der ses bort fra energi (slide 3). For EU under t har bytteforholdet derimod vret undret siden 1990. Bytteforholdene i Sverige og Finland er forvrret over perioden, mens de to landes konomiske udvikling har vret kendetegnet ved hj vkst. En medvirkende rsag er en strk produktivitetsforbedring i nogle af de produkter, hvor disse lande har en komparativ fordel, bl.a. inden for telekommunikation. Nr Danmark har oplevet en forbedring af bytteforholdet kan det bl.a. henfres til, at erhvervsstrukturen lbende er blevet tilpasset. Netop fordi det danske samfund udviser stor forandringsvillighed, er det lykkedes dansk 3 konomi at forblive konkurrencedygtig. Forandringsvilligheden vil ogs vre et vigtigt element for dansk konomi i fremtiden, nr vi muligvis i endnu hjere grad end i dag udfordres p produktionen af hjteknologiske og andre "videnstunge" produkter. Fleksibiliteten i dansk konomi skyldes flere faktorer. Det har vret vigtigt, at man ikke ad politisk vej har sgt at holde kunstigt liv i brancher og enkeltvirksomheder i tilbagegang. Samtidig har vi som flge af et fleksibelt arbejdsmarked samt efteruddannelsesindsats vret i stand til at flytte rundt p arbejdskraftressourcerne. I Danmark er den gennemsnitlige ansttelsestid pr. job ca. 4,8 r, hvilket er lavt i en europisk sammenhng (slide 4). Med en arbejdsstyrke p omkring 2,9 mio. personer svarer det til, at der er ca. 600.000 jobskift i Danmark om ret. *** En srlig side af globaliseringen har vret finansiel integration over landegrnserne. Det er ikke kun international vare- og tjenestehandel, som er steget kraftigt. Udviklingen i internationale kapitalbevgelser har vret eksponentiel. Eksempelvis er omfanget af handler i amerikanske vrdipapirer mellem USA og resten af verden vokset med en faktor 200 i perioden 1980 til 2006. I samme periode er den amerikanske udenrigshandel vokset med en faktor 11 og det amerikanske nominelle BNP med en faktor 5 (slide 5). Det har vret afgrende for den stigning, som vi har set, at kapitalbevgelserne verden over er blevet stadigt mere liberaliseret. Der har vret tale om 4 en gradvis proces, som isr fik momentum i 1980'erne. Inden for rammerne af EU er der gjort meget for at fremme frie kapitalbevgelser. Fjernelsen af valutakursusikkerhed i forbindelse med indfrelsen af euroen har yderligere medvirket til stigende finansiel integration inden for eurolandene. I de seneste r er der ogs udformet nye flles rammebetingelser for de europiske vrdipapirmarkeder. Globaliseringen af finansmarkederne bner for en mere effektiv kapitalanvendelse med potentielt store gevinster for verdenskonomien. For investorer indebrer et mere integreret finansielt marked strre investeringsmuligheder. Kapitalen fr mulighed for at sge over i nye markeder med hjere afkast, og et strre finansielt marked giver bedre mulighed for at sprede sin risiko. Hertil kommer, at lntagere fr mulighed for at rejse kapital fra en dybere og bredere kreds af investorer. Den samlede effekt er en mere effektiv kapitalanvendelse. Kapitalen anvendes dr, hvor effekten er strst. Med den finansielle integration er der dog samtidigt opstet nye risici. Store finansielle ubalancer p tvrs af lande kan finansieres, s lnge de finansielle markeder har tillid til udviklingen. Men den dag tilliden forsvinder, s kan det g meget strkt. USA har uafbrudt fra 2002 og frem til i dag vret i stand til at finansiere et underskud p betalingsbalancen p omkring 4-7 pct. af BNP (slide 6). I denne periode har USAs forbrugs- og investeringseftersprgsel vedvarende vret markant strre end dets indkomst. Dette har vret muliggjort af store udenlandske kapitaltilfrsler. Men hvad hvis disse kapitaltilfrsler pludseligt ophrer? Det vil medfre strkt stigende amerikanske renter og en markant svagere dollar. I sdant et scenario er der en risiko for, at tilpasningen vil vre meget omkostningskrvende for store dele af verdenskonomien. Der vil ske en abrupt tilpasning af priserne p en rkke finansielle aktiver, og dette vil trkke realkonomiske tilpasninger med sig. Heldigvis er de fleste af den opfattelse, at risikoen for en abrupt tilpasning er aftagende, men fortsat til stede. Danmark har ogs taget del i den globale finansielle integration. Danske virksomheder kber jvnligt udenlandske virksomheder op, og udenlandske virksomheder kber danske virksomheder. Salget af TDC til en international 5 kapitalfond sidste r var selv i international sammenhng en af de strste transaktioner af den slags nogensinde. Udviklingen p de danske vrdipapirmarkeder vidner om stigende finansiel integration  isr med eurolandene. Statistiske analyser viser, at rentendringer p 10-rige danske statsobligationer tt flger tilsvarende tyske rentendringer (slide 7). Danske, tyske, engelske og japanske rentendringer samvarierer ogs relativt tt med rentendringer i verdens vigtigste obligationsmarked  markedet for amerikanske statsobligationer (slide 8). I de senere r er konvergensen steget mrkbart. Investorer betragter tilsyneladende i stigende grad de store obligationsmarkeder verden over som t marked. Sammenlignet med obligationer er aktier af en mere heterogen struktur, og integrering af aktiemarkeder p tvrs af lande er knap s fremskreden. Det er dog tydeligt, at aktieindeks i USA, euroomrdet og herhjemme pvirkes af flles faktorer (slide 9). 6 Danmarks integrering i de globale finansielle markeder er uomtvistelig. Og det er en udvikling, som bringer os meget gavn. Men det er ogs benbart, at vi ikke i samme grad som tidligere kan afskrme os fra udefrakommende begivenheder. Jeg nvnte tidligere risikoen for, at finansieringen af det amerikanske betalingsbalanceunderskud pludseligt vanskeliggres. En sdan abrupt tilpasning ville ndvendigvis ogs f nogle flger i Danmark, fx via et fald i eksporten. *** Et andet eksempel p et globalt finansielt fnomen, som af nogen vurderes at udgre en trussel mod den globale finansielle stabilitet, er den skaldte yen-"carry"-handel. Yen-carry-handlen er en investeringsstrategi, hvor en investor lner penge til lav rente i japanske yen og efterflgende placerer pengene til en hjere rente i eksempelvis amerikanske vrdipapirer. Selvom omfanget af yen-carry-handel strategien er umulig at opgre med nogen stor prcision, tiltrkker strategien uden tvivl mange investorer. Det skyldes et betydeligt rentespnd, p i omegnen af 3 procentpoint, mellem yen og dollar fordringer (slide 10). Udvere af yen-carry-strategien er en broget flok. De spnder fra japanske husmdre, der investerer i investeringsforeninger, som placerer sig i newzealandske og australske dollar-obligationer, over hedgefonde til landmnd i steuropa, der finansierer sig i yen. Om yen-carry-strategien udgr en global risiko afhnger i hj grad af strategiens popularitet. Sker der pludselige ndringer i strategiens forudstninger, der medfrer, at investorerne samtidig flokkes mod udgangen, vil det  hvis summerne ellers er store nok  kunne fre til kraftige bevgelser i valutakurser og renter. Bevgelser som vil forplante sig videre i det globale finansielle system og i sidste ende ogs krve tilpasninger i realkonomien. Yen handlen burde iflge konomisk teori ikke kunne betale sig over lngere perioder. Tilpasninger i konomierne medfrer, at renteforskelle over tid opvejes af valutakursndringer  i dette tilflde af en yen styrkelse. Faktum er imidlertid, at strategien i lange perioder har kunnet betale sig. Valutakurser, som ikke er forankret i fastkursregimer, er notorisk svre at 7 forudsige. Det glder ogs for yennen, der i lange perioder lbende er blevet svkket over for dollar  mske netop som flge af, at flere og flere investorer er blevet tiltrukket af yen-carry-handlen ensbetydende med et lbende salg af yen. Meget taler imidlertid for, at man skal vre forsigtig med den slags spekulation, ogs selv om strategien i lange perioder har vret fordelagtig. Yencarry-strategien er risikofyldt. Problemet opstr, hvis yennen styrkes kraftigt og pludseligt. Investorerne vil s pfres store tab. Mange investorers forsg p at komme ud af samme type position vil kun forstrke yennens appreciering. Det vil skabe yderligere tab. Det var netop det, som skete i 1998. Rentespndet mellem yen- og dollar-fordringer tiltrak ogs dengang mange investorer til yen-carry-handlen. S blev yennen i lbet af blot 3 dage styrket med 13 pct. Dette pfrte bl.a. en rkke hedgefonde voldsomme tab (slide 11). Sammenlignet med yennens normale kursudsving var styrkelsen i denne periode en nrmest umulig hndelse iflge de sandsynlighedsfordelinger, som man normalt bruger. Men sdan kan det g, og sdan gr det indimellem. Det er baggrunden for strategiens sammenligning med opsamling af smmnter foran en damptromle (slide 12). konomer har et begreb, som hedder "fede haler". Det er betegnelsen for det statistiske fnomen, at ekstreme hndelser optrder hyppigere end den mest benyttede sandsynlighedsfordeling vil tilsige. Fede haler kan gre ondt p investorer, nr de rammer. *** 8 Den finansielle integration har ikke kun medfrt globale systemiske forandringer og nye muligheder for professionelle investorer. Udviklingen har ogs givet anledning til en rivende finansiel innovation med helt nye muligheder for privatinvestorer. Jeg vil tro, at en del her i salen er bekendt med principperne bag carryinvesteringsstragien, som jeg netop omtalte. Vi har nemlig ogs vores egen lille version af den strategi. I vores tilflde udfres strategien af private lntagere, ofte landmnd siges det, som frem for at optage ln i danske kroner vlger at gre det i schweizerfrancs. Et lavere renteniveau p schweiziske fordringer end p danske betyder, at dette vil vre fordelagtigt  i hvert fald s lnge schweizerfrancen ikke styrkes alt for meget over for kronen (slide 13). Pengeinstitutternes udln til husholdninger i schweizerfrancs er steget stt siden 2001 og opgres i dag til knap 20 mia.kr. (slide 14). I lbet af 2006 fladede stigningen i schweizerfranc udlnene dog ud, og nettoudlnene blev sidst p ret negativ (slide 15). Samtidig var schweizerfrancen svkket til sit laveste niveau i 8-9 r over for danske kroner. Faldet i nettoudlnene kan skyldes forventninger om en reversering af schweizerfrancens svkkelse. Dette bekrftes af statistiske analyser p data for en lngere rrkke. Analyserne finder en signifikant sammenhng mellem en svkket schweizerfranc og aftagende nettoudln. 9 Det er interessant, at de danske carry-spekulanter har et anderledes reaktionsmnster end yen carry-spekulanterne. Yen carry-spekulanterne lber ud af deres position, nr yennen styrkes. De er tilsyneladende bange for, at styrkelsen varsler en kommende strre tilpasning i valutakursen. Vores hjemlige schweizerfranc spekulanter ger deres positioner, nr schweizerfrancen styrkes. De tror tilsyneladende, at styrkelsen er midlertidig. Den danske schweizerfranc carry-lnestrategi udgr selvflgelig ikke en trussel for det globale finansielle system. Dertil er den alt for lille og ubetydelig. Risikoen knytter sig i stedet til den konomiske situation for de enkelte lntagere, sfremt schweizerfrancen styrkes over for kroner. Det vil ogs her kunne gre ondt, hvis de fede haler slr fra sig. En anden ny type finansielle produkter, som vi inden for de sidste r er blevet prsenteret for herhjemme, er de skaldte indekserede obligationer. Bankernes salg af denne type obligationer er vokset kraftigt siden begyndelsen i 1998. Primo april i r var den udestende mngde noteret p Kbenhavns Fondsbrs 52 mia.kr. (slide 16). I Nationalbankens nste kvartalsoversigt vil vi prsentere en analyse af dette produkt. Lad mig nvne nogle af resultaterne allerede nu. Produktet bestr delvist af en relativ sikker obligationsinvestering og delvist af en optionsinvestering. Optionsinvesteringen er knyttet til udviklingen i fx aktier, valutakurser eller rvarer. Produktet har udvidet investeringsuniverset for private investorer. Vi kan nu alle spekulere i, om det er kobberprisen eller den australske dollar, som er p vej op. 10 De indekserede obligationer udmrker sig ved, at et eventuelt tab ofte er begrnset til en forholdsvis lille andel af det investerede belb. Dette er dog ikke tilstrkkeligt til at gre det til en fornuftig investering. De indekserede obligationer er illikvide og har ofte en kompliceret struktur, der kan vre svr at gennemskue for de fleste. Hvad fs til gengld for denne kompleksitet? Et hjt afkast? Ikke ndvendigvis. I Nationalbanken har vi gennemget 67 indekserede obligationer med en nominel vrdi p ca. 18 mia.kr. Obligationerne har alle vret noteret p Kbenhavns Fondsbrs, men er nu indfriet. Det gennemsnitlige rlige afkast p disse obligationer har vret omkring 2,5 pct. vgtet i forhold til obligationernes lbetid og nominelle udestende mngde. Nsten halvdelen af obligationerne var forbundet med et negativt eller intet afkast, mens ca. 15 pct. af obligationerne havde et rligt afkast p 10 pct. eller mere (slide 17). De 67 indekserede obligationer har haft et gennemsnitligt rligt merafkast i forhold til danske statsobligationer af tilsvarende varighed p omkring 0,1 procentpoint. Ved investering i en dansk statsobligation kbes en likvid, risikofri og ganske ukompliceret obligation, hvis nominelle afkast ydermere er kendt p kbstidspunktet. I sammenligning hermed har de indekserede obligationer lidt mere kreditrisiko, meget mindre likviditet og et meget mere svingende afkast. Set i forhold til de ptagne risici m et historisk gennemsnitligt rligt merafkast p 0,1 procentpoint karakteriseres som vrende lille. Optagelse af ln i schweizerfrancs og investering i indekserede obligationer er som de fleste andre investeringsbeslutninger forbundet med finansielle risici. Jeg kan kun opfordre til, at investeringsmssige beslutninger foretages under grundig overvejelse af de indeholdte risici. Globaliseringen er en positiv udvikling, og den har i srdeleshed vret det for Danmark, fordi vi har vret i stand til at omstille os hurtigt. De finansielle markeder er et omrde, hvor konsekvenserne af globaliseringen er mest tydelig. De finansielle markeder reagerer i dag som tt forbundne kar. Det er klogt at huske, at det ogs kan have ubehagelige konsekvenser, nr man som privat investor eller lntager bevger sig ud p disse markeder.

Title: Government Bond Markets in 2009
text: Government Bond Markets in 2009 Speech by Jens Thomsen, Member of the Board of Governors of Danmarks Nationalbank and Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee, Sub-Committee on EU Government Bonds and Bills Markets.1 European Government Bond Summit, Brussels, Belgium, 5 November 2009 1. Introduction I am delighted to be here tonight to offer my view on the development in the financial markets. A little more than a year ago the financial markets were frozen and there was a well-founded concern regarding the financial and economic outlook. 2009 has indeed proven to be challenging in many ways. In the period after Lehman Brothers collapse the international financial crisis escalated. As a consequence the spread between uncollateralised and collateralised money-market interest rates tripled, cf. Chart 1. Most countries launched extensive rescue packages to mitigate the crisis. The interventions stopped the free fall of the financial system. 3-MONTH MONEY MARKET SPREADS IN GERMANY, UK AND USA Basis points 450 Chart 1 400 350 300 250 200 150 100 50 0 jan 07 apr 07 jul 07 okt 07 jan 08 apr 08 jul 08 okt 08 jan 09 apr 09 jul 09 okt 09 Germany UK USA Source: Bloomberg. Against the backdrop of weaker economic outlook governments introduced fiscal stimulus and monetary policies have been relaxed substantially. Central banks have reduced the policy interest rate sharply and provided extensive liquidity to banks and resorted to unconventional tools to ease monetary policy, which has supported financial stability. 1 The mandate of the sub-committee is to aim at promoting further the integration and better functioning of EU government bonds and bills markets thereby impacting positively on the financial markets as a whole. 2 2. Government finances The global economic prospects were gloomy at the beginning of the year and the financial crisis has had greater real economic repercussions than expected, which triggered the adoption of large stimulus packages worldwide. As a result of lower government revenue and rapidly rising expenses, public finances have deteriorated. In the course of 2009 most countries have revised their forecast of government deficits to record highs and government finances are expected to be under extensive pressure in the coming years. Government debt issuance in the euro zone is expected to be around 925 billion euro in 2009, which is an increase of around 30 per cent. In 2010, issuance is expected to be even higher. At the same time the role of DMOs has changed as a result of the financial crisis. The special status of government securities as risk-free assets has been highlighted, and DMOs played a key role in connection with the financing of rescue packages. 3. Government bond markets Primary markets The primary markets have worked reasonably well in light of the severity of the financial and economic crisis. The uncertainty in the financial markets, coupled with risk aversion among investors, led to rising demand for riskfree assets, including government bonds. Even so, the greater supply of government bonds has in periods caused investors to be more selective and some DMOs have found it difficult to obtain sufficient demand at auctions and when issuing syndicated loans. Especially in the latter part of 2008 and the beginning of 2009, DMOs paid a concession premium in order to attract investors. In addition, yield spreads to Germany widened considerably in a number of European countries, cf. Chart 2. This reflected a flight-to-quality, as the German bond market is considered to be the most liquid in Europe. In addition, investors attributed higher credit risk premiums due to increasing concerns about fiscal sustainability in view of the rapidly growing budget. Since mid-2009 the primary markets have improved. DMOs no longer pay concession premiums and yield spreads between European countries have narrowed. The market has been able to absorb the considerable higher volume of government debt issuance better than expected. 3 10-YEAR YIELD SPREADS TO GERMANY Basis points 160 Chart 2 140 120 100 80 60 40 20 0 jan mar maj jul sep nov jan mar maj jul sep nov jan mar maj jul sep nov 07 07 07 07 07 07 08 08 08 08 08 08 09 09 09 09 09 09 Italy France The Netherlands Spain Belgium Source: Bloomberg. Issuance strategies The challenging issuance climate and uncertainty about future borrowing requirements have prompted several DMOs to pursue more flexible issuance strategies. This has included issuance in government securities outside key on-the-run issues, and use of various loan programmes, including CP and EMTN programmes. DMOs have also introduced new issuance techniques to secure successful auctions. At the same time, DMOs have an increased focus on investor relations in order to avoid that investors disregard an issuer on the basis of incomplete information. The improvement of the financial markets and lower uncertainty concerning issuance needs has meant that DMOs to a larger degree are returning to a more predictable issuance strategy. Roll-over risk and competition from government guaranteed bonds In the beginning of the year government deficits and financial rescue packages were primarily funded by issuing short-term papers such as T-bills and commercial papers. This raised concern about roll-over risk, especially in the light of expected high government deficits in the years to come. The concern of roll-over risk eased during the year as the gradual improvement of the government bond market enabled DMOs to lengthen the maturity profile of their issuance. So far debt managers have by and large covered the required record issuance need for 2009 at reasonable costs. The concern in the beginning of the year regarding possible competition from government guaranteed bonds has proven to be less of an issue than expected. This can primarily be attributed to the fact that the high liquidity of government securities has a value for investors. Less liquid issuances of local governments or state agencies have 4 to a higher degree suffered from private sector issuers with a government guarantee. In 2010, the government bond market may see increasing competition from other sectors, including covered bonds and corporate bonds, if the financial market continues to improve and investors gain risk appetite. This would be a positive sign of health in the financial system but also raise a concern about the government bond market in view of the record issuance requirements. Secondary markets The secondary market has been more permanently hit by the crisis than primary markets. After the shock in September 2008, liquidity in the secondary market dried up, resulting in a significant widening of bid-ask spreads and a dramatic reduction of volumes, cf. Chart 3. The situation has improved in 2009 with a narrowing of bid-ask spreads, but the secondary markets have still not normalised. It is important to restore transparency and confidence in the government bond market. Some countries are successfully bringing more competition in the secondary market by implementing market making obligations based on relative performance among primary dealers instead of fixed maximum spreads and minimum volumes. BID-ASK SPREADS IN 10-YEAR BENCHMARK BONDS Ticks 240 Chart 3 200 160 120 80 40 0 apr-08 jul-08 okt-08 jan-09 apr-09 jul-09 okt-09 Belgium Netherlands France Germany Finland Portugal Source: MTS platforms. Future challenges Over the summer, the financial markets have been characterised by stronger confidence in real economic developments, and the extensive political measures have contributed to increasing the risk appetite of investors. Spreads in the money market have come down from a high of several hun- dred basis points to a level below pre-Lehman. Similarly, the spreads be- tween European issuers have narrowed considerably. These factors indicate 5 a significant improvement in financial conditions since the historical low in October 2008. The panic mood has ceased, but the enhanced market stability is to a high degree the result of continued public support measures. Market conditions have still not normalised and the estimated government issuance need for 2010 is record high in many countries due to high redemptions and large budget deficits, cf. Chart 4. GENERAL GOVERNMENT BUDGET DEFICITS Per cent of GDP 14 Chart 4 12 10 8 6 4 2 0 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 Euro area UK USA Source: European Commission, European Economic Forecast Autumn 2009. Compared to one year ago, debt managers and banks are however less nervous. The financial markets have improved and in light of the expectations of the future government funding requirements turnover in the primary and secondary market should increase. Both debt managers and bankers have a mutual interest in restoring confidence in the market.

Title: Speech at the Danish Bankers Association's annual meeting
text: Nils Bernstein Speech at the Danish Bankers Association's annual meeting on 6 December 2006 Thank you for the invitation to speak here at the Danish Bankers Association's annual meeting. The Danish economy is still characterized by a boom, and there are no signs that it is about to fade away. The recovery began in mid-2003 and has since strengthened. The recovery was initially supported by income tax cuts and has been gradually compounded by a remarkable recovery in the international economy. In this picture, Europe has generally been behind the rest of the world, but now that growth in the U.S. economy seems to be slowing, activity among our main trading partners in Europe is rising. The growth in the Danish economy has led to a decline in unemployment, which has not been seen lower since the oil crisis hit us in the 70s. This means that, unlike previous recovery, the balance of payments remains strong and the surplus in public finances has a solid structural foundation. However, the picture of the Danish economy cannot be fully drawn without pointing out the risks at hand. Global imbalances remain conspicuous, with the huge U.S. current account deficit as the dominant move. It is still the overwhelming opinion that the imbalances will correct themselves over time. The U.S. economy is slowing down as a result of a shrinking housing market. However, the risk of more abrupt adjustments cannot be ruled out. However, the danger signals for the Danish economy come from within. The development depends on how we handle the situation ourselves. We in this country have had low inflation and moderate wage increases for a long time. It is a phenomenon that we share with many other countries and which, among other things, is the result of a growing recognition of the beneficial effects on the economy of low inflation. The low unemployment rate, combined with a continued robust increase in demand for Danish goods, entails a risk that the pressure on the labour market will take hold as higher inflation. It is well known that this can later lead to greater unemployment. Although it is not considered the most likely course of events, the risk of a harmful overheating of the economy 2 Growing. This is the reason why Danmarks Nationalbank has recommended  and continues to recommend  that there be a limitation of the overall increase in demand as a measure to create greater security for a continued favourable development in the Danish economy. At Danmarks Nationalbank, we have noted that the government has chosen to look at the time. The critical focal point in the coming years is, as mentioned, the labour market. The population of the most working groups is declining, setting limits on the growth of the labor force. Employment is likely to remain largely unchanged, in contrast to previous years, when there has been an increase of 70,000 since the recovery began in 2003. The continued recovery will be dampened by labour shortages. We have seen increasing wage increases this year, and domestic price pressures have been gradually increasing. It is unknown how much the adjustment process will ultimately impact inflation. The housing market rightly attracts a lot of attention. We have seen very strong increases in the price of real estate, not least in the Capital Region. The latest figures suggest that price increases are continuing, but at a subdued pace. In some of the most expensive areas, there are scattered signs of slightly declining prices, and it has become more common to refuse compared to the price offered. One of the most important factors behind rising house prices has been the low interest rate. In 1998, 80 per cent of total household loans were from banks and mortgage banks at fixed rates. That figure has now fallen to 40 per cent. Thus, more than half of the outstanding loans have interest rate adjustment or completely variable interest rates, and borrowers have to look forward to a higher performance on their loans in 2007 as a result of the increase in short-term interest rates over the past year. Taking into account that households also have interest income, households' net after-tax interest expense will increase by a little more than 2 mia.kr. or 0.3 per cent of consumption. In particular, it is by influencing the temporal location of consumption and investment that interest rates affect activity. Although interest rates have risen, the real interest rate after tax remains very low  not much above 1% for most people. Therefore, the level of interest rates continues to have an expansionary effect on the Danish economy. The progress of the economy is also reflected in the financial system. Banks' balance sheets are growing strongly. At the same time, there are record profits, labor shortages, rising wages and large bonus payments. 3 The banks' lending is growing by just over 20 per cent year-on-year. The composition of the lending of banking institutions on professions and households follows a well-known pattern. Lending to households comes first in a consumption-driven recovery, and growth in it has been in double digits since 2004. The banks have gone strong into housing finance with so-called mortgages. In addition, many households  well supported by the marketing of a number of financial institutions  have gained greater risk appetite. Lending to businesses comes later in a recovery when corporate investments can no longer be financed from their own resources. Growth in business lending double-digits at the end of 2004 and is now up to 20% year-on-year. The high rate of increase in lending is an average figure for all financial institutions. The spread between institutions is significant. In some financial institutions, lending increases by more than 50 per cent year-on-year. The strong loan growth is clearly seen in the banks' balance sheet composition. The difference between lending and deposits of financial institutions has grown significantly in recent years. Total loans now exceed total deposits by three-digit billions. As a result, banks have become increasingly dependent on financing in the financial markets in the form of money market loans from other banks and the issuance of securities, nationally and internationally. At the same time, it becomes important for the individual financial institution to maintain access to these sources of financing. The sources are more sensitive than traditional deposits to changes in market conditions and the assessment of the institution's own financial condition. This can increase the vulnerability of financial institutions. The Minister for Economic and Business Affairs is putting the finishing touches on a bill that gives banks access to issue covered bonds (SDOs) on an equal footing with mortgage banks. Why is it now necessary to change the Danish system of financing real estate through the mortgage banks? Mortgage credit is a well-functioning and stable system that has provided real estate owners with access to finance on capital market terms with a transparent cost structure. Let me put it bluntly. The change has come to us from the outside and also has positive elements. It intensifies competition between Danish financial institutions and gives Danish institutions access to work on the same terms as foreign credit institutions. It must also be borne in mind that the change in the law will not lead to a major upheaval of Danish housing finance overnight. A lot has already happened in the past few years. Here I am thinking of the fact that the financial institutions have very successfully introduced the so-called mortgages. From this perspective, SDOs issued by financial institutions can promote financial stability as a stable source of financing for mortgage lending, thus covering the large deposit deficit in a more satisfactory way. 4 When the CB legislation is changed, Danmarks Nationalbank prefers a robust and simple model. The banks have requested the lifting of the current restrictions on repayment profiles and maturities. We can agree with this, as we also propose that the loan limit for home loans be reduced to 70 per cent of the value of the home. This also makes it easier for institutions to comply with the ongoing requirement that a loan based on covered bonds must never exceed 80 per cent of the value of the mortgage during the entire term of the loan. Should there be a slight tightening in this, it is not accidental. In connection with the work with SDO, two committees have been set up, which look at the balance principle and so-called joint funding, respectively. Danmarks Nationalbank is prepared to adapt and make the Danish balance sheet principle more flexible, so that it is better in line with modern risk management methods. In this context, it is important that a new balancing principle provides the same certainty as the existing system. Joint funding occupies many of those present. It is a market condition that the issuance of bonds at advantageous prices requires large volume. At the same time, it is the Danish Bankers Association's wish: "that the customer throughout the customer relationship experiences that it is the bank that stands as the creditor for the loan and thus is the customer's bank connection, even though the bank actually manages the loan on behalf of the funding company". I understand that it is important for the individual bank that decisions can be made locally at the counter. On the other hand, it is not clear to me how much fundamental legal principles need to be changed to achieve this situation. Already today, banks do business on behalf of other legal entities such as mutual funds, insurance companies, etc. Now, whether the wish can ultimately be fulfilled will be the task of the Ministry of Justice to assess. It is Danmarks Nationalbank's assessment that the Danish banking system is robust today. Earnings are very good, and the buffers are large but declining. For the banks as a whole, the buffers in relation to the act's minimum capital requirements have fallen over 3 years from 7.5 per cent of loans and guarantees to 4 per cent. The regulation of Danish banks is undergoing major changes in recent years. At first, the accounting rules were changed so that write-downs on loans can only be made on the basis of an objective assessment of the value. Provisions based on a precautionary principle can no longer be made. In 2007, the new capital adequacy rules will come into force. The solvency of a credit institution will now be calculated with risk weights that correspond better to the actual risk in the portfolio. The legal capital requirement will be smaller in dollars and cents, but will also fluctuate more. 5 I would like to stress that the changes in accounting and capital adequacy rules mean that legislation does not automatically create reserves in credit institutions to the same extent as before. The responsibility now largely lies with the management, and it is an extremely important management task to establish a sufficient buffer in determining the solvency of the individual institution. I would like to conclude by saying that we at Danmarks Nationalbank welcome the growth in the financial sector, which is a mirror image of the good Danish economy. And on behalf of Danmarks Nationalbank, I would like to thank you for the good cooperation.

Title: Government bond market in light of the recent turmoil
text: Government bond market in light of the recent turmoil Speech by Jens Thomsen, Member of the Board of Governors of Danmarks Nationalbank and Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee, sub-committee on EU Government Bonds and Bills Market.1 European Government Bond Summit, Brussels, Belgium, 24 October 2008 Introduction I am delighted to be here today to offer my view on the ongoing turbulence in the financial markets. In the not so distant past the financial markets played a role by applying pressure on Member State governments to run sound public finances in Stage III of the EMU. Today the tables have been turned. A reasonable description of the present agenda is more along the lines of how the public finances can promote sound financial markets (see slide 2). Liquidity In turbulent times the price of liquidity increases. Since august of 2007 there has been four consecutive waves of illiquidity, during which the perceived default and liquidity risk of banks have risen and widened the spread between unsecured and secured lending and where the fourth and last spike following the default of Lehman Brothers has been the most severe (see slide 3). The decomposed TED spread shows how T-bills have become especially valuable in times of crises (see slide 4). During the four spikes the lending against US T-bill has driven down the T-bill rate. The same effect has not been quite as prominent in the European money market (see slide 5). The most recent flare up of the turbulence has however lead to significantly increased demand for short term government securities leading to lower interest rates for the German T-bills. Prior to the recent turbulence in September the search for safety drove down both the T-bill and the highest rated commercial paper yield. Lately the status of the commercial paper programs as a safe heaven has eroded, as the CP-markets have frozen (see slide 6). Outstanding amounts of asset backed commercial papers took a significant dive at the outset of the turbulence in 2007 (see slide 7). Recently the outstandings of commercial papers for financial issuers have been declining. Note however that the latest data does not reflect the impact of the Commercial Paper Funding Facility (CPFF) provided by the Federal Reserve. 1 The mandate of the Sub-Committee is to aim at promoting further the integration and better functioning of EU government bond markets thereby impacting positively on the financial markets as a whole. 2 Credit risk and issuance terms The increased price of liquidity has been followed by an increase in of the price of credit. The recent announcements of bank recapitalisations and guarantee schemes have curtailed the upswing in the CDS spread in the financial sector. However spreads are still high compared to pre-August 2007 levels (see slide 8). Even sovereigns have not been immune to the increased credit risk valuations (see slide 9). Following the announcement of the rescue packages, the CDS-spreads for sovereigns seem to have stabilized. In relation to issuance terms in this volatile market the bond yields have been declining compared to level in July 2008 (see slide 10). This movement has primarily been driven by a flight to safety. Nevertheless the demand for government securities can be quite volatile. The latest round of financial turmoil has indeed lead to pronounced increase in the volatility both in the stock and bond market (slide 11), which from an issuers standpoint makes it difficult to manoeuvre in terms of coming out with timely issuances in such an unpredictable market environment. In addition increased credit risk and demand for liquidity have widened the yield spread to German government securities and thereby aggravating the relative issuance terms for other EMU-countries (see slide 12). Under the assumption that the yield spread between member states purely can be explained by differences in credit risk and liquidity, one may use prices on credit default swaps (CDS) as an approximation for the credit risk premium. The liquidity risk may then be defined as the residual of the yield spread after deducting the credit risk premium (see slide 13). The calculation shows that the widened yield vis-a-vis Germany in 2008 compared to 2007 is predominately caused by increased credit risks. The financial turbulence has elucidated the role of the government securities as safe havens (see slide 14). Under normal market conditions the swap market may function as a substitute for government securities especially in terms of it's virtues in regards to pricing. However the increasing credit and liquidity premiums imply that this type of substitution is no longer valid. Market conditions In general banks are under pressure. They experience rising funding costs and declining market value (see slide 15). The capacity of the balance sheet is constrained making it more difficult to handle the intermediation phase between issuers and end-investors. In addition, the constrained balance sheets combined with increased volatility have lead to widened bid offerspreads in the secondary government bond markets, hence the efficiency of the European government bond market has temporarily gone down (see slide 16). 3 The role of the DMOs After listing the areas in which the government debt management experiences the effect of the financial turbulence. I now turn to discuss in what role the DMOs may play in handling the crisis (see slide 17). Involvement in handling the stressed situation in the financial sector Help to ensure state guarantees to secure confidence between financial counterparties  and thaw up the frozen interbank market. Issue sufficient funds to perform the announced recapitalisations of banks. It has been stated that the government ownership through recapitalisations should be a temporary solution. When it comes time to wind up the government ownership of the banks timing can be hard; should the government for instance sell its shares, when the share prices are high, i.e. in periods of high growth where the government typically does not have a funding need? What lies ahead? Ahead of us lies a period, where a majority of the governments in the Euro area will experience an increased need for funding, hence higher issuance from sovereign issuers is to be expected (see slide 18 and 19) Government bond markets in light of the recent turmoil The European Government Bond Summit, 24 October, 2008 By Jens Thomsen 1 Changing perspectives In 2003 the headline was: The role of financial markets in promoting sound public finances in EMU Today the perspective is turned around: The role of public finances in promoting sound financial markets in EMU 2 Price of liquidity in turbulent times is very volatile Four consecutive rounds of uncertainty increasing the price of liquidity 3 Source: Bloomberg.
