Title: Speech at the annual meeting of local banks
text: SPEECH GOVERNOR SIGNE KROGSTRUP'S SPEECH AT THE ANNUAL MEETING OF LOCAL BANKS1 THE SPOKEN WORD APPLIES PART 1: PROSPECTS FOR THE DANISH ECONOMY Slide 1 Thank you for the invitation to speak here today. I will start with a brief overview of where the economy stands today  just over a year after the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic. And then from talking about one crisis that we're emerging from, I'm going to spend the rest of the time talking about another crisis that's still ahead of us  the climate crisis. Slide 2 If we start by taking a look at abroad, last year  as we all know  saw the strongest economic downturns in recent times. Economic activity declined globally by nearly 4 percent. But it covers up big differences across countries and industries. For example, China and the US have outdone the euro area. And manufacturing professions have performed better than service occupations. I'll get back to that shortly. While in some ways it may feel that way  when we look down through the streets  we're not yet on the other side of the pandemic. But the vaccine rollouts around the world have given us a light at the end of the tunnel. 1 I would like to thank Marcus Molbak Ingholt in particular for his help in writing the speech and Carsten Andersen, Oliver Hammershoj Bentsen, Mette Hojen, Carina Moselund Jensen, Lasse Jygert, Ole Mikkelsen and Karoline Garm Nissen for their suggestions and comments. Page 1 of 17 In the very short term, we expect that global activity will still be limited by, for example, not being able to travel freely. But as people get vaccinated and economies fully reopen, we believe there is a prospect of a strong recovery in economic activity. The global economy has been and still is  largely supported by an extraordinarily accommodative monetary and fiscal stance. The policy measures help to mitigate the consequences of the infection restrictions. It has held a hand under both businesses and citizens. In the U.S. just, 2.8 trillion in recent months has been passed  the equivalent of 13 percent of GDP. The massive stimulus is really kicking off the U.S. recovery. That's contributing to the U.S. economy expected to be back at pre-pandemic levels by the middle of this year. In the euro area and the UK, it won't be until next year. Slide 3 If we turn our attention to Denmark and rewind to the time before the pandemic hit, the Danish economy found itself in a moderate boom without significant imbalances. In other words, we were well equipped to counter the economic downturn. And how has the Danish economy fared? The latest figures show that GDP fell by just under 3% last year. And here in the first quarter, we saw another big drop in activity. The good news is that activity seems to return rapidly as the community opens up. For example, the Danes' use of payment cards shows that consumption has quickly recovered. In our latest March forecast, we estimated that GDP would increase by about 11/2% this year. Since then, we've gotten a little more positive. We are because the restrictions were lifted sooner than expected. Consumption returned faster. And Danish exports performed better than predicted in our forecast. Overall, with the rollout of vaccines, the risk picture has become more balanced. But we still see a number of risks on both sides. On the one hand, there are factors that can lift economic activity above what we expect. For example, the vaccine rollout could go faster than expected. Our consumption and investment can return to normal patterns faster. And the effect of economic stimulus could be stronger than expected. Page 2 of 17 On the other hand, there are factors that could end up dragging down economic activity further than we expect. For example, related to the evolution of the pandemic and the vaccine rollout. There is also a risk that the higher government spending from the pandemic could lead to debt crises in some countries. And that the pandemic has given rise to a flourishing of protectionism  that is, an "every country for itself" mentality. Finally, we run the risk that some companies can't keep their heads above water when the government bailouts expire. In Denmark, however, we believe that you  the banks  are well equipped to support viable companies when the aid packages expire. Banks have a significant capacity to expand lending and to absorb any losses. The release of the countercyclical capital buffer has contributed to this capacity. The purpose of the capital buffer is precisely to build up capital in times of upturn, so that in a future crisis there is capital to maintain lending and absorb losses. Therefore, it is important that the buffer is rebuilt as we emerge from the crisis, so that we have something to resist with. And as you have probably noticed, the Systemic Risk Council expects to recommend that the reconstruction of the buffer begin in mid-2022. All in all, there is still a great deal of uncertainty about the timing and pace of the recovery of the Danish economy. That is why we have also pointed out in the past that it is important that politicians are ready to adapt fiscal policy. Slide 4 As I mentioned earlier, the economy right now is running at multiple speeds. It is seen both at home and abroad. On the one hand, parts of the economy are hampered by contagion fears and restrictions. These include tourism. On the other hand, there are also parts of the economy where activity has returned  or is even higher than before the pandemic. This can be seen, for example, in supermarkets, in the IT industry and, not least, in the construction industry, where an increasing number of companies are even reporting a shortage of labour. Slide 5 One place where activity has increased particularly during the pandemic is in the housing market. Prices have risen significantly throughout the country, but it is especially in the capital that there is extra momentum in the housing market. Page 3 of 17 The price increases are based on a lot of home trades. 30 per cent more homes are now being sold per month than before the pandemic, and trading activity for houses is still at an all-time high, although they fell slightly in April. It's going really fast. Such a development in itself gives reason to raise eyebrows. The many trades may be due to the fact that Danes have changed their housing demand during the pandemic. We have not been able to travel and go to a restaurant as usual. And at the same time, we've had to work from home. That may have led many to prioritize or advance home purchases. At the same time, the pandemic may have exposed the selling thoughts of some homeowners who had plans to move to a smaller residence or exit the market. If there are no more homes on the market, that alone will increase the price. In parts of the housing market, several warning lights are starting to light up. This is especially the case with the larger cities and especially in Copenhagen. The housing burden for condominiums here is relatively high. It's a trend we've seen over recent years. At the same time, there has been a tendency for lending to grow faster than incomes in Copenhagen since 2015. This has meant that lending relative to disposable income today is approaching pre-financial crisis levels. Overall, Copenhagen homeowners have thus become more vulnerable to declines in their income and rising interest rates. Interest rates today are historically low, and in 2020, for the first time in many years, we saw an increase in the use of interest-only loans. This is especially true for the most indebted homeowners, where half of the borrowers took out loans without installments. It is not appropriate for such a large proportion of this group to go into debt without paying off. Instead, it should be a sound principle that when you take on a lot of debt, the debt should subsequently be reduced to a lower level. Overall, we therefore see more signs of risk build-up as a result of the rising house prices  and especially in the metropolitan area. There is therefore good reason for vigilance. As you may have noticed, the Systemic Risk Council has announced that at its next meeting in June it expects to recommend to the Government to take new measures to limit risk build-up due to rising house prices. Page 4 of 17 It is important to prevent unsustainable risk build-up. Therefore, it is advantageous to look at measures that can reduce fluctuations in the housing market. For example, it may be a requirement for repayments for the most indebted homeowners or lower interest deductions. It is also important that the new housing tax, which fluctuates with house prices, is introduced as planned in 2024. These measures will have a structural, stabilizing effect on the housing market  both today and in the future. Page 5 of 17 PART 2: CLIMATE CHANGE AND THE ROLE OF THE FINANCIAL SECTOR Slide 6 I will now talk about climate change and the green transition  and not least about how you  the financial sector  play a key role on the way to the important climate goals. Climate change and the green transition are among the biggest challenges we face as a society. We're all going to be affected. And we're all going to have to deal with what is our contribution. Of course, we also do this at Danmarks Nationalbank  just as you do in your local banks. A common feature between the corona crisis and climate change is that society is transformed into a new reality in a very short time. In both cases, this has major economic consequences. On the contrary, a difference between the two transitions is that the corona crisis restrictions are temporary, while the green transition becomes permanent. In comparison with the corona crisis, this increases the economic consequences of the green transition. Slide 7 In this part of the presentation, I will touch on the objectives of a green transition. I will talk about the necessary policy measures  and how the transition will affect the financial system. And I want to talk about the role of the financial sector in the transition to a more climate-friendly production and lifestyle. Next, I will talk about the role of central banks in the transition  and more specifically Danmarks Nationalbank's role and work with the climate. It's relatively new that central banks are talking about climate. But at the same time it is quite natural. Let me be very clear: It is not Danmarks Nationalbank's job to drive the green transition. But it is our role to ensure a robust economy and contribute to financial stability. Therefore, Danmarks Nationalbank must take into account how the climate and the transition affect the business cycle and the financial system. When we do this, we help to support  and ensure a good framework for  the transition. Page 6 of 17 Slide 8 The objectives of the Paris Agreement and the Danish Climate Law are extremely important. They provide a good starting point for climate action, which ensures behavioural change and the necessary investments. And the private sector is today taking more and more important initiatives towards achieving climate goals. As examples from the financial sector, I can mention, that pension funds invest greenly, that banks and mortgage banks issue green loans and obligatio- ner, and that your trade association, Finance Denmark, has prepared a mo- part for accounting for the funded carbon footprint of loans and investments.2 Manufacturing companies are also in the process of reducing their carbon footprint. This is done through a focus on energy efficiency and through research and development in green technologies. These are welcome initiatives that make key contributions to the green transition. When the private sector takes so many important initiatives, it's because it's increasingly clear that it makes business sense  on balance sheets and bottom lines. That it is bottom lines and balance sheets that drive the work is as it should be in a market economy. That's how healthy competition works. But that's not enough. Despite the good private initiatives, projections from the Danish Council on Climate Change, among others, show that we are far from meeting the 70% target by 2030 and the goal of climate neutrality by 2050.3 In other words, more is needed to ensure society's bottom line. That's because companies' bottom lines don't fully capture the cost to society of companies emitting greenhouse gases. Not even though consumers have increasingly started to demand the green. Policy action is therefore necessary. 2 Finance Denmark, "CO2 model for the financial sector: Principles for measuring and accounting financed 3 emissions from lending and investment", November 2020. The Danish Council on Climate Change, "Known roads and new tracks for 70 percent reduction: Direction and measures for the next ten years of climate action in Denmark", March 2020. The Danish Council on Climate Change, "Status Report 2021: Denmark's National and Global Climate Action", February 2021. Page 7 of 17 Slide 9 An important purpose of policy action is to create a "level playing field". It must pay off for all companies to invest greenly while healthy competition remains. Policy measures must ensure that companies that invest in energy-efficient technology, for example, are not outcompeted by companies that do not invest green. Without the policy measures, there will be a risk that the greener producer will be outcompeted by the market. Ideally, these would have to be global measures, as it is not essential to global warming where greenhouse gases are emitted in the world.4 However, agreement on an effective global solution is not forth coming, and national action is therefore necessary. Slide 10 The policy tools to ensure the transition come in three forms: inclusion, investment and information.5 By inclusion, I mean that the cost to society of global warming must be included in the price of emitting greenhouse gases. It can be done in different ways. Many economists point to tax incentives. In particular, it is greenhouse gas taxes that are considered to be a cost-effective tool to ensure the inclusion of greenhouse gas emissions in prices.6 Another method to ensure inclusion is technical standards targeted at lower greenhouse gas emissions. Technical standards implicitly increase the cost of greenhouse gas emissions. This includes the social costs in the private price of emissions. The goal of inclusion is ultimately to lower the demand for and supply of greenhouse gas-intensive goods and services. Next, we come to investing. Both public and private investment is needed. They must "go hand in hand". 4 5 IMF, "Fiscal Monitor: How to Mitigate Climate Change", IMF, oktober 2019. The concepts of 'inclusion', 'investment' and 'information' are inspired by ECB President Christine Lagarde's 6 speech at bis Innovation Summit 2021. The Economic Councils, "Economy and Environment 2020: Danish climate policy towards 2030", March 2021. Page 8 of 17 Public investment in infrastructure, for example, is important and can act as a catalyst for private know-how and financing. At the same time, private investments in green research and development and in energy renovation are key. Finally, we have information. Here, requirements for manufacturing companies to report greenhouse gas emissions  also through value chains  are particularly important. It increases the transparency of companies' dependence on greenhouse gas emissions  and makes it easier for banks and investors to assess how exposed business models are to the transition. And how does Danmarks Nationalbank work with climate change? Slide 13 Work on climate change is on the rise in many central banks around the world. Another example of this development is the evaluation of the ECB's monetary policy strategy, which is now underway  and is expected to be published this year. Here climate is one of the main topics. How is it that climate has become a focal point for central banks when it is not the central banks' job to ensure the green transition? This is due to the fact that over the past few years it has become increasingly clear to what extent climate change and the green transition have the potential to challenge central banks' objectives of price stability and financial stability. Many central banks therefore take climate change into account because it is their job to ensure stable prices and financial stability. It is important to understand and respond to the changes and the transition, precisely in order to live up to the mandate. It can be said that taking climate into account has become due diligence in the world of central banking. Something you have to get a handle on. Title: Comment on the Law on Refinancing
text: Comment on refinancing law Deputy Governor Karsten Biltoft says: "For Danmarks Nationalbank, it is important that the bill is implemented as planned later this month. The bill addresses the refinancing problem of unfunded loans. In this connection, it is welcome to note that S&P, as the rating agency Fitch has done in the past, speaks positively on the Government's bill. According to S&P, the bill ensures the refinancing, whether due to a lack of investor confidence more generally or problems in a single institution. Danmarks Nationalbank agrees with S&P's assessment that there will continue to be a solid investor base for the bonds. In addition, S&P notes that the bill itself will not reduce the amount of adjustable-rate short-term loans. Danmarks Nationalbank agrees that it makes sense to continue the work of spreading the auctions. " Page 1 of 1

Lovforslaget tager hnd om refinansieringsproblemet ved ikke for-finansierede ln. I den forbindelse kan det med tilfredshed noteres, at S&P, ligesom ratingbureauet Fitch tidligere har gjort, udtaler sig positivt om regeringens lovforslag. Iflge S&P sikrer lovforslaget refinansieringen, uanset om det skyldes manglende investortillid mere generelt eller problemer i et enkelt institut. Nationalbanken er enig i S&Ps vurdering af, at der fortsat vil vre en solid investorbase for obligationerne. S&P bemrker derudover, at lovforslaget ikke i sig selv vil reducere omfanget af korte rentetilpasningsln. Nationalbanken er enig i, at det er fornuftigt at fortstte arbejdet med at sprede auktionerne. " Side 1 af 1

Title: Feature article: The IMF meets globalization
text: CHRONICLE - Politiken, October 19, 2006 The IMF meets globalization By Governor Nils Bernstein Globalisation creates a need for reforms in international economic cooperation. Denmark has just supported reforms in the IMF. The world has changed since the International Monetary Fund, the IMF, came into being over 60 years ago in the shadow of World 2. World war. Today, far more countries play a central role in world economic development, and international capital movements have multiplied. Increasing integration of economies has led to increased prosperity and new opportunities, but also risks. With globalization has come large balances of payments between leading economies. With a deficit of 6 1/2 percent of GDP, the U.S. now seizes 70 percent of global savings. The IMF has continuously adapted to international economic challenges. Sometimes in the wake of crises such as after the nearly 10-year-old crisis in Asia that led to a much-needed openness about the IMF. Other times, adjustment occurs during good times, as we are witnessing in these years of record global growth and few countries in need of loans. Globalization sets the agenda not only for international economic development in the 21st century, but also for international economic cooperation. This also applies to the tasks of the IMF and the representation of member states in the governing bodies. In Singapore, Denmark therefore helped to ensure that the IMF adapts to the challenges of globalisation. This will be done through a major reform of countries' representation in the IMF and a focus on the IMF's macroeconomic and financial surveillance across national borders. Economic and financial crises cannot be avoided, but one must insure oneself against them in the best possible way. New challenges for the IMF were created with the aim of promoting trade and economic growth and avoiding the mistakes of the Deep Depression of the 1930s. The IMF's tasks were and are threefold: 1) to monitor and advise on economic matters, 2) to provide short-term loans to countries with balance of payments problems, and 3) to provide so-called technical assistance, i.e. expert advice, to the economic-political institutions of its members. In principle, the currencies of the countries were linked together in a fixed exchange rate system, and stability was supported by the possibility of financial assistance. Short stabilization loans thus came to the fore. But in the early 1970s, the global fixed exchange rate system collapsed. Thus, the borrowing needs of the developed countries were also on the decline. IMF "loan customers" eventually became instead the emerging economies of Europe, Asia and Latin America, as well as the poorest countries, with many African countries becoming independent and then members of the IMF. Only 3 of the IMF's original 40 members were from Africa, while all 53 countries in Africa had joined the IMF in 1990. Now, emerging economies have also grown large, and the need for new loans from the IMF is severely limited. The poorest countries still need assistance, but the debt relief initiative implies a significantly lower indebtedness to the IMF. So far, the IMF has forgiven the debt of 22 of the poorest and most indebted countries, and many more countries may qualify for debt forgiveness. In addition, the IMF has never been the main lender to the poorest countries, nor should it be. The IMF is not an aid organization. Long-term lending for the development of the poorest countries is first and foremost a task of the IMF's sister organization, the World Bank. All in all, IMF's lending now amounts to 28 billion, or about 165 billion, while the amount was almost five times higher 4 years ago. Over the past decade, Russia, Argentina and Brazil, among others, have been among the big borrowers, but they have now repaid their loans. Many other countries have followed suit, not least in Asia. If you only associate the IMF with lending in crisis situations, you might think that the IMF's role is played out. But a key role for the IMF is to help ensure that countries do not get into economic trouble  to prevent crises rather than "merely" solve them. In addition, globalisation creates new challenges and opportunities that increase the need for well-functioning multilateral institutions such as the IMF. Increased trade and integration of economies increase contagion across national borders and thus the benefits of cooperation over self-interest. The number of people to the IMF is at a record high with 184 members  behind only the UN's 192 member countries. But the IMF's member states deposit a "membership contribution" in the form of a so-called quota, and everyone wants value for money. Preferably more than the possibility of loans, when nevertheless  and usually unpredictably when  a crisis occurs in the world economy again. What do member states want with the IMF? For developed countries, the problem is not new. The global agenda has long been more crucial than goodies for individual countries. The overall world economic development must be the focus of the IMF, as the current global imbalances and recurring discussions between the US and China about China's export of goods and fixed exchange rate policy show the need for. Economic stability in the world and in individual countries is paramount for developed countries, which is also the overall goal of the IMF. An economic crisis can quickly spread in a globalized world, as the financial crisis in Asia in 1997/98 showed with all due clarity. But in recent years, the agenda has been set by the 7 major industrial countries of the G7. It was also the G7 that first reached an agreement in principle on debt forgiveness to the poorest countries, although it would ultimately have to be financed by all the members of the international financial organizations. For developed countries, the main interest must be that the IMF, with its 184 member countries, contributes to a much greater extent to promoting stability in the world economy and solving global problems. For emerging economies and, not least, Asian countries, the less need for loans and high economic growth means that their interests point in the same direction as those of developed countries. Growth should also come with increased responsibility for the world economy, not least for large economies such as China and India. But many Asian countries probably still have a trauma to the IMF because they found the IMF's efforts in the 1997/98 financial crisis failed. Regardless of the need to be careful blaming the doctor for all his hardships. The interest in emerging economies is therefore to have more influence on the IMF and then ultimately on the global economic issues. Unfortunately, for the poorest countries, the need has not changed significantly. Countries continue to need assistance, but typically not the short-term stability loans that are the IMF's mission. Nevertheless, the IMF plays an important role, including by advising on macroeconomic conditions and providing technical assistance for building sound economic policy institutions. The IMF helps these countries deal with the macroeconomic challenges associated with the UN's 2015 goals  including reducing poverty and disease in the poorest countries. Thus, the IMF helps with, for example, managing the increasing development assistance and managing debt development. For the poorest countries, it is therefore important to be heard in the IMF and to have a say in decisions that greatly affect the everyday lives of the world's poorest. Throughout the ages, criticism of the IMF has been significant, for example regarding the role of the IMF in Asian countries and in the poorest countries. And the critical countries have repeatedly asked for more influence in the IMF. In September, IMF members clearly supported reforming the IMF at the annual meetings in Singapore. Denmark's support hardly comes as a surprise. It is well known that small countries are more dependent on open and democratic cooperation than larger countries. The choice of member states is a recognition that globalization means that all countries have become very dependent on each other. These are the types of interests that can best be served by a world-wide organization like the IMF, over which everyone has a say. New times in the IMF? In Singapore, Denmark helped to allocate higher quotas and thus higher voting weights in the IMF to China, Korea, Turkey and Mexico, which by all standards are clearly underrepresented. Economic growth translated into higher influence. The decisions in Singapore were only a first step to ensure a fairer distribution of influence within the IMF, as a simultaneously adopted 2-year plan should lead to more adjustments to the countries' voting weights and a modernization of the calculation base. There is a consensus to strengthen the representation of the poorest countries in the IMF. Many poor countries have had such low economic growth that an immediate adjustment of the voting weights in the IMF on the basis of economic size would involve fewer votes. But there was a consensus to find other ways to improve the opportunities for these countries' representatives to be heard as well. Equally important was confirmation in Singapore that IMF member states prefer crisis prevention to crisis loans. There is a need to strengthen the IMF's macroeconomic and financial surveillance of the world economy and individual member states. Neither a deterioration nor the status quo is good enough, not only because there is a latent risk of new economic and financial crises, which is often forgotten in favorable times, but also because globalization itself has strengthened the need for a global management of economic-political challenges. As a concrete example of the new course, the IMF's Executive Director, Rodrigo de Rato, is now conducting so-called "multilateral consultations", in which the IMF in an attempt to contribute to resolving global imbalances in the world economy is holding meetings with the eurozone, the United States, China, Japan and Saudi Arabia. Of course, there is no guarantee that the consultations will resolve global imbalances  just as the regular meetings of the G7 have not been able to  but dialogue is the first step. The consultations contribute to a more central role for the IMF in the struggle to ensure global economic and financial stability. For a small country like Denmark, it is positive that the leading countries in i.a. The G7 and G20 have backed the multilateral consultations and that they take place with the IMF in the driver's seat. Globalisation reinforces the need for well-functioning international economic policy cooperation. And already the IMF's founders, John Maynard Keynes of England and Harry Dexter White of the United States, fully understood the gains for the world economy by tackling the challenges together. The competing devaluations and trade restrictions of the interwar years did not benefit anyone. Multilateral cooperation can make all parties look beyond their own narrow short-term interests for the good of all. But it requires all members to also assess that they have influence over the IMF. Ahead is a lot of work to be done to implement the reforms of the IMF over the next two years. This work will be essential for the IMF to further develop its importance for all member countries and effectively pursue its main goal: healthy economic growth and stability in a globalized world. NILS BERNSTEIN
text_original: KRONIK - Politiken, 19. oktober, 2006 Valutafonden mder globaliseringen Af Nationalbankdirektr, Nils Bernstein Globaliseringen skaber behov for reformer i det internationale konomiske samarbejde. Danmark har netop stttet reformer i IMF. Verden har ndret sig, siden Den Internationale Valutafond, IMF, blev til for over 60 r siden i skyggen af 2. Verdenskrig. Langt flere lande spiller i dag en central rolle for den verdenskonomiske udvikling, og de internationale kapitalbevgelser er mangedoblet. Stigende integration af konomierne har frt til get velstand og nye muligheder, men ogs risici. Med globaliseringen er fulgt store betalingsubalancer mellem toneangivende konomier. Med et underskud p 6  pct. af BNP lgger USA nu beslag p 70 pct. af den globale opsparing. IMF har lbende tilpasset sig de internationale konomiske udfordringer. Nogle gange i klvandet p kriser ssom efter den snart 10 r gamle krise i Asien, der frte til en strkt pkrvet benhed omkring IMF. Andre gange sker tilpasning under gode tider, som vi er vidner til i disse r med rekordstor global vkst og f lande med behov for ln. Globaliseringen stter ikke kun dagsordenen for den internationale konomiske udvikling i det 21. rhundrede, men ogs for det internationale konomiske samarbejde. Det glder ogs IMF's opgaver og medlemslandenes reprsentation i de styrende organer. I Singapore var Danmark derfor med til sikre, at IMF tilpasser sig globaliseringens udfordringer. Det skal ske gennem en strre reform af landenes reprsentation i IMF og fokus p IMFs makrokonomiske og finansielle overvgning p tvrs af landegrnser. konomiske og finansielle kriser kan ikke undgs, men man skal forsikre sig bedst muligt imod dem. Nye udfordringer for Valutafonden IMF blev oprettet med det forml at fremme handel og konomisk vkst og undg fejltagelserne fra 1930'ernes dybe depression. IMFs opgaver var og er tredelte: 1) At overvge og rdgive om konomiske forhold, 2) at yde kortsigtede ln til lande med betalingsbalanceproblemer, samt 3) at yde skaldt teknisk assistance, dvs. ekspertrdgivning, til medlemmernes konomisk-politiske institutioner. I udgangspunktet blev landenes valutaer knyttet sammen i et fastkurssystem, og stabiliteten blev understttet af muligheden for finansiel assistance. Korte stabiliseringsln kom sledes i hjsdet. Men i starten af 1970'erne brd det globale fastkurssystem sammen. Dermed var ogs industrilandenes lnebehov p retur. IMF "lnekunder" blev efterhnden i stedet vkstkonomierne i Europa, Asien og Latinamerika samt de fattigste lande, hvor mange afrikanske lande blev selvstndige og derefter medlemmer af IMF. Kun 3 af IMFs oprindelige 40 medlemmer var fra Afrika, mens samtlige 53 lande i Afrika var kommet med i IMF i 1990. Nu har ogs vkstkonomierne vokset sig store, og behovet for nye ln fra IMF er strkt begrnset. De fattigste lande har stadig brug for bistand, men gldslettelsesinitiativet indebrer en vsentlig lavere gldstning til IMF. Indtil videre har IMF eftergivet glden til 22 af de fattigste og mest forgldede lande, og mange flere lande kan kvalificere sig til gldseftergivelse. Dertil kommer, at IMF aldrig har vret den vsentligste lngiver til de fattigste lande og heller ikke skal vre det. IMF er ikke en bistandsorganisation. Langsigtet lngivning med henblik p udvikling af de fattigste lande er frst og fremmest en opgave for IMFs ssterorganisation, Verdensbanken. Alt i alt belber IMFs udln sig nu til 28 mia.dollar eller ca. 165 mia.kroner, mens belbet var nsten fem gange hjere for 4 r siden. Gennem det seneste rti har bl.a. Rusland, Argentina og Brasilien vret blandt de store lntagere, men de har nu tilbagebetalt deres ln. Mange andre lande har fulgt trop, ikke mindst i Asien. Hvis man kun forbinder IMF med lngivning i krisesituationer, kunne man synes, at IMFs rolle er udspillet. Men en hovedrolle for IMF er at bidrage til, at landene ikke kommer i konomisk ufre  at forebygge kriser frem for "blot" at lse dem. Hertil kommer, at globaliseringen skaber nye udfordringer og muligheder, som ger behovet for velfungerende multilaterale institutioner som IMF. get samhandel og integration af konomierne ger smittevirkninger p tvrs af landegrnser og dermed fordelene ved samarbejde frem for egenrdighed. Tilslutningen til IMF er da ogs rekordhj med 184 medlemmer  kun overget af FNs 192 medlemslande. Men IMFs medlemslande indskyder et "medlemsbidrag" i form af en skaldt kvote, og alle vil gerne have noget for pengene. Gerne mere end muligheden for ln, nr der alligevel  og som regel uforudsigeligt hvornr  igen opstr en krise i verdenskonomien. Hvad vil medlemslandene med IMF? For industrilandene er problemstillingen ikke ny. Den globale dagsorden har gennem lang tid vret mere afgrende end godbidder til de enkelte lande. Den overordnede verdenskonomiske udvikling skal vre i fokus i IMF, hvilket bl.a. de nuvrende globale ubalancer og tilbagevendende diskussioner mellem USA og Kina om Kinas vareeksport og fastkurspolitik viser behovet for. konomisk stabilitet i verden og i de enkelte lande er i hjsdet for industrilandene, hvilket ogs er det overordnede ml for IMF. En konomisk krise kan hurtigt sprede sig i en globaliseret verden, hvilket den finansielle krise i Asien i 1997/98 viste med al nskelig tydelighed. Men gennem de seneste r er dagsordenen blevet sat af de 7 store industrilande i G7. Det var ogs G7, der frst nede til principiel enighed om gldseftergivelsen til de fattigste lande, selv om den i sidste ende skulle finansieres af alle medlemmerne af de internationale finansielle organisationer. For industrilandene m hovedinteressen vre, at IMF med sine 184 medlemslande i langt hjere grad bidrager til at fremme stabilitet i verdenskonomien og lse globale problemstillinger. For vkstkonomierne og ikke mindst de asiatiske lande betyder det mindre behov for ln og den hje konomiske vkst, at deres interesser peger i den samme retning som industrilandenes. Med vkst br ogs flge et get ansvar for verdenskonomien, ikke mindst for store konomier som Kina og Indien. Men mange asiatiske lande har formentlig stadig et traume i forhold til IMF, fordi de fandt IMFs indsats ved den finansielle krise i 1997/98 forfejlet. Uanset at man skal vre varsom med at klandre lgen for alle sine genvordigheder. Interessen for vkstkonomierne er derfor at f mere indflydelse p Valutafonden og derefter i sidste ende p de globale konomiske sprgsml. For de fattigste lande har behovet desvrre ikke ndret sig markant. Landene har fortsat brug for bistand, men typisk ikke de kortsigtede stabilitetsln, som er IMFs opgave. Alligevel spiller IMF en vigtig rolle, bl.a. ved at rdgive om makrokonomiske forhold og at yde teknisk bistand til opbygning af sunde konomisk politiske institutioner. IMF hjlper disse lande med at hndtere de makrokonomiske udfordringer forbundet med FNs 2015 ml  om bl.a. nedbringelse af fattigdom og sygdom i de fattigste lande. IMF hjlper sledes med fx hndtering af den stigende udviklingsbistand og styring af gldsudviklingen. For de fattigste lande er det derfor vigtigt at blive hrt i IMF og at have indflydelse p beslutninger, der i hj grad pvirker hverdagen for klodens fattigste. Gennem tiderne har kritikken af IMF vret markant, fx hvad angr IMFs rolle i de asiatiske lande og i de fattigste lande. Og de kritiske lande har tilbagevendende bedt om mere indflydelse i IMF. I september valgte IMFs medlemmer klart at bakke op om en reformering af IMF ved rsmderne i Singapore. Danmarks sttte kommer nppe som en overraskelse. Det er velkendt, at sm lande er mere afhngige af et bent og demokratisk samarbejde end strre lande. Medlemslandenes valg er en erkendelse af, at globaliseringen betyder, at alle lande er blevet meget afhngige af hinanden. Det er den type interesser, der bedst kan varetages af en verdensdkkende organisation som IMF, som alle har indflydelse p. Nye tider i Valutafonden? I Singapore var Danmark med til at tildele hjere kvoter og dermed hjere stemmevgt i IMF til Kina, Korea, Tyrkiet og Mexico, som efter alle mlestokke er klart underreprsenteret. Den konomiske vkst blev udmntet i hjere indflydelse. Beslutningerne i Singapore var kun et frste skridt for at sikre en mere rimelig fordeling af indflydelsen i IMF, idet en samtidig vedtaget 2rsplan skal fre til flere justeringer af landenes stemmevgte og en modernisering af beregningsgrundlaget. Der er enighed om at styrke de fattigste landes reprsentation i IMF. Mange fattige lande har haft en s lav konomisk vkst, at en umiddelbar tilpasning af stemmevgtene i IMF p grundlag af konomisk strrelse ville indebre frre stemmer. Men der var enighed om at finde andre veje til at forbedre mulighederne for, at ogs disse landes reprsentanter bliver hrt. Lige s vigtig var bekrftelse i Singapore af, at IMFs medlemslande foretrkker kriseforebyggelse frem for kriseln. Der er behov for en styrkelse af IMFs makrokonomiske og finansielle overvgning af verdenskonomien og de enkelte medlemslande. Hverken en forringelse eller status quo er godt nok, ikke kun fordi der er en latent risiko for nye konomiske og finansielle kriser, hvilket ofte glemmes i gunstige tider, men ogs fordi globaliseringen i sig selv har styrket behovet for en global hndtering af de konomisk-politiske udfordringer. Som et konkret eksempel p den nye kurs, er IMFs administrerende direktr, Rodrigo de Rato, nu i gang med at foretage skaldte "multilaterale konsultationer", hvor IMF i et forsg p at bidrage til lsning af de globale ubalancer i verdenskonomien afholder mder med euroomrdet, USA, Kina, Japan og Saudi Arabien. Der er selvsagt ikke garanti for, at konsultationerne lser de globale ubalancer  ligesom de regelmssige mder i G7 ikke har kunnet det  men dialog er det frste skridt. Konsultationerne bidrager til, at IMF fr en mere central rolle i kampen om at sikre den globale konomiske og finansielle stabilitet. For et lille land som Danmark er det positivt, at ogs de toneangivende lande i bl.a. G7 og G20 har bakket op om de multilaterale konsultationer, og at de finder sted med IMF i frersdet. Globaliseringen styrker behovet for et velfungerende internationalt konomisk-politisk samarbejde. Og allerede IMFs grundlggere, John Maynard Keynes fra England og Harry Dexter White fra USA, forstod til fulde gevinsterne for verdenskonomien ved at tackle udfordringerne i fllesskab. Mellemkrigsrenes konkurrerende devalueringer og handelsrestriktioner var ikke til gavn for nogen. Et multilateralt samarbejde kan f alle parter til at se udover egne snvre kortsigtede interesser til alles bedste. Men det krver, at alle medlemmer ogs vurderer, at de har indflydelse p IMF. Foran ligger der et stort arbejde med at gennemfre reformerne af IMF over de nste to r. Dette arbejde vil vre afgrende for, at IMF kan videreudvikle sin betydning for alle medlemslande og effektivt forflge sit vigtigste ml: Sund konomisk vkst og stabilitet i en globaliseret verden. NILS BERNSTEIN

Title: Governor Lars Rohde's speech notes at press conference on banning trade in kroner in Russia and Belarus
text: DANMARKS NATIONALBANK DANMARKS NATIONALBANK 29 March 2022 29 March 2022 SPEECH Governor Lars Rohde's keynote speech at press conference on ban on trade in kroner in Russia and Belarus THE SPOKEN WORD COUNTS Russia's invasion of Ukraine is a game-changer and we now have a war bordering on the EU. It affects the entire global community. It is a farewell to the dividends of peace and a hello to rearmament. I would like to start by making it clear that we cannot accept that the Danish krone can be misused and used for financing in Russia. The fixed exchange rate policy means that the value of the krone is fixed against the euro. The Danish krone can therefore be used as a possible replacement currency for the euro. It is crucial that the economic sanctions are effective and cannot be circumvented by Russia. That is why we also believe that it is necessary to implement the same restrictions on the use of Danish kroner as those implemented at European level for the euro. Let us turn our attention to the sanctions and the economic effects. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the EU and other G7 countries have imposed coordinated and unprecedented economic sanctions. The sanctions have had an immediate and significant impact on Russia's economy. The stock market in Russia has fallen significantly. The same applies to the Russian Ruble, which has fallen significantly in value. This has meant that the Russian central bank has had to keep the interest rate at 20 percent in order to stabilize their exchange rate. Overall, it has become significantly more expensive to live in Russia. These are just a few examples of the effects that the sanctions have caused. Several international organizations expect that the sanctions will bring the Russian economy into a deep recession this year. They estimate that Russia's GDP will fall by more than 10 percent this year. This is more than the Russian economy contracted during the financial crisis. In addition, Russia is considered to be in imminent danger of state bankruptcy as a result of the sanctions. In addition, the sanctions will have long-term implications for the Russian economy. Less trade and so-called brain drain from skilled Russians who seek to leave the country will reduce Russia's growth potential in the future. But it is not only the Russian economy that is affected by the sanctions. The war in Ukraine will also have noticeable economic consequences for both companies and households in Denmark and in our trading countries. Danmarks Nationalbank estimates that the war in Ukraine will take 1 percentage point out of growth in Denmark this year. First and foremost, the war and sanctions lead to a lower supply of energy and other raw materials. This will translate into significant price increases for e.g. energy, and thus erode households' purchasing power. Increased uncertainty about the future course of the war will also result in lower consumption and investment appetite. As a starting point, however, the Danish economy is strong. Employment is high, there is a lot of savings in the private sector and we have healthy public finances. So even though sanctions against Russia also have economic consequences for ourselves, the Danish economy may be able to withstand an expected growth slowdown. Tak for ordet.

Title: Speech at PwC banking seminar
text: SPEECH GOVERNOR LARS ROHDE'S SPEECH AT PWC BANKING SEMINAR THE SPOKEN WORD APPLIES 22. november 2021 INTRODUCTION --- Planche 1: Today's program --- Thanks for the invitation. The last year and a half has been a rollercoaster ride. It went fast on the way down, but it has also gone fast on the way up again. The same is true for the banking sector. At the same time as the pandemic took the spotlight, several reforms to the requirements for banks have been ready behind the scenes. It is now time for us to take them forward again. I will spend my time talking about the following topics: a5 The Danish economy d0 from pandemic to recovery a5 Resolution of the bailouts d0 finally we can see the end of it a5 The current situation in the banking sector d0 the banks are well prepared for the recovery a5 And finally, the European Commission's proposal on capital requirements d0 closure basel III package. FROM PANDEMIC TO RECOVERY --- Planche 2: The pandemic caused a sharp setback globally but affected countries very differently --- The pandemic d0 as we all know d0 severely brought economic downturns in recent times. Virtually all countries were hit at the same time. And globally, economic activity fell nearly 4 percent last year. Just as quickly as the rug was pulled out from under us, almost as quickly the economies regained their footing. But there has been d0 and there is Page 1 of 12 still d0 big differences in how quickly the recovery is going across countries. In an international comparison, the Danish economy has so far performed relatively well during the pandemic. When we look back at the last 18 months, the setback in Denmark was milder and the recovery faster. If I have to give my take on why, I will highlight three factors. Firstly, the outbreak of COVID-19 did not take hold in Denmark as in many of the larger European countries. This is partly thanks to quick action by the authorities. I'm thinking in particular of the first lockdown last March. The rapid response meant that restrictions became milder and more short-lived. For example, industry and construction were at no time shut down in Denmark, just as we did not use outright curfews. Secondly, a number of extraordinary public initiatives have kept the hand of Danish companies and households. It made sense at the time and helped limit the size of the setback. Third, it's harder to knock an economy off course if it's already in balance. And I believe that the Danish economy was before the pandemic hit. We found ourselves in a moderate boom with no prospect of overheating d0 with households and firms having consolidated since the financial crisis, and with solid public finances. In addition to the three, let me just mention a few other factors that also contributed to the Danish economy's immune system, so to speak. The business structure has played a significant role. Denmark's economy is not so dependent on tourism, and Danish exports are relatively robust to fluctuations in the global economy. It has also borne fruit that Denmark is one of the most digitized countries in the world. Digitized countries have generally fared better through the pandemic because technology made it easier to continue everyday life undisturbed during lockdowns. --- Planche 3: The Danish economy is back in a moderate boom --- With a look back at how the Danish economy has performed, I will now turn my gaze forward. The Danish economy is currently doing well. We are probably a pinch ahead in the recovery and the business cycle compared to our Nordic neighbours and the other countries we normally compare ourselves to. The Page 2 of 12 economic activity reached the same level as before the pandemic earlier this year. So did employment. The economy is above its cyclical level. In other words, we are back in a moderate boom. But the way out of the pandemic is uncertain and untested. This autumn, the number of infected people has increased, and the development in Europe has once again taken centre stage. Although the biggest challenges to economic activity may lie behind us, the economy will continue to depend on the development of infection. Another big question right now is: How persistent are the pressures we see in global supply chains, on prices, and on labor markets? There is no clear answer, but I will offer a few of my observations. Supply chain disruptions are the result of repeated shutdowns and reopenings, as well as various unfortunate circumstances. This kind of stop-and-go has led to shifts in our consumption and in corporate production. We expect pressure to subside as the pandemic subsides and the global balance between goods and services consumption recovers. Over the past few weeks, there have been tentative signs that the pressure is easing slightly. But the world must still arm itself with patience. International organizations expect us to enter next year before the humps are settled. As for inflationary pressures, the annual increases in consumer prices in the US and in the euro area are the highest we've seen in a number of years. Much of the price increases are due to sharp increases in energy prices and changes in taxes and duties. This implies that price pressures are temporary. For example, international organizations such as the IMF and the World Bank expect energy prices to normalize over the course of next year. But here I would like to draw a line in the sand. There is a difference between what is happening in the United States and what is happening in the euro area and at home. Prices have generally risen more in the U.S., and price increases are broader based across goods and service groups. This is partly due to the fact that the economic recovery has been stronger in the United States. And there are several indications of significant pressures on the U.S. labor market and on U.S. wages. That could lead to more sustained price pressure going forward. Page 3 of 12 In the euro area, pressure is likely to build up more slowly. Here is still significant slack in the economy and a modest wage pressure. In Denmark, there is currently no evidence that the rate of wage increase has run out. Although wage growth rates in the second and third quarters were at the highest level since the late 2000s, the overall wage increase throughout the pandemic is not significantly higher than agreed in the pre-pandemic collective bargaining agreements. When it comes to the pressure on the labour market at home, the sharp increase in employment after the reopening has made it difficult for companies to find labour. The recruitment difficulties have been compounded by the fact that many companies have had to rehire staff at the same time, and that some manpower has been retained in the health sector as testing and vaccination staff. The challenges of recruitment can increase salary pressures. That may sound worrisome d1 but we should remember that wage pressures are at the heart of a market economy. It is the mechanism that supports the fact that unproductive enterprises perish while productive enterprises remain. However, we expect that the pressure will partially subside as vacancies are filled, but that the pressure will still be at a high level. This is compatible with the Danish economy moving further into the boom. At the same time, as I said, the uncertainty is great. We are again building testing capacity, and this can contribute to prolonged pressure on the labour market. Here I have outlined some of the assumptions that underlie our forecast for the Danish economy. We estimate that some of the pressure we are seeing right now will subside and that the growth trajectory will therefore be balanced. The economy is fundamentally healthy, and Denmark's competitiveness is good. We can handle a period of capacity pressure. But the way forward is untested. Therefore, we also see a greater risk than usual that the economy may develop differently from our forecast. There is a risk that growth will be significantly stronger. What particularly concerns us is that households have built up large fortunes, and therefore the prerequisites are present for a lot of consumption to be unleashed in a short period of time. Such an unusually large jump in consumption can lead to an overheating of the economy. With that risk in mind, we have recommended that the Government should be prepared to tighten fiscal policy more than is currently envisaged. Page 4 of 12 UNWINDING OF BAILOUTS FROM THE LOCKDOWNS --- Planche 4: State bailouts also benefited banks --- As mentioned earlier, the Danish Parliament adopted far-reaching assistance schemes for the Danish business community when society was shut down due to the pandemic. Several of the measures were in the form of direct compensation to companies. As an example, the salary compensation scheme has limited the number of redundancies and helped to maintain important employee competencies in the companies. In addition, a number of deferred tax and VAT payments provided access to significant liquidity. Since the pandemic hit, the tax authorities have extraordinarily deferred payments totaling DKK 330 billion. As the deferred payments fell due, companies were given the opportunity to take out government loans of the same size. The authorities have also allowed some companies to take out bank loans with a state guarantee as collateral. The banking sector has pointed out through the pandemic that in this crisis, the sector was not part of the problem, but part of the solution. I can understand the desire to spread a joyful message. But I guess that's the least you can expect. Yet it has been in stark contrast to the situation during and after the financial crisis. The banks have not made use of the compensation schemes. On the whole, they have been ready with liquidity and loans to the private and viable companies that wanted it. So far, so good. But the trees, as you know, do not grow into the sky. It is worth remembering that without the state support, the situation would have been different d0 even for the banks. Support schemes d0 through the back door d0 also benefited the banks. Banks and mortgage lenders would have looked into higher losses if the state hadn't kept its hand under customers. -- Planche 5: Aid to weak companies hampers business dynamism d0 The pandemic, as I said, is still here. In the autumn, the contagion has once again taken hold of our society. Hopefully, the worst part is behind us. The state support is being phased out. Almost no more compensations are paid. The temporary liquidity arrangements are set to expire over the coming years. The majority of tax and VAT loans are due in April next year. Page 5 of 12 It is good that we can now see the end of support schemes. It's not healthy to be on the support d0 although it may be temporarily necessary. In line with the economic recovery, supporting business has been increasingly problematic. It is obviously expensive for the state, but also more generally for the economy, where market forces have been stymied. The terms of tax loans have been attractive. The loans are interest-free and granted without distinction to the borrower's creditworthiness. This has d0 not surprisingly d0 attracted many companies that were already weak. They may already have a hard time making it through a credit rating. Even before the pandemic, banks estimated that many of the corporate customers who have subsequently taken out tax loans were weak. A larger proportion of these companies had loans which, according to their own bank, either had a significant increase in credit risk or were directly credit-decomponeted. Some of these companies are kept artificially alive with the government tax loans. Market forces usually contribute to supporting the efficient allocation of resources. The Danish economy is characterized by being flexible and adaptable. In the years leading up to the pandemic, for the same reason, there were only a few unproductive companies - so-called zombie companies. In Denmark, unproductive companies are outcompeted and have to go bankrupt. It's important to get the business dynamics going again. This requires, among other things, that it is again the banking sector that is responsible for the provision of credit, and not the state. -- Planche 6: Banks ready to phase out liquidity support --- How expensive will the dismantling of the schemes become, then? What will happen to the companies that have accepted the liquidity support when it expires? Can they do without the support again? Or are we looking into a wave of bankruptcies? Let it be said right away: the settlement will lead to bankruptcies. Anything else would be unnatural. During the pandemic, the number of bankruptcies has been lower than in the years leading up. There must be bankruptcies in a healthy market economy, and there is a backlog in that account. It is also in your own interest that we get market forces going again. The banking sector, unlike the state support schemes, must give credit on Page 6 of 12 background of thorough credit ratings. That is your core competency. You have to stick to your credit policies, and then you have to fall what the fall is supposed to do. The alternative is that now sow the seeds of your next crisis. But I also want to calm down. As I said, the Danish economy is doing well. There are labour shortages d0 including the labour force that may have become stuck in unproductive companies during the pandemic. In addition, banks have come through the pandemic sensibly without major scratches. I'll come back to that. Banks have the capacity to take over after the tax loans have expired. The sector is well positioned to lend to viable businesses, and the particularly affected parts of the economy make up a limited part of banks' loan books. Now remember: you yourself have emphasized that this time the banking sector is not part of the problem, but of the solution. That should also be the case when tax loans start due in April next year. In parenthesis noted, the dismantling of the support schemes can still be costly for the state. The government has also acknowledged this, and DKK 2 billion has been allocated for losses on the schemes. RECENT DEVELOPMENTS IN THE FINANCIAL SECTOR --- Planche 7: Banks are currently as resilient as they are in the run-up to the pandemic --- Now back to the situation in the banking sector. Fortunately, the pandemic was never as the banking sector as feared. Today, big banks' earnings expectations are back to pre-pandemic levels d1 and in several cases above. It looked blacker last year. Right after the pandemic hit, banks accounted for significant write-downs. A significant part of the write-downs from that time represented either a downward adjustment of expectations for economic development or for discretionary management decisions. Many of the expected losses have not yet materialized. The status is that the big banks are as robust as they were before the pandemic. Their capitalization has strengthened overall during the pandemic. However, it should be noted here that the additional padding did not come completely by itself. But during the pandemic, I noticed a sudden responsiveness to good outside advice. It is gratifying that, for once, our advice was heeded. Page 7 of 12 Conversely, it is sobering that here, on the other hand, we can continue to see some large banks with limited capital adequacy. --- Planche 8: Signs of ongoing risk build-up, therefore the countercyclical buffer needs to be rebuilt --- Now that the banking sector is back to its starting point, so should the framework for the sector. Just like before the pandemic, we are now seeing signs of risk buildup in the financial system. The economic recovery was swift, and asset prices in the stock and housing markets, among others, have risen significantly. At the same time, financial conditions remain accommodative. In the years leading up to the pandemic, the Minister for Industry, Business and Financial Affairs, on the recommendation of the Risk Council, chose to start building the countercyclical capital buffer. The buffer shall ensure that institutions build up capital during periods when risks in the financial system are building up. This should make them more resilient when the risks subsequently materialise. Back then, there was a heated debate every time the buffer rate was raised. Subsequently, when the pandemic hit, the buffer turned out to be an expression of due diligence. This time, the build-up should be done faster. It's important not to get started too late. In June, the Systemic Risk Council recommended to the Minister for Industry, Business and Financial Affairs to raise the buffer to 1 per cent with effect from September 2022. The Minister followed the recommendation and I have noted that the decision has been met with if not joy, then understanding in the sector. The Risk Council has already announced that it expects to recommend another increase up to 2 per cent at its meeting in December. The council also expects that the build-up to the rate will subsequently continue up to 2.5 per cent. --- Planche 9: Wide spread of deferred amortisation contributes to the build-up of risks in the housing market --- One of the risks mentioned in particular has drawn my attention. It deserves some extra words along the way. There has recently been some debate about the housing market. During the pandemic, things moved quickly: trading activity was high, and the price level has lifted significantly. Page 8 of 12 However, I have long talked about the housing market and struck a blow for healthier structures in the market. A robust housing market is essential for a robust Danish economy. It is important both for you in the banks, for homeowners in the country and for the development of the Danish economy. If you have any doubts about the importance, I can remind you that many of the major setbacks that have occurred in the economy have come after problems in the housing market. With the Danish economy out of the crisis, now is a good time to implement measures that could strengthen resilience. When house prices rise, there is a tendency for indebtedness to rise as well. Homeowners increase debt by buying more expensive homes or taking out loans in the home equity. So far, credit growth overall has remained moderate. But growth is on the rise, especially in those areas that have seen large house price increases. In Copenhagen, there has not only been a significant boost in house prices, but also in lending. Diverse developments across areas and groups of homeowners can lead to the emergence of high-risk pockets. Add to that the fact that in the last few years, several home buyers have opted for deferred amortization. This is despite the fact that the authorities have introduced a number of loan rules. Most worryingly, a large part of the mortgage banks' new lending to highly indebted homeowners is still without repayments. In June, the Systemic Risk Council recommended to the government to further restrict access to interest-only mortgages. But unfortunately, the government has chosen to ignore that. I have to admit that it's obviously never the right time to do the right thing. BASEL III AND OUTPUT FLOOR --- Planche 10: The many capital requirements risk getting in the way of each other -- As I said, things are going well in the banking sector. Against this background, it may seem tempting for boards of directors to benefit shareholders. But banks should carefully consider how big dividends and share buybacks should be. After all, even if the shareholders' money stays in the bank, it remains their money. At the same time, more equity leads to lower risk for both shareholders and creditors d0 and thus a more robust banking system. Page 9 of 12 On the whole, there is a lot of myth-making about banks' equity. So let me be clear: Equity is not an expense. If a bank increases its own funds, its expenses do not increase. Equity is part of the financing base of any enterprise. Of course, equity must be remunerated just like other sources of financing d0 but the requirement for returns will, as I said, decrease as equity increases. Myths or not, the coming years will see demands for more capital in banks. In October, the European Commission presented its proposal for the implementation of the final part of the Basel Committee's global capital requirements package d0 also known as Basel III. The Committee introduced the first parts of the package in the aftermath of the financial crisis, and the Commission's proposal is thus the provisional end of well over a decade of new capital requirements. Capital requirements have generally been tightened. It's gratifying. There was a need for both more and better capital in the banks. But from being a solo track with one capital requirement, the set of rules has grown into an orchestra with many instruments. This makes it harder to ensure that all the instruments keep the beat. The many new requirements mean, for example, that some large institutions cannot actually use their capital buffers in a stress situation. Then they will come into conflict with the newly introduced leverage requirement. There is, in yet another new Danish word, a lack of buffer usability. The leverage requirement is an additional capital requirement which, unlike the others, does not reflect a specific statement of the risk of an institution. The demand first appeared in the international debate in the years after the financial crisis. Those years were marked by a deep distrust of banks and their risk statements globally. On the one hand, the large institutions, which had been given permission to use their own internal models for the inventory, were accused of taking the task too lightly. On the other hand, the so-called standard model used by the smaller banks was accused of a lack of risk sensitivity. So these are some of these new and old challenges that the Basel Committee and now the European Commission will address. The question then is: Will the new rules lead to more harmony? --- Planche 11: More good notes in the European Commission's proposal to implement Basel III ---- Page 10 of 12 I think the European Commission has put forward a reform that has a lot of good music in it. First and foremost, the rules on how the large institutions can use internal models are tightened. This has been necessary to ensure high credibility around their risk statements. This will and must lead to higher capital requirements. My basic position is that capital requirements and real risk must go hand in hand. The use of internal models can help an institution's capital requirements to better reflect the specific risk of the institution. But to get there, it requires both great insight and large amounts of high-quality data. Those conditions haven't always been present. Therefore, for example, it makes sense to reduce the use of internal models in areas that are difficult to model. Here I would like to interject that Europe is in fact already in the process of aligning, harmonising and tightening the requirements for internal models. Within the enhanced banking cooperation, the ECB has carried out a targeted review of internal models (TRIM) in institutions supervised over a number of years. Unfortunately, the Danish institutes have avoided such a round. But also in Denmark, the departments will soon have to live up to new European guidelines. Secondly, the rules on how risk should be calculated under the Standard Model are revisited. The key word here is more risk sensitivity. In particular, I note that in the future it will require comparatively more capital to provide mortgages with high loan-to-value rates than with low ones. And then there's the much-debated output floor. I've mentioned it on a previous occasion: That idea hasn't grown in our backyard. Such an overarching and unnuanced floor requirement is contrary to the fact that capital requirements and real risk must go hand in hand. And while much has been done to get more risk sensitivity into the underlying standard model, it never beats well-functioning internal models. It's not just me who has had opinions on the floor requirement. The prospect of particularly higher capital requirements on mortgage lending has gotten the whole of financial Denmark out of its chair and ready to beat the drum for alternative solutions. But we also have to deal with reality. The output floor has been a long time coming. It replaces an old and even more incomprehensible floor requirement that you may have already happily forgotten. And with the EU- Page 11 of 12 The Commission's proposal on European rebates on mortgage-secured mortgages and lending to unrated business customers addressed two of the problem areas highlighted by the Business Minister's expert group back in 2018. The Commission's proposal for the technical implementation of the flooring requirement d0 the so-called single stack approach d0 has the advantage of being simple. There is no need for more complexity in the rules on capital requirements. It is already a matter of keeping your tongue straight in your mouth when the instruments have to play in tandem with each other. And now that we're back at the music, let's not forget the other new one in the orchestra: the leverage ratio d0 which is a floor requirement that is not at all risk-based. In that constellation, perhaps even a binding output floor d0 with some risk sensitivity d0 is preferable? If nothing else, it has the potential to strengthen buffer usability d0 and that's sweet music to my ears. Thanks for the word. Side 4 af 12 AFVIKLING AF HJLPEPAKKER FRA NEDLUKNINGERNE --- Planche 4: Statslige hjlpepakker kom ogs bankerne til gode --- Som tidligere nvnt vedtog Folketinget vidtgende hjlpeordninger til dansk erhvervsliv, da samfundet blev lukket ned p grund af pandemien. P den baggrund kan det virke fristende for bestyrelser rundt omkring at tilgodese aktionrerne. Men bankerne br nje overveje, hvor store udbytter og aktietilbagekb skal vre. Komiten introducerede de frste dele af pakken i klvandet p finanskrisen, og Kommissionens udspil er sledes det forelbige punktum for godt og vel et rti med nye kapitalkrav. Kapitalkravene er generelt blevet skrpet. Det er gldeligt. Der var behov for bde mere og bedre kapital i bankerne. Men fra at vre et solonummer med t kapitalkrav, er regelsttet vokset til et orkester med mange instrumenter. Dermed er det blevet svrere at sikre, at alle instrumenterne holder takten. De mange nye krav betyder fx, at nogle store institutter reelt ikke kan anvende deres kapitalbuffere i en stresssituation. S vil de nemlig komme i konflikt med det nyligt indfrte gearingskrav. Der er med endnu et nydansk ord manglende buffer usability. Gearingskravet er et supplerende kapitalkrav, som  modsat de vrige  ikke afspejler en specifik opgrelse af risikoen i et institut. Kravet dukkede frste gang op i den internationale debat i rene efter finanskrisen. De r var prget af en dyb mistillid til bankerne og deres risikoopgrelser globalt. P den ene side blev de store institutter, som havde fet tilladelse til at bruge deres egne interne modeller til opgrelsen, beskyldt for at tage for let p opgaven. P den anden side blev den skaldte standardmodel, som de mindre banker anvendte, beskyldt for manglende risikoflsomhed. Det er alts nogle af disse nye og gamle udfordringer, som Baselkomiten og nu EU-Kommissionen vil adressere. De danske institutter har  desvrre  undget en sdan omgang. Men ogs herhjemme skal institutterne snart leve op til nye europiske retningslinjer.
