Det bekymrende er, at p trods af de mange redningspakker eller initiativer, er der ikke ijnefaldende tegn p forbedring  tvrtimod. Det kritiske gldsniveau er ikke et punkt eller en prcis grnse, der ns, men en udvikling, hvor tingene bliver gradvis vrre. En forsker har i en nylig undersgelse pvist, at nr bruttoglden stiger til op omkring 80-90 pct. af BNP  det vre sig den offentlige gld, virksomhedernes gld og i nogen grad husholdningernes gld - s belaster det vksten i samfundet negativt. Denne udfordring skrpes af, at de vestlige lande alle vil have demografien imod sig i de kommende mange r. De ldres andel vokser og der bliver Side 2 af 8 relativt frre til at forsrge flere. Sundhedsudgifterne vil i srlig grad vokse p grund af det stigende antal ldre. Vi er p vej ind i en periode, som ndvendigvis vil blive prget af konsolidering. Vi skal vnne os til en ny "normal", hvor der m ske en hrdere prioritering af de offentlige udgifter. *** Og s til Danmark. Efter et par kvartaler med vkst tt p nul voksede BNP igen pnt i 2. kvartal. Set under t, ser frste halvr fornuftigt ud. Men vi m forvente, at vi i hvert fald har et par noget svage kvartaler foran os. For 2011 som helhed forventer vi, at vksten ender p 1 pct. og p godt 1 pct. de kommende par r frem til 2013. Det er en nedjustering p knap  procentpoint i forhold til vor seneste prognose. Nedjusteringen har baggrund i en svagere vkst p vore eksportmarkeder og en svagere privat eftersprgsel. Bde forbrugere og virksomheder er fortsat tilbageholdende med at bruge penge. Den svagere vkst p eksportmarkederne kommer efter en rkke negative std til verdenskonomien: Rvarepriser, der var kommet meget hjt op, ulykkerne i Japan, som ikke blot ramte landet selv, men gennem den internationale arbejdsdeling ogs ramte andre dele af verdenen. Hertil kommer gldsproblemerne i Europa og USA, som jeg allerede har omtalt. Vkstudsigterne herhjemme er stort set p linje med euroomrdet, men lavere end i USA, hvor den potentielle vkst er hjere som flge af befolkningsvkst. Vkstforlbet i dansk konomi har siden rtusindeskiftet vret ujvnt. Vi startede med en lavkonjunktur efter dot-com boblen, efterfulgt af en strk hjkonjunktur, som gik over i en egentlig recession. Den er vi nu p vej ud af. Hjkonjunkturen fra 2005 til 2007 endte i en regulr overophedning af konomien. Det vil sige, at ledigheden blev presset ned til et niveau, som var klart uholdbart, og beskftigelsen til et ligeledes uholdbart hjt niveau. Det er et vigtigt budskab, at beskftigelses- og ledighedsniveauerne fra den seneste hjkonjunktur, alts fra 2005 til 2007, ikke gres til ml i den fremadrettede konomiske politik. Disse niveauer kan kun opns ved en ny overophedning. Hvad kan vi s realistisk stte os som ml frem til 2020? Det afhnger af produktivitetsudviklingen og befolkningsudviklingen. Og det er ikke strrelser, man nemt ndrer p. Danmark har i en lang periode haft en skuffende lav vkst i produktiviteten samtidig med en befolkningsudvikling, der indebrer en faldende tilgang i de arbejdsdygtige aldersklas- Side 3 af 8 ser. Det har snket vksten i konomiens potentielle produktion, det vil sige den vkst, som kan fastholdes over en lngere periode uden, at der opstr uholdbare pris- og lnstigninger. Oven i disse vkstbestemmende faktorer er kommet en recession, som yderligere trykker den potentielle produktion, i hvert fald for en periode, idet recessionen med dens arbejdslshed forringer arbejdsstyrkens kompetencer, og kapitalapparatets lbende fornyelse svkkes. For de kommende par r sknnes vksten i den potentielle produktion til omkring 1 pct. om ret. Da vi i jeblikket ligger under den potentielle produktion  der er et skaldt negativt produktionsgab - er der plads til, at produktionen i et par r vokser hurtigere end vksten i den potentielle produktion, svarende til, at det negative produktionsgab lukkes. Lukningen af det negative produktionsgab krver efter Nationalbankens opfattelse ikke det, der for tiden betegnes som vkstpakker. Vi forventer, at gabet lukkes over de kommende par r som flge af den almindelige konjunkturudvikling. At fremme den proces vil vre udtryk for et forsg p at finjustere konjunkturudviklingen, som under alle omstndigheder er meget vanskelig at time, og som i kombination med de opstemmede forbrugs- og investeringsmuligheder kan resultere i, at vi pny rammer over den potentielle produktion. Der er erfaring for, at den politiske reaktionsfunktion i s fald ikke er symmetrisk. I klart sprog: Den politiske vilje til at gribe ind, hvis det gr for hurtigt, svarer ikke helt til lysten til at skubbe p, hvis man synes, at det gr for langsomt. I et lngere perspektiv  det vil sige p den anden side af 2013 - bliver den potentielle vkst formentlig kun en smule hjere end 1 pct. om ret. Finansministeriet sknner 1,3 pct. frem mod 2020. Overgangsvis lidt mere nr, og hvis, tilbagetrkningsreformen gennemfres. Varigt hjere vkstrater kan vi kun opn, hvis det over tid lykkes os at ge vksten i timeproduktiviteten. Og det sker ikke fra den ene dag til den anden. Vi har formentlig endda udviklingen i erhvervsstrukturen imod os. Vi m derfor i en lngere periode indstille os p en lavere vkst i dansk konomi, end vi har vret vant til, og end vi mentalt har indstillet os p. Vi er p vej mod en ny normal. Det m den konomiske politik indrette sig p. Det betyder ikke ndvendigvis flere ledige, men det dmper den hastighed, hvormed velstanden stiger her i landet. Danmark er et af de lande, som i kraft af et godt udgangspunkt har kunnet lempe mest under krisen og samtidig et af de lande, hvor de planlagte opstramninger er mindst. Fokus i den konomiske stabiliseringspolitik br vre stift rettet mod holdbarheden af de offentlige finanser, s vi ikke mister markedernes tillid. Mister vi frst den, vil en negativ renteeffekt langt kunne overskygge eventuelle yderligere ekspansive tiltag. Den nuvrende meget Side 4 af 8 lave rente er med til at holde hnden under konomien for mange  bde husholdninger og virksomheder. *** Mlt p beskftigelsen har dansk konomi tabt over 150.000 job siden toppunktet i efterret 2008. Disse job er blevet tabt i lbet af meget kort tid. En stor del af disse job blev omvendt ogs vundet i lbet af relativt kort tid fra 2005 og frem. Beskftigelsestoppen i 2008 reprsenterer et historisk hjdepunkt. Det var et toppunkt, som blev net under en klar overophedning af konomien illustreret med en ledighed p under 50.000 personer, samtidig med stor import af udenlandsk arbejdskraft. En ledighed p 50.000 er langt under ethvert estimat p det strukturelle niveau, og tilsvarende m beskftigelsen og arbejdsstyrken vurderes at have vret over deres "strukturelle niveauer". Lad mig gentage: Det er bde urealistisk og uhensigtsmssigt at gre toppunktet i beskftigelsen i 2008 til en mlstning for den konomiske politik. Trods en vis stigning de seneste mneder, er ledigheden stadig moderat. Vi venter en lille stigning frem mod begyndelsen af 2012, men herefter falder ledigheden ned mod sit strukturelle niveau. * * * En stor del af beskftigelsesfremgangen under opsvinget var drevet af stigning i bygge- og anlgsaktiviteten. Byggebeskftigelsen steg med nsten 40.000, og nede i begyndelsen af 2008 sit hjeste niveau siden begyndelsen af 1970'erne. Bygge- og anlgssektoren er som bekendt meget konjunkturflsom og den ekstraordinrt store aktivitet i bygge- og anlgssektoren var et langt stykke hen ad vejen et overophedningsfnomen, som drnede ogs andre sektorer for ledige hnder. Det var klart uholdbart. Beskftigelsen i byggeriet, som i hj grad er et hjemmemarkedserhverv med kun beskeden eksport, er nu iflge nationalregnskabet tilbage p niveauet forud for hjkonjunkturen, og beskftigelsen har endog vret stigende i de frste mneder af indevrende r. Pr. 1. juni pbegyndtes en boligfradragsordning, som endnu ikke har haft lejlighed til at virke fuldt ud. Alt i alt er der ikke noget der taler for, at der skulle vre behov for at gre yderligere for at stimulere beskftigelsen i byggeriet, som ydermere kmper med betydelige produktivitetsproblemer. Det styrker ikke varigt vkst og velstand at kanalisere resurser over i sektorer med lav vkst i produktiviteten. De arbejdskraftresurser, der er blevet frigjort fra sektoren, m mest hensigtsmssigt finde ny beskftigelse andre steder. Det krver selvflgelig, at vi her i Danmark er konkurrencedygtige i forhold til udlandet. Og her har vi noget at indhente. Side 5 af 8 *** Jeg vil nu vende mig mod en enkelt af de udfordringer, den finansielle sektor str overfor i den kommende tid. Forud for den finansielle krise var likviditeten rigelig og billig. Selv sm pengeinstitutter kunne finansiere sig p de internationale finansielle markeder til fordelagtige priser og lod sig friste heraf. Det betd, at en rkke institutter - og ikke kun sm - fik op-bygget betydelige indlnsunderskud. Krisen har med al tydelighed vist, at en hj udlnsvkst finansieret af ln p de internationale finansielle markeder, er risikabel. For sm og mellemstore pengeinstitutter har den gammeldags forretningsmodel - hvor man ikke lner flere penge ud, end man fr betroet fra egne kunder - derimod vist sin styrke. Den finansielle krise trkker stadig spor, og der er fortsat et stykke vej, fr sektoren kan st p egne ben. S man kan ikke bare lne sig tilbage og afvente roligere forhold. Det er derimod ved at vre sidste udkald, og for nogle institutter vil der vre behov for at foretage helt ndvendige tilpasninger af forretningsmodellen, s de bliver levedygtige. Gldsudstedelserne med individuel statsgaranti udlber i lbet af 2012 og 2013. Udfordringen med at refinansiere denne gld forstrkes af, at flere institutter vil have behov for at optage ny gld samtidigt. For enkelte institutter udgr udstedelserne en vsentlig del af deres samlede balance. En situation, hvor et strre antal pengeinstitutter samtidigt kommer i likviditetsproblemer, kan give anledning til finansiel ustabilitet. Der er tale om en stor udfordring, som I str overfor. Og som landets centralbank har det naturligvis givet os anledning til overvejelser. Nationalbanken har derfor, som bekendt, besluttet at udvide sikkerhedsgrundlaget for de pengepolitiske ln med pengeinstitutternes udln af god bonitet. Det rejser en lang rkke af sprgsml, som vi for tiden overvejer. Jeg vil her komme ind p de vigtigste. Kan det overhovedet lade sig gre uden at komme i konflikt med negative pledge klausuler i bestende ln? Det mener vi efter konsultation af juridisk sagkundskab, da der er tale om sdvanlig centralbankvirksomhed. P den anden side kender vi ikke alle udformninger af sdanne klausuler og har ikke praktisk mulighed for at afdkke dette sprgsml fuldt ud. Det bliver derfor jeres egen opgave at sikre jer mod sdanne klausuler. Der vil blive tale om, at udln kan indg i sikkerhedsgrundlaget p lige fod med anden sikkerhed og dermed kan anvendes som sikkerhed for svel intradag som interdag kredit. Side 6 af 8 Vi overvejer derudover at indfre en lngere lbende udlnsfacilitet i Nationalbanken p baggrund af det samlede sikkerhedsgrundlag til en variabel rente. Udvidelsen trder i kraft fra 1. oktober, og der er tale om en generel ordning, som vil lbe indtil videre. Lignende ordninger kendes fra centralbanker i andre lande, herunder ogs fra den Europiske Centralbank. Udln som sikkerhed for ln i Nationalbanken er muliggjort af en ndring af vrdipapirhandelsloven, som giver mulighed for, at udln kan stilles som sikkerhed, uden at den enkelte lntager skal have besked om det. Nationalbanken kan njes med at modtage en liste over de udln, der pantsttes. Det udgr sikringsakten. Fr lovndringen var pantstning af udln i praksis meget svrt. De nrmere detaljer for ordningen er ved at blive fastlagt og vil blive meldt ud samlet, inden vi bner vinduet den 1. oktober. Udfordringen er p den ene side at udforme ordningen, s den reelt kan med-virke til at lette overgangen til en situation uden statsgarantier. P den anden side vil Nationalbanken ikke g p kompromis med, at der skal vre fuld sikkerhed bag vores udln. Det vil sledes vre et ufravigeligt princip, at det kun er udln med god bonitet, der kan belnes. Men samtidig skal der ikke opbygges et stort bureaukrati i Nationalbanken, hvor vi selv skal kreditvurdere de enkelte ln. Vi vil foretrkke at anvende den kreditvurdering, der allerede foregr i institutterne. Vi kigger i den forbindelse p Finans-tilsynets bonitetskategorier, herunder kategorien "normal bonitet", der bl.a. stiller krav om, at udlnene passes anmrkningsfrit fra kundens side. Vi er opmrksomme p, at der skal ske en oversttelse af IRB-institutternes rating-modeller til normal bonitet. For at vi kan acceptere, at vurderingen af udlnenes bonitet foretages af det enkelte pengeinstitut, skal den eksterne revisor bekrfte, at instituttet har de ndvendige forretningsgange og procedurer herfor. Vi overvejer ogs, i hvilket omfang den eksterne revisor skal erklre sig om listen over udln, der stilles som pant. Udlnenes belningsvrdi vil blive fastsat efter et haircut. Dette haircut skal sikre, at Nationalbanken kun ptager sig en ubetydelig kreditrisiko. Vi har endnu ikke lagt os fast p det prcise haircut, men i faststtelsen af haircuttet er det naturligt at skele til ECBs regler. Samtidig er det vores juridiske vurdering, at hvis et pengeinstitut kommer i solvensproblemer  og der ikke kan findes en kber - vil instituttet ende i Finansiel Stabilitet A/S  uanset om der allerede er truffet beslutning om Bankpakke 3 eller ej. Det taler for ogs at skele til vrdiansttelsesprincipper og haircuts i Finansiel Stabilitet A/S. Side 7 af 8 Vi har som sagt endnu ikke lagt os fast p det prcise haircut. S er der sprgsmlet om afgrnsningen af udln. I Danmark er en stor del af udlnene fx ydet som kassekreditter, som har et variabelt trk. Sprgsmlet er, om kassekreditter er anvendelige som sikkerhed og under hvilke betingelser? Det kunne for eksempel vre et ekstra haircut, der tager hjde for den iboende variation i kassekreditter. Det kigger vi p. Renten er en srdeles vigtig parameter. Et rentetillg til den pengepolitiske rente kan vre et effektivt styringsredskab, som kan medvirke til at give de rette incitamenter i forhold til pengeinstitutternes anvendelse af forskellige typer af sikkerhed. Heroverfor str hensynet til fastkurspolitikken, som uden sidestykke er Nationalbankens vigtigste opgave. Hvis der kommer stor dybde i anvendelsen af det nye belningsgrundlag, vil et rentetillg kunne skabe usikkerhed omkring den pengepolitiske rente. I den forbindelse spiller det en rolle, at ECB ikke anvender et rentetillg. En alternativ styringsmekanisme kunne vre et maksimum over det enkelte instituts anvendelse af sikkerhedsgrundlaget. P den anden side indsnvrer kvantitative restriktioner ordningens fleksibilitet. Endelig kort om jeres likviditetsberedskab. Vi er i tt dialog med Finanstilsynet om, under hvilke betingelser det nye belningsgrundlag kan indg i  152. Det forventer jeg vil vre fuldt afklaret forud for den 1. oktober. * * * Endelig vil vi generelt inspireret af sektoren opkrve et gebyr til dkning af vores administrative omkostninger. Lad det vre sagt med det samme: Det er ikke hensigten, at pengeinstitutter fremover skal basere deres forretningsmodel p muligheden for at belne udln i Nationalbanken. I skal heller ikke stte jer p hnderne i forhold til refinansieringen af de individuelle statsgarantier. Nationalbanken har tidligere opfordret til, at I forbereder jer p udlbet af de individuelle statsgarantier. Opfordringen glder fortsat og er ikke blevet mindre aktuel. Udvidelsen af Nationalbankens belningsgrundlag skal ikke vre en sovepude, men er tnkt som en brobygger til en fremtid uden statslige garantier. Tak for opmrksomheden. Side 8 af 8

Title: Statement at the Conference Experience with and Preparations for the Euro
text: Governor Nils Bernstein's statement at the Conference "Experience with and Preparations for the Euro" to be held from 10 to 12 May 2006 at the Raiffeisen Landesbank Oberosterreich in Linz, Austria Session 2: A View from the Outside  Effects on the Introduction of the Euro It is a great pleasure and honour to have been invited to give a view from an out-country on the effect of the introduction of the euro. Conferences like this offer an excellent opportunity for mutual exchange of experiences and discussion of issues related to monetary policy and financial sector developments. I will focus my statement on the effect of the euro for Denmark on four topics: Monetary policy, financial integration, trade integration and the requirements for fiscal policy and other economic policies. Finally, I will summarise our experience with the euro as the nominal anchor for inflation expectations within the Danish fixed-exchange-rate regime. First, let me describe the effects of the introduction of the euro on monetary policy in Denmark. Denmark maintains a fixed-exchange-rate policy vis-a-vis the euro area. Since the start of the third stage of the Economic and Monetary Union in the EU on 1 January 1999, the formal framework for the fixed-exchange-rate policy has been the European Exchange-Rate Mechanism, ERM II. Denmark participates in ERM II with a narrow fluctuation band of /- 2.25 per cent around the central rate. The central rate is a conversion of the central rate of the krone vis-a-vis the D-mark in the previous European Exchange-Rate Mechanism (ERM I), and the central parity of the Danish krone vis-a-vis the anchor has now been unchanged for more than 19 years.1 Due to this long-standing experience with a firm fixed-exchange-rate policy, the introduction of the euro has not implied any major changes for the overall monetarypolicy framework in Denmark. During its more than seven years of existence, the euro has served as a stable nominal anchor for the inflation expectations in Denmark. The fluctuations in the krone vis-a-vis the euro are now so moderate that most ordinary households and business enterprises no longer take them into consideration. On average, prices on retail goods have been broadly constant for a long period. 1 The monetary policy in Denmark is described in details in Danmarks Nationalbank (2003), Monetary Policy in Denmark. 1 During most of the ERM I period the D-mark was the nominal anchor of the Danish economy, and Germany has been Denmark's largest single export market since the late 1970s. Even though a number of other European currencies were closely pegged to the D-mark during the ERM I period, the introduction of the single currency in replacement of 12 national currencies has made the anchor more clearly visible for Danish households and business. The euro has a weight of more than 50 per cent in the effective krone-rate index compared to just above 20 per cent for Germany alone. It may also be argued that the anchor was more diffuse during the ERM I period due to the multilateral nature of the system and the widening of the fluctuation bands to /- 15 per cent in 1993. The ERM II is a so-called hub and spokes model where each participating currency has a central parity vis-a-vis the euro but not vis-a-vis the other participating currencies as they did in ERM I. Together with the narrow Danish /- 2.25 per cent fluctuation band the introduction of the euro and the transition from ERM I to ERM II have therefore made the communication of the fixed-exchange-rate policy somewhat easier. Since the introduction of the euro in 1999 the krone has been stable against the euro, close to the central rate, and it has been possible to stabilise the krone with relatively limited use of interventions in terms of both frequency and amounts. During the most recent years the monetary-policy interest rate spread has amounted to 15-25 basis points. The long-term yield spread between Denmark and Germany has virtually disappeared and even been negative in some periods. Anecdotal evidence indicates that the participants in the foreign-exchange market often take positions in the expectation of a stable krone. This contributes in itself to a stable exchange-rate development and confirms the credibility of the Danish fixed-exchange-rate policy and stable economic conditions. Let me now turn to the second topic, financial integration. The introduction of the euro has acted as catalyst for a renewed interest in financial integration in Europe  both within the euro area and between the euro area and the non-participating EU countries. However, even though the euro area is clearly Denmarks most important trading partner there has been no sign of currency substitution in Denmark. By the end of 2005 euro-denominated deposits accounted for less than 0.2 per cent of the resident households' total deposits in the Danish banking sector. Tourists can though normally make their payments in euro in Danish shops without paying unfair margins. The mortgage-credit institutes offer euro-denominated loans, but these loans accounted only for 5 per cent of the total volume of outstanding domestic mortgage-credit loans at end-2005. This should probably be viewed in light of the low interest-rate differential between Denmark and the euro area. At low interest-rate spreads, the Danish households and firms apparently find it more convenient to borrow in their base currency, i.e. in Danish kroner, since this is the currency denomination of the households' wages and salaries. 2 The last decade or so has also been characterised by some significant changes in the structure of the Danish credit-institute sector.2 The Danish mortgage-credit system has been transformed from a system based mainly on long callable fixed-interest rate mortgages to a system with many different types of loans and a high share of adjustablerate mortgages. However, the driving forces behind this development have been liberalisations and increased domestic competition. It does not seem in any significant way to be related to the introduction of the euro and the Danish fixed-exchange-rate policy vis-a-vis the euro. The period since the introduction of the euro has also witnessed a number of major cross-border mergers involving Danish banks. In 1997, the Swedish Nordbanken and the Finnish Merita formed a group into which the Danish Unibank and the Norwegian Christiania Bank were included in 2000. In 2001 the group was renamed Nordea. Nordea has considerable market shares in Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Finland and is by most standards the second largest banks in Denmark. Furthermore, in 2001 Svenska Handelsbanken acquired the Danish Midtbank, and in 2004 the Icelandic Kaupthing Bank acquired the Danish bank FIH. There has also been an increased internationalisation of the Danish banking sector through the establishment abroad of branches and subsidiaries of Danish banks. Danske Bank acquired for instance the Swedish ostgota Enskilda Banken in 1997 and the Norwegian Fokus Bank in 1999, and in 2004 Danske Bank entered into an agreement to purchase National Irish Bank (based in Ireland) and Northern Bank (based in Northern Ireland). The increased international representation in the Danish Banking sector has until now mainly involved banks from the Nordic countries. Among the Nordic countries only Finland is a member of the euro area. Sweden is a member of the EU, but is not a member of ERM II, and Norway and Iceland are not members of the EU at all. The structural changes in the Danish banking sector during the last decade do therefore not seem to be related to the introduction of the euro in any significant way. Rather, the development has been driven by some of the "traditional" factors that motivate crossborder mergers and acquisitions in the banking industry such as cost reductions due to scale economies. In view of the still relatively low level of cross-border mergers and acquisitions activity within the euro area-banking sector in general, the absence of major cross-border mergers into the Danish banking sector by euro area banks does not appear to be a result of Denmark being outside the euro area. Nor are there any indications that the level of financial integration as measured by the development in the number of branches and subsidiaries of foreign banks is lower in Denmark than in the euro area. 2 Cf. Thomsen, J. (2005), Experience of Danish Credit Institutions in ERM2, Banni vestniks Journal for Money and Banking, vol. 54, July-August, pp. 78-82. 3 My third topic is the effect of the euro on trade integration. Empirical evidence suggests that launch of the single currency has increased the intra-euro area trade.3 Furthermore, there are no indications that the euro area member states are trading less with countries in the rest of the world. However, due to the relatively short time span since the introduction of the euro such empirical studies should always be interpreted with caution. In theory one should expect the introduction of the euro has also had a positive effect on the Danish export sector. The unification of 12 currencies into a single currency has reduced the exchange-rate uncertainty and other costs faced by the Danish exporters. Danish hourly wage costs are among the highest in the world, and the gap to Denmark's competitors has widened in the last decade. Despite of this, exports have fared well, and in 2005 Denmark had a surplus equivalent to around 5 per cent of GDP on external trade in goods and services. 4 This is also a large surplus by international standards. The current-account surplus, which in addition to goods and services includes interest on the external debt and current transfers, showed a surplus of around 2.5 per cent of GDP in 2005. However, it is difficult to trace any effect of the introduction of the euro on Denmark's foreign-trade relations due to some other major structural tendencies. Denmark operates one of the world's largest merchant fleets, and the sea freight exports have more than doubled in less than ten years. Shipping is now the second-largest export sector after the manufacturing industry.5 An increased production of oil and gas from the Danish North Sea fields also contributes significantly to the surplus on the balance of goods and services. My last topic is the requirements for fiscal policy and other economic policies under a fixed exchange-rate regime vis-a-vis the euro. A fixed-exchange-rate policy implies that the stance of monetary policy is from time to time out of line with domestic short-term cyclical needs. When the key monetary-policy interest rates in Denmark are closely linked to euro-area interest rates, there is no room for domestic stabilisation by means of monetary policy. This problem might appear particularly severe in Denmark, where the business cycle during the last two decades or so often seems to have been negatively correlated with the cyclical conditions in Germany and the euro area. However, in light of the consistent Danish fixed-exchange-rate policy it is also possible to draw a completely opposite conclusion: cyclical divergence is immaterial to the success of a 3 Cf. e.g. the survey in Pedersen, A. M. (2004), Currency Unions and Foreign Trade, Danmarks Nationalbank Monetary Review, 4 2nd Quarter, pp. 35-50. Cf. Beier, N. C. and Pedersen, E. H. (2005a), Wages, Competitiveness and the Balance of Payments, Danmarks Nationalbank 5 Monetary Review, 1st Quarter, pp. 43-60. Cf. Beier, N. C. and Pedersen, E. H. (2005b), Sea Freight and the Danish Economy, Danmarks Nationalbank Monetary Review, 4th Quarter, pp. 41-56. 4 fixed-exchange-rate policy provided that the fiscal policy and other economic policies are in line with the requirements of a fixed-exchange-rate regime.6 In the Danish case two fairly general experiences has been seen regarding the relationship between monetary policy and fiscal policy in a fixed-exchange-rate regime: First there has been an unconditionally willingness to subordinate monetary policy to the exchange-rate strategy in order to get a stable exchange rate. Secondly a mediumterm horizon in the annual fiscal budget planning process without ad hoc based and short-sighted changes in the fiscal policy contributes to an environment that is supportive to the fixed-exchange-rate policy.7 Denmark is subject to the objectives and requirements of the Stability and Growth Pact on equal terms with euro area member states, although no sanctions are imposed in case of non-compliance. However, being a satellite  and not the core  within the European exchange-rate cooperation, the fiscal policy in Denmark has to be at least as prudent  if not even more  if a credible fixed-exchange-rate regime is to be maintained. Today the macroeconomic fundamentals of the Danish economy are sound and fairly robust: Low inflation, surpluses on the current account as well as on the general government budget, and a relatively low level of unemployment. However, this has not always been the case! Today's firm commitment to a fixed exchange rate in Denmark has its background in bad macroeconomic policies and, consequently, poor performance of the Danish economy in the 1970s and the beginning of the 1980s. It was the switch to a stability-oriented fiscal policy and a firm fixed-exchange-rate policy during the 1980s that let the Danish economy on a path of stable economic development as well as low and stable inflation.8 The political situation in the 1970s was characterised by frequent elections and shortterm orientation of the macroeconomic policy. This resulted in a stop-go nature of the fiscal policy with frequent "packages". When the first oil crises came in 1973 Denmark had already experienced a deficit on the current account of the balance of payment for each consecutive year since 1963 leading to a limited room of manoeuvre in economic policy. Furthermore, the labour market system was based on automatic inflation indexation of wages. This implied a more or less direct feed of the oil price shocks into wages and prices. The 1970s saw a broad range of economic policy interventions, but without clear success. Unemployment was increasing rapidly9, government deficits were approaching 10 per cent of GDP, the balance of payments deficit persisted, and inflation was running at double-digit numbers. In principle, a fixed-exchange-rate policy was 6 Cf. Jensen, H. F. (2001), Costs and benefits of ERM II: The Danish experience, in: National Bank of Poland (2001), The Polish Way 7 to the Euro, Conference 22-23 October 2001, pp. 252-262. Cf. the background paper "The relationship between fiscal policy and monetary policy in a fixed exchange rate regime" to the 8 speech given by Governor Jens Thomsen at the Central Bank of Cyprus on 24 November 2003. An elaboration of the origin of today's fixed-exchange-rate regime in Denmark is found in Christensen, A. M. and J. Topp (1997), Monetary policy in Denmark since 1992, in: Monetary policy in the Nordic countries: Experiences since 1992, BIS Policy 9 Papers, No. 2, pp. 5-23. In particular if one abstracts from an early retirement scheme introduced in 1979. 5 pursued within the European exchange-rate co-operation, but the krone was devaluated several times against the Deutsche mark during the second half of the 1970s and the early 1980s. Therefore, de facto the exchange rate did not serve as the economy's "nominal anchor". As the result of high inflation and lack of credibility, long-term central-government interest rates reached more than 20 per cent in the beginning of the 1980s and the long-term interest-rate differential between Denmark and Germany was above 10 per cent. The government debt increased rapidly, and a fear that Denmark was on the verge to state bankruptcy began to rise. In the early 1980s, a radical change in policies took place after a shift in government. In relation to a change of government in September 1982 the incoming government declared that devaluation would no longer be considered as an economic-policy instrument. This was subsequently followed by a significant tightening of the fiscal policy and an abolition of the automatic cost-of-living adjustment of wages. The promise to pursue a firm fixed-exchange-rate policy was soon put to a serious test when Sweden  one of Denmark's largest trading partners  devalued its currency by 16 per cent one month later. Denmark did not devalue. This and the other tightening measures meant that the credibility of Denmark's fixed-exchange-rate policy was soon enhanced.10 In the following years the government budget improved, and the inflation and interest-rate differentials to Germany fell significantly. The medium-term horizon in the Danish fiscal policy framework during the last two decades or so has been crucial for the conduct of the fixed-exchange-rate policy. The discretionary fiscal policy measures carried out within this framework have also often contained elements of structural policy. Hereby consideration has been taken to both the short-term macroeconomic stabilisation as well as to the medium-turn and long-term growth-potential of the economy. The most important permanent structural element during the second half of the 1980s was a tax reform that lowered the tax on capital income  positive or negative  and thus the value of the full deductibility of interest payments.11 Other economic policies have also contributed to a more flexible economy with better incentive structures. During the period 1994-2000 several labour market reforms has played an important role in reducing structural unemployment. The reforms have effectively reduced the maximum-benefit-duration period from 8-9 years in 1994 to 4 10 It should be mentioned that the transition to a firm fixed exchange rate policy in Denmark was not fully completed until 1987. The Deutsche Mark was revalued several times within the ERM in the period 1983-1987, including vis-a-vis the krone, but not on the initiative of Denmark. Since 12 January 1987 there has been no change in the central rate of the krone vis-a-vis the D- 11 mark and subsequently euro. Before the tax reform in the mid-1980s (effective from 1987) the tax value of interest rate deductions were up to 73 per cent. After the maximum tax value of interest rate deductions was lowered to 51 per cent. A further reduction of the tax deductibility of interest payments was implemented during the 1990s. The tax value of interest rate deductions reached the current level of 33 per cent in 2001. 6 years in 2000. Furthermore more intensive use of activation measures (job training and education for unemployed, etc.) has been implemented.12 Let me finalise this speech by concluding that the introduction of the euro has been successful and that the ERM II works well as the formal framework for the Danish fixed-exchange-rate policy. In practice Danish business and Danish trade unions have become perfectly aware that Denmark is in a price stability environment that is anchored by ERM II-participation. A few may even know the ECB's definition of price stability. More will know that the objective of price stability is taken serious by the ECB. For the past 15 years or so inflation in Denmark has been in accordance with this definition without an independent monetary policy to support it and with a fiscal policy that is medium-term oriented and sound as well, but normally not geared to manage short term inflation objectives. In short scientific language: ERM II has helped anchoring inflation expectations at 2 per cent. Thank you very much for your attention. 12 Cf. Gaard, S. and Kieler, M. (2004), Two decades of structural reform in Denmark: a review, Oesterreichische Nationalbank 32nd Economic Conference, May 27 and 28, Vienna. 7

Title: Answers to questions about mortgage lending of adjustable-rate bonds
text: Governor Nils Bernstein's answers to questions about mortgage lending of adjustable-rate bonds Question from Jyllands-Posten: about the possibility for banks and mortgage banks to mortgage adjustable-rate bonds in Danmarks Nationalbank? Reply from Governor Nils Bernstein: "Danmarks Nationalbank does not keep its hand under the housing market. If interest rates rise on adjustable-rate bonds, homeowners will have to pay. This is also the case even if interest rates rise extraordinarily much, possibly in the context of a currency crisis. It is true that adjustable-rate bonds are included in our loan-to-value basis. But it targets usual monetary policy operations. If we find that the system is being abused in the sense that the mortgage option is used to keep the hand under the market, we will intervene and, if necessary, have a comradely talk with the institute. We've done that before. The loan-to-value option shall not be included as a prerequisite for a particular mortgage product." Page 1 of 1

Title: Tale: Outside the euro in the financial crisis - the Danish experience.
text: Speech by Governor Nils Bernstein at Copenhagen Business School, 22 March 2010 Check against delivery DANMARKS NATIONALBANK The Danish krone during the crisis It is now my turn to discuss how Denmark  as a non-euro area EU, ERM II member state  has navigated through the financial crisis. The really interesting question is, perhaps, what difference it would have made, if we had been part of the euro area. That is difficult to say, as other things might not have been equal. For example: who knows whether Denmark's economic policy would have been the same, if we had not been governed by the fixed-exchange-rate policy? (Chart 2) Since the euro was rejected in a referendum in 2000, it has been a widespread view, that Danish membership of the euro area is first and foremost a political question. Combined with the other three opt-outs, the issue is whether Denmark wants to participate fully in the important political decisions on the future of Europe. From a purely economic point of view, Danish participation in the euro can be expected to lead to slightly lower interest rates, a small increase in foreign trade and lower transaction costs. In normal, calm periods, interest rates will only be marginally lower than under the current fixed-exchangerate regime. Over a longer horizon, adopting the euro will have a certain positive overall effect on growth in Denmark. But it is difficult to quantify this effect, which is hardly likely to be felt in the short term. Danmarks Nationalbank's rough estimate is that, in the long term, euro area membership would permanently boost GDP by between 0.5 and 1 per cent. Since the introduction of the euro in 1999, Denmark has performed well outside the euro area. This is due to our long-standing stability-oriented economic policy with a focus on medium-term objectives and structural reforms, not least in the labour market. It is important that Denmark continues along this path  even if we eventually join the euro. The current economic policy discussion should be viewed in that context. 2 All along, we have been aware that the advantages of euro area membership would be accentuated in periods of financial turmoil. The lessons from the financial crisis have more than confirmed this. The world before Lehman fell The seeds of the financial crisis were sown already in July 2007, when the rating agencies decided to downgrade bonds issued to finance sub-prime mortgages. This increased uncertainty in the markets. The effect soon spread to more creditworthy securities. In the money markets, the uncertainty was reflected in a widening spread between collateralised and uncollateralised money-market loans. The confidence crisis developed in stages over the latter part of 2007 and up to September 2008. In August 2008, Danmarks Nationalbank with a government guarantee and the Danish Contingency Association acquired Roskilde Bank on the brink of collapse. This was an important medium-sized bank, with a significant funding in foreign currencies. This should be seen in the light of a Danish banking sector with a total deposit deficit of 600 billion kr. Danmarks Nationalbank's primary reason for stepping in was to avoid a systemic crisis. In that situation we couldn't accept doubts that loans to Danish banks would be honoured. Capital outflows from smaller areas The financial crisis intensified from mid-September 2008 after the collapse of Lehman Bros. Risky assets such as shares and credit bonds plummeted. The heightened uncertainty prompted investors to seek safe havens. This led to portfolios shifts towards more secure assets. There was a worldwide trend for foreign exchange to flow out of small capital areas and into larger ones. In other cases, portfolios were actually closed by investors who had bought assets, financed by short-term loans in foreign currency  such as dollars  that were subject to regular renewal. Investors who were unable to obtain renewed funding in early October 2008, when the international loan markets1 froze, were compelled to sell assets immediately, regardless of the price. The interest-rate increases by Danmarks Nationalbank, - which I will return to - did not have any impact on investors, who were forced to sell out, when the global loan markets contracted. Liquidity constraints  the need for euro and dollars Initially the money-market turmoil was strongest in the dollar market, and many financial institutions outside the USA experienced a shortage of dollar 1 The interbank market for uncollateralised lending, the CP market, and the FX swap market. 3 funding. As the crisis escalated, the euro market was eventually also affected. In the spring of 2008, the ECB established a swap line with the Fed, with a view of lending dollars to euro area banks. The majority of the Danish banks did not have access to this facility. Many financial institutions in Europe already depended on short-term funding in both dollars and euro. As a result, most of them were on the same side of the order flow. Moreover, the usual dollar funding channels dried up, to a certain extent because the suppliers themselves had an increasing need for dollars, which in itself was partially due to mounting concerns about counterparty risk. This put pressure on both the demand and supply sides of the dollar market. Impact on the Danish krone The dysfunctional markets for, primarily, euro and dollars had a considerable impact on the market for Danish kroner. Danish banks needed access to funding in euro and dollars; a need that was to some extent satisfied by issuing CP and trading in the FX swap market. In principle, the use of FX swaps has no impact on the exchange rate of the krone. But as the crisis evolved, funding and hedging in the FX swap market became expensive, and the spot markets became a more attractive source of foreign exchange. As a result, the krone came under pressure. Developments in the euro area were particularly significant for the krone. In late September and early October 2008, extensive demand for euro liquidity meant that the average allotment rate, in the ECB's weekly main refinancing operations, exceeded Danmarks Nationalbank's lending rate. In other words, the interest-rate spread turned negative. Usually the spread is positive to compensate for the exchange-rate risk. In early October, just before the ECB began to offer unlimited liquidity at a fixed rate of interest (the lending rate), the ECB's average allotment rate was observed to be a full 39 basis points higher than Danmarks Nationalbank's lending rate. As a result, the krone came under pressure. Speculation against the krone At the peak of the crisis, many market rumours were circulating, claiming that Danmarks Nationalbank was in difficulties. A large foreign bank wrote that Danmarks Nationalbank no longer had any reserves for intervention and that the exchange rate was approaching its limit, i.e. a deviation of 2.25 per cent from the central rate. If that situation does occur, the ECB has an obligation to intervene in support of the krone. So far this has never happened. The ERM II agreement includes a provision on unlimited intervention credit 4 between the ECB and the participating central banks, including Danmarks Nationalbank. Such credit must be repaid within three months. There was extensive market focus on the size of our foreign-exchange reserve. More specifically, a limit of DKK 100 billion was mentioned for Danmarks Nationalbank to be able to defend the krone. The currency positions of the Danish banks in the market were, on the whole, not unfavourable to the krone (Chart 3). The banks reduced their market positions, to more or less neutral levels, but never held long currency positions, when Danmarks Nationalbank made intervention purchases to support the krone. This reflected some degree of confidence on the part of the Danish banks, that Danmarks Nationalbank would be able to observe the unofficial de facto band. There was anecdotal "evidence" that certain foreign investors were speculating against the krone (Chart 4). The first speculation rumours concerned options, with a strike price outside the implicit narrow band around the central rate. For example, a large hedge fund was reputed to have bought options against the krone weakening. The size of the financial backing behind this speculation is, however, uncertain. "Out-of-the-money" options involve little cost, but hedging by sellers of such options may have led to considerable sales of kroner. Generally speaking, international speculators had a certain interest in testing the strength of the support for the fixed-exchange-rate policy. This caused further uncertainty about the krone. Intervention The spring of 2008 saw gradual weakening of the krone, and Danmarks Nationalbank responded by intervening  to a limited extent (Chart 5). As late as in July 2008, we mirrored the ECB when it raised its key interest rates. Danmarks Nationalbank took the usual course of action when the krone came under pressure. First, we sell foreign exchange for kroner. If this has not had the desired effect after some time, we raise interest rates. To counter the tensions in the dollar market, Danmarks Nationalbank intervened in the FX swap market on 18 September, i.e. before the crisis really erupted. Dollars were offered against kroner for a total of DKK 3 billion with a maturity of 7 days. Likewise, in early October, Danmarks Nationalbank intervened in the euro market, offering euro for a total of DKK 17 billion with maturities of 7 days and 1 month. Danmarks Nationalbank had not previously intervened in the FX swap market in recent times. 5 The intervention in the FX swap market turned out to have only a temporary impact on the market. The Danish market for euro and dollar liquidity is considerable, and intervention via the FX swap market also entails drawing substantial amounts on the foreign-exchange reserve. Pressure on the krone prompted Danmarks Nationalbank to intervene heavily directly in the foreign-exchange market in late September and the first weeks of October. Intervention sales of foreign exchange totalled DKK 1 billion in September and reached a monthly all-time high of DKK 64 billion in October. There were considerable day-to-day fluctuations. On some days, intervention purchases approached DKK 15 billion. Intervention by Danmarks Nationalbank was concentrated in the periods around 7 and 24 October, when we raised our interest rates. We could literally see our reserves pouring out of our coffers. I felt like driving a car without brakes. Monetary-policy interest rates Sustained strong pressure on the krone led Danmarks Nationalbank to increase monetary-policy interest rates on several occasions in October (Chart 6). On 7 October, the lending rate was raised by 0.4 percentage point. The following day, the ECB reduced its key interest rate by 0.5 percentage point, thereby widening the interest-rate spread once more. It was very unpleasant to have to raise interest rates and accept a widening spread at a time when other central banks were lowering theirs to support the financial sector. The only way to interpret this was that something must be rotten in the state of Denmark! But we had no other choice. These interest-rate increases had no short-term impact on the krone. In the hours immediately after Danmarks Nationalbank's announcements, the krone weakened further and intervention sales of foreign exchange were necessary. The interest-rate instrument did not have the desired effect. Few domestic counterparties bought kroner in response to the interest-rate increases. On 15 October, the ECB introduced full allotment in its weekly main refinancing operations, and the pressure on the krone eased temporarily. Euro area banks were now able to obtain sufficient liquidity from the ECB, which was reflected in market spreads to the euro area. On 24 October, further capital outflows  driven by foreign investors  led Danmarks Nationalbank to raise interest rates further. Subsequently, the spread to the euro area was 1.75 percentage points, which was enough to make domestic insurance and pension companies in particular turn towards the Danish kroner once again. 6 Issuance of CP The substantial intervention sales in October drained the foreign-exchange reserve. In previous crises, it had been possible immediately to increase the reserves by issuing short-term CP loans and later replacing these by longerterm loans if necessary. Experience from the autumn of 2008 showed that we, on the behalf of the government, could not issue sufficient CP at the peak of the crisis. Furthermore, it took quite a while before the government was able to raise longer-term foreign loans at an acceptable price. We did not want to borrow at a rate that signalled an urgent need for foreign exchange. The crisis confirmed the old saying that money is hardest to come by when you need it the most. By 15 October, the foreign-exchange reserve had been reduced to DKK 104 billion, the lowest level in ten years (Chart 7). How long would it take before the situation would begin to improve? After 14 October, Danmarks Nationalbank was finally able to issue CP on behalf of the Danish government (Chart 8). This continued on an almost daily basis throughout the rest of 2008. Other initiatives We managed to keep our head above water, but this was not solely due to our own intervention and interest-rate increases. A number of other factors played an important role. The shortage of euro and dollar liquidity, combined with dysfunctional financial markets  notably the frozen interbank market  led the ECB and the Fed to establish swap lines with other central banks, including Danmarks Nationalbank. Via these swap lines, national central banks were able to offer euro and dollar liquidity to domestic banks. Danmarks Nationalbank established a swap line with the Fed on 24 September 2008. The need for this facility was highlighted by the fact that volumes offered in our dollar auctions were drawn upon in full. The swap line with the Fed  totalling USD 15 billion  was fully exercised after three auctions. On 27 October 2008, Danmarks Nationalbank and the ECB established an equivalent swap line for 12 billion euro. Although this limit was not reached, the security of Danish banks in relation to euro funding was undoubtedly boosted. The swap facility has been very helpful in addressing the banks' liquidity needs. It should be emphasised that this facility did not affect the foreign-exchange reserve or support the krone directly. It supported the krone indirectly by calming the market for FX swaps; and the ECB's backing sent a strong positive signal to the market. 7 Issuance of 30-year government bonds was another key factor. There was extensive demand in the Danish market for domestic bonds with longer maturities  particularly on the part of pension funds, which needed to hedge their long-term commitments. In November and December 2008, the Danish government took the extraordinary step of issuing 30-year bonds. As a result, Danish pension funds restructured their portfolios from foreign to domestic securities. This supported the krone. Last  but not least  it was equally important that the government, at short notice in early October 2008, decided to issue a guarantee for all deposits with and loans to Danish banks. It is impossible to say exactly what the impact of this measure, known as Bank Rescue Package I, was. Non-residents withdrew krone deposits totalling DKK 70 billion from Danish banks in October 2008. This package contributed strongly to keeping capital outflows during the crisis at a manageable level. Timing and determination were essential elements in terms of ensuring confidence in Danish banks. As I see it, the Danish banks would have been far worse off without this guarantee, and Danmarks Nationalbank's ability to keep the krone stable might have been called into doubt. But while the government provided bank guarantees totalling around 2.5 times Denmark's GDP, the potential claims on the foreign-exchange reserve increased. If a bank failed, the guarantee might be called in at short notice. If loans had been raised abroad, this would have affected the foreignexchange reserve. Therefore, the need to increase the reserve was even more important. The turning point in the krone crisis came in late October, when stabilisation of the krone market enabled us to buy back foreign exchange. Largescale buy-backs took place from 4 November 2008. Partial normalisation of the situation made it possible for us to follow suit when the ECB lowered its interest rates by 0.5 per cent on 6 November. In December, the monetary-policy spread gradually narrowed by a total of 0.75 percentage point. Conclusion (Chart 9) During 2009, Danmarks Nationalbank gradually reduced interest rates so that the spread to the euro area narrowed again. Today, the monetary-policy spread is only 5 basis points. But the actual money-market spread is around 50 basis points, mainly due to the substantial amount of excess liquidity in the Euro area. 8 Over the last year, Danmarks Nationalbank has built up the foreignexchange reserve to a much higher level than it used to be. It now exceeds DKK 400 billion. The dollar swap line with the Federal Reserve has expired. So, in many ways the situation has normalised. But we have learnt what it means to be outside the euro area when you are a small economy with a fixed-exchange-rate regime. This should give food for thought. We made it through. I will not ponder upon  at least not openly  what could have happened if speculation against the krone hadn't subsided. We are still in a fixed exchange rate regime. As recent developments have shown, euro membership is not  and should not  be a guarantee for easy access to foreign borrowing. That depends on one's ability to keep its own house in order. There is no substitute for sound economic policy inside or outside the euro. But when you are a small open economy and a storm of this magnitude sweeps through the markets  you would rather not have your own currency to worry about. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech at the Danish Bankers Association's annual meeting
text: Speech by Governor Nils Bernstein at the Danish Bankers Association's annual meeting, Monday 30 November 2009 The spoken word applies DANMARKS NATIONALBANK The recession in the world economy now appears to be over. Growth is again positive in most OECD countries. World trade is slowly getting going again after a sharp dip. As far as Denmark is concerned, we currently only have a preliminary overview of how things went in the first half of the year. How it has gone since early summer, we do not have a full overview of yet. But according to Danmarks Nationalbank's best estimates, Denmark is now also slowly emerging from the recession, which started around the turn of the year to 2008. In this country, we reached a mid-year low in total production, which was more than 7% lower than the last peak in 2007. Most forecasts show that we will only slowly move forward again, and in our estimation, we will reach the level of production we left off in 2007 at the earliest. With large spare business capacity, unemployment will grow in the next year or more. Much will depend on when consumers get their desire to buy back and how much exports will again contribute to growth. Right now, it is especially the extensive stimulus packages here and abroad and inventory adjustments that have halted the decline, pushing the economy forward again. We have yet to see if progress will become self-sustaining when growth packages and expansionary fiscal and monetary policies end. There is an unusual amount of uncertainty attached to the process in the coming years  a lot can go wrong  but it is our best estimate that it will now progress slowly. One of the challenges we are up against is the financing of the large government deficits, which are the counterpart to the expansionary fiscal policy in this country and abroad. If the rollback of expansionary fiscal policy happens too late, fears of debt spirals and inflation could lead to rising interest rates. If, on the other hand, the rollback occurs prematurely, financial markets could again come under severe pressure. New aid packages may be needed. This balancing act is very much a matter of gaining investor confidence in the viableity of future economic policy. 2 If confidence fails, interest rates will rise at the risk of creating a downward spiral with larger budget deficits and increased interest expenses. The risk of this can dampen growth. It is therefore essential to draw up a sustainable plan for the consolidation of public finances. And a sustainable and credible plan requires not only agreement on the ends  but also on the means. * * * Now that the financial crisis is returning, it makes sense to look at the process in perspective. And think about what lessons can be drawn from events. We are talking about the most serious financial crisis since the 30s, so it is obvious that thick and learned books will be written about the reasons for this. I just want to note today that a strong economic recovery in the United States, helped in the first place by tax cuts and a very accommodative monetary policy, spread to the rest of the world at the same time as the Chinese economy grew in importance. The U.S. economy was strongly driven by the optimism and buying appetite of the U.S. consumer, while the Chinese economy gained its strength through impressive export growth and massive business investment. The United States suffered a very significant current account deficit, which was financed to a significant extent by surpluses in China, and in the oil-producing countries, which benefited from strong growth in the world economy. Liquidity in the financial system worldwide became cheap and abundant. The hunt for returns took many forms, and the risk appetite was great. * * * This development also affected us here in Denmark. As a small and open economy, we benefited from the international recovery. The abundant liquidity of the international capital markets meant that banks could supplement the traditional deposits with borrowing abroad, as the basis for rapidly increasing lending. In addition to traditional commercial finance, the development was characterized by an upswing in new construction and modernization  not least in the residential area. The favourable economic conditions also meant that activities in the financial sector increasingly went beyond the borders of the country, where bank purchases were carried out on an unprecedented scale. The increasing borrowing of many banks abroad made the sector dependent on continued access to international liquidity. The plentiful and inexpensive loan options gave extra power to the recovery. The Danish boom was fuelled by exports, private consumption and investment, and at the same time had a run-in of public consumption. The Danish economy reached the limit of its own capabilities at the end of 2007, independent of the incipient financial crisis, and was independently on the decline when Lehmann Brothers collapsed in September 2008, peddling the financial markets in shock and giving the impetus to the economic crisis. The decisive financial shock came to us from the outside. But we ourselves had made ourselves vulnerable when the crisis hit. We cannot prevent new crises, but we can and must learn from what we have been through. 3 When we look back over the past half dozen years, it is obvious to everyone that the development in the real estate market in Denmark reinforced the ups and downs of the business cycle. And thus contributed to the difficulties we are struggling with today. Danish house prices rose almost continuously from 1993 to 2007. The increase was extraordinarily strong in 2005 and 2006. The growth in property prices during the recent recovery can be largely explained, up to 2005, by low interest rates  especially at the short end  loans with deferred amortisation, growth in disposable incomes, falling unemployment and tax breaks. But the price increases became self-reinforcing. In anticipation of continued price increases, a new home was purchased before the old one was sold. Property became an object of speculation. Driven by expectations and the concurrent cyclical recovery, the price of semi-detached and terraced houses rose from the beginning of 2005 and a year onwards by almost 25%. The increase in the metropolitan area was somewhat higher. A boost of that magnitude cannot be explained by the underlying economic conditions alone. Expectations played an independent role. The price increases in the real estate market provided increased fuel for the recovery. Free values grew and gave consumers extra purchasing power. We saw a violent expansion of construction with clear signs of overheating. And last but not least, lending grew extra strongly in financial institutions that were particularly committed to the real estate sector. It is characteristic that under the shelter of developments in the real estate market, activities thrived that are now being investigated by the police. * * * The reversal of these imbalances is amplifying the impact of the international recession. The fall in prices in the property market has not only hit the construction sector, but also intensified consumption decline when compared to other countries. And if we look at the financial sector, it is characteristic that the financial institutions that have become distressed are to be found in the first place among those that pursued the most expansionary lending policy in the real estate market. What, then, can we learn from it? A market economy will never be crisis-free. We must accept that there are periods of setbacks. As a small, open economy, we cannot guard against the sudden failure of foreign demand and exports falling almost 20 per cent in six months, as has happened. But we can aim for an economic policy that does not independently amplify the fluctuations in the business cycle. We haven't been good at that. During the boom, economic policy was ongoing and amplified the recovery. 4 Not enough was done to hold back. We pushed the economy into higher gear, so to speak, in a situation where the wheels were already well under way, partly due to a low level of international interest rates. And overall, we in Denmark gave the housing market too much tailwind. It is the imbalances that were created globally and at home during the boom that we are now grappling with. * * * In just under a year, as you know, the state's guarantee for all deposits and loans to banks in Denmark expires. The scheme is the most far-reaching and necessary step that was taken in Denmark when the financial crisis really swept over us in the autumn of 2008. A guarantee of this magnitude must necessarily have a short lifespan, and we must now adapt and plan for the scheme to expire. No one should speculate that there will be an extension. The scheme will be replaced by an increased deposit guarantee of DKK 750,000, and there is the possibility, until the end of next year, to take out guarantees for stand-alone loans with effect until the end of 2013. With a deposit guarantee of DKK 750,000, the vast majority of private depositors will be covered. The temporary scheme of guaranteeing stand-alone issuances is immediately most accessible to larger financial institutions. Danmarks Nationalbank is aware that the sector is working with umbrella schemes, where several smaller institutions can join forces on joint issuances, based on state guarantees. Danmarks Nationalbank welcomes these initiatives and the possibility of including such issuances in our loan-to-value basis. As far as we can judge, larger deposits and other financing have to some extent found their way to some financial institutions in the lee of the general state guarantee. Some adjustment is to be expected with the expiration of the warranty. However, for the overall credit intermediation system, it is important that the institutions concerned exercise due diligence and obtain other financing in good time or reduce their lending profits. The larger institutions must assume their responsibility to make the money market work smoothly again. The financial crisis has clearly demonstrated that banking is not a normal commercial activity. As a counterpart to the comprehensive banking packages, I expect banks to live up to their social responsibility and importance and actively contribute to making markets work without a government guarantee. * * * It is part of the picture of the future financial architecture in Denmark that the legislation on "Financial Stability's" access to purchases of banks expires at the same time as the general state guarantee. In my opinion, the State's takeover of distressed financial institutions has worked as intended, i.e. the banking activity in relation to the traditional customers has continued as far as possible, even though the share capital and other subordinated capital have been lost. 5 Access to purchases by "Financial Stability" should be continued  but without any guarantee other than the statutory deposit guarantee. In order for the financial system to function without excessive risk-taking, not only owners of responsible capital must be able to suffer losses  but also large depositors and other lenders without collateral. The important thing is not the survival of the financial institution, but the continuation of the activities. In the future, Financial Stability must, in the specific situation, have the right to carry out restructurings that are deemed appropriate for that reason. In the future, the sector should contribute continuously to the deposit guarantee scheme as insurance and in such a way that the additional costs of aggressive financial behaviour are borne by the right people. Work on this should be launched - and completed with a view to legislation before the summer holidays, so that the scheme can come into operation at the end of the existing legislation next autumn. * * * I would like to conclude by thanking the outgoing Chairman and the Danish Bankers Association for a good and trusting cooperation during a difficult period. I welcome the President-elect back to office and look forward to the continuation of the good cooperation.

Og ser vi p den finansielle sektor er det karakteristisk, at de pengeinstitutter, der er blevet ndlidende, i frste rkke skal findes blandt dem, der frte den mest ekspansive udlnspolitik p ejendomsmarkedet. Den midlertidige ordning med garanti for enkeltstende udstedelser er umiddelbart mest tilgngelig for strre pengeinstitutter. Nationalbanken ser positivt p disse initiativer og p muligheden af at lade sdanne udstedelser indg i vores belningsgrundlag. De strre institutter m ptage sig deres ansvar for, at f pengemarkedet til at fungere smidigt igen. Title: Speech at the Danish Mortgage Bankers Association's annual meeting
text: Basis of speech. The spoken word applies Governor Nils Bernstein Speech at the Danish Mortgage Bankers Association's annual meeting on 24 April 2008 Thanks for the invitation. *** At the Mortgage Council's annual meeting last year, I said of the economic situation in the United States: "Nor does it appear that the problems of companies that specialize in home loans to less creditworthy households will spread to other parts of the capital markets". It wasn't an assessment I was alone in. I take it as a reminder that economic predictions need to be taken with a grain of salt. One can say without exaggeration that it has gone somewhat differently than predicted. The economic outlook for the United States and Europe has been gradually revised downward over the past year or so. And what started as problems for companies specializing in so-called subprime loans have spread to other parts of the financial sector d0 including outside the United States d0 and are now putting a damper on production and employment. Which, in turn, acts negatively back on the financial companies. Today, the assessment is that the United States is entering a recession, which will last at least until the second half of 2008, after which it will at best proceed slowly. Europe is likely to avoid recession, but must prepare for modest growth rates between 1% and 2% in the coming years. The development has come as a surprise to most, even though the boom in the United States had peaked before the subprime problems. A positive feature is that developing countries and emerging economies have so far largely escaped the economic downturn. That has mitigated the decline in the global economy. At the same time, the rate of price appreciation has taken a jump upwards all over the world, driven by rising energy and food prices. Price increases place narrow limits on continued easing of economic policy. There is a risk of pushing up inflation expectations and triggering a price and wage spiral. Of course, the rising prices of food are being felt especially in the poor countries and are rapidly moving upwards on the international agenda. *** 2 Today, there is talk of losses in the financial sector that could run into 1 trillion. An amount that is 3 times as large as the Danish national product, without comparison in general. The losses have affected both financial companies and others, first and foremost in the United States, but also in Europe. The biggest losses have been recorded in some of the world's largest banks, and one has been on the verge of bankruptcy. These are companies that have had thousands of highly skilled and highly paid employees and managers available to avoid just such losses. The process has given rise to introspection in both financial companies and authorities who belatedly saw the problems and intervened. How could it go so wrong, and how can you prevent it from happening again? Much has already been written about the causes. And the course will certainly become the subject of many learned treatises in the coming years, which will be able to benefit from the bright light of hindsight. Basically, financial business boils down to bridging the gap between those who need to spend more than they earn and have at their disposal at any given time and those who are in the opposite situation. This intermediation means that companies can invest in anticipation of future income. And that we as households can buy a house or apartment with a 20 per cent down payment. And that governments from time to time may have deficits in the state budget. Financial intermediation d0 at its best d0 ensures that savers get the best possible return for the chosen risk and that it is the most rewarding investments that are promoted. Cross-border dissemination takes place and the financial sector is among the foremost in globalisation. The importance of an efficient financial sector cannot be overstated in a modern society. However, the volume of financial intermediation has grown so rapidly in recent years, in combination with sophisticated product development, that risk assessment systems and incentive structures have not always been able to keep up with the battle for market share. Where development has created an atmosphere of euphoria, greed and sloppiness have been able to thrive. An important mechanism to correct this, of course, is that someone has burned their fingers and has felt the consequences. But it probably won't. A safe guess today is that there will be stricter rules. Now that it goes the other way, it is important to find the right balance between stricter rules and the need for financial communication to continue to serve socially useful purposes. Last autumn, the G7 countries requested the so-called Financial Stability Forum (FSF), which includes finance ministries, central banks and the Treasury. 3 the visions of the major countries, to carry out an analysis of the causes and weaknesses that have led to the crisis and to come up with proposals to improve the resilience of financial markets and institutions. It is interesting reading and should be the curriculum for anyone employed in the financial sector. The FSF makes 67 proposals under 5 main headings: The first group of proposals is about tightening the requirements for the capital, liquidity and risk management of financial institutions. There needs to be more to resist. The immediate difficulty, of course, is the implementation in a situation where the demands could make matters worse. The second group of proposals aims to increase transparency in markets by publishing all relevant risks and providing greater certainty in valuations. This has added to the uncertainty that financial institutions have only drip-wise declared their losses and that it has been difficult to value assets that are no longer traded. A third group of proposals targets the role of credit rating agencies in financial intermediation. It is necessary to improve the quality of the assessment process in order to avoid conflicts of interest and to increase the understanding of the results. The authorities must reassess their use of the work of the agencies. Fourthly, it is proposed that for each of the largest cross-border banks in the world, a group of representatives of the supervisory authorities of the relevant countries be created. This is in recognition of the fact that the authorities today are too ill-prepared to deal with possible crises in banks that with subsidiaries and branches work across national borders. Finally, central banks are encouraged to have greater flexibility, including expanding their lending facilities. One of the lessons of the current crisis has been that central banks have not had the adequate lending facilities available to banks in liquidity squeeze. As it appears, there are greetings for all of us: the private companies, governments, regulators and central banks. Most of the proposals are recommended to be implemented by the end of the current year. The rest in 2009. *** How does all this affect us here in Denmark? As paradoxical as it may sound, the slowdown in the international economy, as it now stands, comes quite conveniently for Denmark. The business cycle has been strong for a number of years, helped by low interest rates and expansionary fiscal policy. Employment is at a record high and unemployment the lowest in a generation. The current account surplus has fallen significantly, 4 but fortunately, no financial imbalances have built up during the recovery. Households as a whole are well consolidated and have a lot to resist, even though the housing market has been weak for a year and a half. The main imbalance is that the Danish economy has been close to its capacity limit for some time. The shortage of labour has increased the demand for wage increases, and the gap between the growth of Danish and foreign wages has grown in recent years. Consumer prices reached a 3.1% annual increase in March; as abroad mainly driven by rising energy and food prices. Consumer expectations that prices will rise are growing. The shortage of labour limits the growth of the Danish economy. In Danmarks Nationalbank's latest forecast from March, the central estimate is that the Danish economy will slow down in the coming years. But that we will not reach an unemployment rate that is compatible with sustainable wage growth in the long term until 2010. In the past, financial turmoil was usually accompanied by currency turmoil in Europe. Until now, there have only been minor traces of this. It is natural to give the smaller number of European currencies as a result of the euro is much of the credit for this. It is an advantage for Denmark that the euro exists and is now the currency of 15 countries. This, together with the European Central Bank's liquidity injection in response to the financial turmoil, has reduced the risk of major real economic damage. The financial system in Denmark is not untouched by the financial turmoil. But, fortunately, less than in several other countries. This is because Danish investors have only to a lesser extent invested in d0 and thus lost on d0 subprime-related assets. We have our own good mortgage products. However, we have also seen in Denmark how, due to the uncertainty, banks have become more reluctant to provide unsecured loans to each other in the money market, especially on the longer maturities. Funding has thus become shorter and more expensive. And this particularly affects those financial institutions that in recent years have accumulated a large deposit deficit in confidence that they could provide cheap liquidity in the money market or by issuing bonds. In the current situation and in accordance with international recommendations, we at Danmarks Nationalbank, like other central banks, are considering our loan facilities. These considerations have not been completed. But it is our opinion that well-run Danish banks should not unnecessarily get into a liquidity squeeze due to the international financial turmoil. With these words, I say thank you for the attention and wish a continued good annual meeting.
